entries.shortExplanation: 노란색 means "yellow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 노란색 (noransaek) means "yellow". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노란색이에요 ("it is yellow"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노란색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

entries.nuance: 노란색 is the noun for yellow and the modifier 노란 goes before a noun, as in 노란 꽃 for a yellow flower.

examples.en: This place's noodles are really chewy.

examples.note: 쫄깃하다 = good chewy, 질기다 = bad tough

entries.nuance: 쫄깃하다 is the GOOD kind of chewy: bouncy and springy like fresh noodles, tteok, or well-cooked octopus. Koreans treat it as high praise for 식감 (texture), so saying 면이 쫄깃해요 at a restaurant is a real compliment. Do not confuse it with 질기다, which is the bad 'tough/rubbery' chewy.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 바삭하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.en: Fried chicken has to be crispy to be good, as expected.
The fritters just came out, so they're super crispy.

examples.ko: 여기 돈까스는 겉이 바삭하고 안은 부드러워요.
examples.romanization: yeogi donkkaseuneun geochi basakago aneun budeureowoyo.
examples.en: The pork cutlet here is crispy outside and soft inside.

entries.nuance: 바삭하다 is the light, crisp crunch of fried chicken, twigim, fresh toast, or crackers. It is the key selling point of fried food in Korea, hence the famous phrase 겉바속촉 (crispy outside, moist inside). Mixing it up with 딱딱하다 (hard/stiff) — 바삭하다 is a light airy crunch, not rock-hard.

Applying it to dry foods — 얼큰하다 is for broths/soups, so 얼큰한 치킨 sounds wrong.
Confusing it with 느끼하다 — they are unrelated; 얼큰하다 is hot-spicy, 느끼하다 is greasy.

entries.explanation: 비리다 (birida) = "fishy (smelling/tasting of raw fish)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비린 맛 ("a fishy taste") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 비린내 = the fishy smell, very common

examples.ko: 이 회 좀 비린 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i hoe jom birin geot gatayo.
examples.en: This sashimi seems a bit fishy.
Squeezing lemon reduces the fishy smell.
It's so fresh it's not fishy at all.

entries.nuance: 비리다 is almost always negative: the off, fishy taste or smell of seafood (or even blood) that isn't fresh. The noun 비린내 (fishy smell) is used just as much as the adjective. Saying 안 비려요 ('not fishy') is high praise for raw fish — freshness is judged largely by the absence of 비린 맛.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
The modifier is 비린, not 비리는 — it's an adjective, so 비린 맛 / 비린내, never the verb-style 비리는 맛.
Using 비리다 for general bad smells — it specifically means fishy/raw-seafood; for spoiled-rotten use 상한 냄새.

entries.shortExplanation: 떫다 means "astringent, puckery (like unripe persimmon)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 떫다 (tteolbda) means "astringent, puckery (like unripe persimmon)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 떫은 맛 ("an astringent taste"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 떫다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

examples.en: This persimmon isn't ripe yet, so it's astringent.
Under-steeped tea is a bit astringent.

entries.nuance: 떫다 is that dry, mouth-puckering astringency of unripe persimmons, strong tea, or tannic wine — the sensation that makes your tongue feel rough. It is a distinct taste category in Korean alongside sweet/salty/sour/bitter/spicy, and persimmons (감) are the classic reference point. The conjugation is regular: 떫어요, 떫은, 떫고.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 떫다 (astringent) with 쓰다 (bitter) — coffee is 쓰다, an unripe persimmon is 떫다.
Treating it as a verb: it's an adjective, so 떫은 감 / 떫어요, never 떫는 감 or 떫는다.

entries.explanation: "clean-tasting, crisp (of flavor); also neat/tidy" is 깔끔하다 (kkalkkeumhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 맛이 깔끔하다 ("the flavor is clean/crisp"). Watch the particle attached to 깔끔하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. examples.note: 목 넘김 = the way it goes down the throat

examples.en: The gukbap here is clean-tasting, so I come often.

entries.nuance: Beyond meaning 'tidy/neat,' 깔끔하다 is a big food-review word for a clean, crisp, non-greasy flavor — the opposite of 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying). It's used to praise clear broths, light beer, or anything that finishes without a heavy aftertaste. You'll hear 깔끔해요 constantly in mukbang and restaurant reviews.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 깔끔하다 only means 'tidy' — in food contexts it specifically praises a clean, non-greasy taste.
Pairing it with rich greasy dishes — calling fatty pork belly 깔끔하다 is contradictory; that's 느끼하다.

entries.explanation: 달콤하다 (dalkomhada) = "sweet (pleasantly, with a nice sweetness)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 달콤한 디저트 ("a sweet dessert") shows how it actually behaves. examples.en: This cake is sweet just right and delicious.

entries.nuance: 달콤하다 is a pleasant, appealing sweetness, often subtler or more romantic-sounding than plain 달다 (which can imply 'too sweet'). It works for desserts, fruit, and even aromas, and shows up constantly in the combos 새콤달콤 (sweet-sour) and 달콤짭짤 (sweet-salty). Figuratively it also means 'sweet/blissful,' as in 달콤한 휴식.

Adjective forms only: 달콤한 / 달콤해요, never 달콤하는.

Treating it as a verb: 질긴 고기 / 질겨요, not 질기는.

entries.nuance: 등본 (short for 주민등록등본) lists everyone registered at your address and is requested constantly — for jobs, bank accounts, contracts. The idiomatic verb is 떼다 (to pull/issue), not 받다: 등본 떼러 가요. Foreigners get the equivalent 외국인등록사실증명, but everyone still says 등본 colloquially.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 받다 instead of 떼다 for getting the document — natives say 등본을 떼다
Confusing 등본 (household list) with 초본 (your personal address history); offices ask for one specifically

Assuming you can walk in — most 출입국 tasks require a 하이코리아 reservation first

entries.nuance: 재발급 is what you ask for when something is lost, stolen, or damaged — bank cards, ID, residence card, transit card. Use the verb 재발급받다 (to have it reissued) for yourself, or 재발급해 주세요 to ask staff. Compare 갱신 (renewal when something simply expires), which is a different request.

Using 재발급 when the document merely expired — that's 갱신 (renewal)

entries.explanation: 신청서 (sincheongseo) means "application form". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 신청서를 작성하다 ("to fill out an application form"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 신청서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 작성하다 is the right verb, not 쓰다 here
내다 = to hand in (casual for 제출하다)

examples.en: Please fill out this application form first.

entries.nuance: 신청서 is any fill-in application form, from visa extensions to library cards. The collocation verb is 작성하다 (fill out), which sounds more correct than 쓰다 in offices. To hand it in, staff say 내세요 or 제출하세요. You'll hear 신청서 작성해 주세요 at virtually every Korean counter.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 쓰다 instead of 작성하다 for completing a form in formal settings
Confusing 신청서 (the form you fill in) with 신청 (the act of applying)

entries.explanation: "receipt/acceptance (of an application); intake" is 접수 (jeopsu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 접수하다 ("to submit/register (an application)"). Watch the particle attached to 접수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. entries.nuance: 접수 is the bureaucratic word for an office accepting and logging your application or documents. At a hospital or office you 접수하다 first, then wait for your number. 접수가 됐어요 means your paperwork is officially in the system. It's slightly formal but used everywhere from clinics to government windows.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 접수 (intake/submission) with 영수증 (a payment receipt) — different 'receipt'
Saying 접수받다 when you mean to submit; you 접수하다, the office 접수받다

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전기세, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 전기세를 내요.. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 전기세.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.en: The electricity bill is scary in summer.

examples.en: I ran the AC a lot, so I'm scared of the electricity bill.

examples.ko: 전기세 아끼려고 안 쓰는 콘센트는 다 뽑아요.
examples.romanization: jeongise akkiryeogo an sseuneun konsenteuneun da ppobayo.
examples.en: To save on electricity, I unplug all the outlets I'm not using.
The electricity bill came out double last month's.

entries.nuance: 전기세 (formally 전기 요금) follows a progressive rate (누진제), so heavy summer AC use can spike the bill dramatically; '전기세 폭탄' is a common summer complaint. Strictly 요금 is more correct than 세 (which means 'tax'), but everyone says 전기세 in daily life.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 전기세 (electricity bill) with 전기 (electricity itself).
Although it ends in 세 (tax), it is a usage fee; the textbook term is 전기 요금.

Memorize one useful chunk: 전기세를 내요..

usagePhrases.en: The gas bill is high in winter.
The gas bill is a burden.
I try to save on the gas bill.

examples.ko: 겨울에 보일러를 많이 틀어서 가스비가 많이 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure boilleoreul mani teureoseo gaseubiga mani nawasseoyo.
examples.en: I ran the boiler a lot in winter, so the gas bill was high.

examples.ko: 가스비 아끼려고 보일러를 외출 모드로 해 놔요.
examples.romanization: gaseubi akkiryeogo boilleoreul oechul modeuro hae nwayo.
examples.en: To save on gas, I keep the boiler on away mode.

examples.romanization: ibeon gyeoureun gaseubiga jangnyeonboda deo bissayo.
examples.en: This winter the gas bill is more expensive than last year.

entries.nuance: 가스비 (formally 도시가스 요금) spikes in winter because the 보일러 runs on gas for both heating and hot water. News about rising 가스비 is a recurring topic, and tenants often link a high 가스비 directly to how much they used the 보일러.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 가스비 (gas bill) with 가스레인지 (gas stove).
Avoid 가스비를 사다; bills are 내다 (pay) or 나오다 (come out).

entries.explanation: "wallpapering" is 도배 (dobae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도배를 해요. ("I get the place wallpapered."). Watch the particle attached to 도배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 이사 오기 전에 도배를 새로 했어요.
examples.romanization: isa ogi jeone dobaereul saero haesseoyo.
examples.en: Before moving in, I had it freshly wallpapered.

examples.ko: 곰팡이 때문에 도배를 다시 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gompangi ttaemune dobaereul dasi haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Because of mold, I have to redo the wallpaper.

examples.ko: 집주인이 도배랑 장판을 새로 해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuini dobaerang jangpaneul saero hae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The landlord redid the wallpaper and flooring for me.

entries.nuance: 도배 (papering the walls) and 장판 (the vinyl floor) are the two things Koreans almost always refresh when moving into or renting out a place; they're often mentioned as a pair. A tenant may negotiate for the landlord to redo 도배 before moving in, especially if there's old or stained 벽지.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 도배 (the act of wallpapering) with 벽지 (the wallpaper material itself).
도배 needs 하다 to be a verb; do not treat it as a standalone action word.

entries.explanation: 장판 (jangpan) = "vinyl floor covering". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장판이 깨끗해요. ("The floor covering is clean.") shows how it actually behaves. entries.nuance: 장판 is the smooth vinyl sheet laid over the heated 온돌 floor in most Korean homes; the verb that goes with it is 깔다 (to lay/spread). Do not confuse 장판 (the vinyl floor sheet) with 바닥 (the floor itself).
Use 장판을 깔다 (lay) not 장판을 입다 or other random verbs.

entries.explanation: 콘센트 (konsenteu) means "electrical outlet, wall socket". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 콘센트가 어디에 있어요? ("Where is the outlet?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 콘센트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.en: When going out, I unplug outlets I'm not using.

entries.nuance: 콘센트 (a Japanese-origin loanword, not 'consent') is the wall socket; the plug itself is 플러그 and the verbs are 꽂다 (plug in) and 뽑다 (unplug). The number of 콘센트 is a real concern in older or small rooms, and unplugging unused ones is a common 전기세-saving habit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not assume 콘센트 means 'consent'; it means the wall outlet.
Do not confuse 콘센트 (the socket on the wall) with 플러그 (the plug on the cord).

entries.nuance: 관리비 is the monthly building-maintenance fee covering things like cleaning, security, elevator, and often part of the utilities; it's charged on top of 월세 and surprises many newcomers. Always ask what the 관리비 covers (수도세, 난방비, 인터넷 etc.) before signing, since a 'cheap' rent can hide a high 관리비.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 관리비 (monthly maintenance fee) with 보증금 (the refundable deposit).
관리비 is usually separate from 월세; don't assume rent already includes it.

entries.nuance: 부추 (garlic chives) are the flat, garlicky-smelling greens used for 부추전, 부추무침, and as a 만두 filling — not the same as thin 쪽파 (scallion). Regional note: the exact same vegetable is called 정구지 in much of 경상/전라, so you may hear that at markets. It's sold by the 단 and bruises easily, so use it fresh.

Confusing 부추 (garlic chives) with 쪽파 (thin scallion)
Counting it with 개 instead of 단

entries.nuance: 숙주 (mung bean sprouts, full name 숙주나물) are the thinner, headless white sprouts — different from 콩나물, which have the yellow soybean head. At the store the two sit side by side, so check the label. 숙주 spoils fast and turns mushy within a day or two, so buy it the day you'll cook 쌀국수, 잡채, or 만두.

Mixing up 숙주 (mung bean) with 콩나물 (soybean, has the yellow head)
Over-blanching it until it goes limp instead of staying crisp

entries.nuance: 무 is the fat white Korean radish (daikon), milder and juicier than the Western red radish. It's the base of 무국, 깍두기, 동치미, and 무생채, and a whole one is large — so '반 개' (half) is a normal amount to buy. Note 시원하다 for radish soup means a clean, refreshing broth, not temperature.

Picturing the small red Western radish instead of the large white 무

entries.nuance: 계란 is the everyday word for egg and what you'll see on most cartons and menus; 달걀 is the slightly more 'proper'/textbook word for the same thing, so both are correct. entries.explanation: 재택근무 (jaetaekgeunmu) means "working from home; remote work". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 재택근무를 하다 ("to work from home"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 재택근무 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

examples.en: Our company allows working from home.
Today is a WFH day, so I'm working at home.

entries.nuance: 재택근무 is the formal term for working from home, often shortened to 재택 in casual speech (오늘 재택이에요). It surged after COVID, so asking 재택근무 가능해요? is a normal question when job hunting.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 집에서 근무 as a fixed term; the set word is 재택근무
Confusing it with 외근, which means going OUT for work, not staying home

entries.explanation: "working overtime (late into the night)" is 야근 (yageun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 야근을 하다 ("to work overtime"). entries.nuance: 야근 specifically means staying late at the office at night, the classic symbol of Korean work culture. Its natural opposite in slang is 칼퇴 (leaving exactly at quitting time), and 야근 수당 (overtime pay) is what everyone wants for it.

Saying 야근을 가다 instead of 야근을 하다

entries.shortExplanation: 연차 means "annual paid leave (a day off)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연차 (yeoncha) = "annual paid leave (a day off)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연차를 쓰다 ("to use a leave day") shows how it actually behaves. entries.nuance: 연차 is your annual paid vacation entitlement, counted in days, and 연차를 쓰다 (use a leave day) or 연차를 내다 (file for leave) are the everyday phrases. A half day off is 반차, a handy related word for slipping out early.

entries.shortExplanation: 장바구니 means "shopping cart (online or physical basket)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장바구니 (jangbaguni) means "shopping cart (online or physical basket)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 장바구니에 담다 ("to add to the cart"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 장바구니 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

examples.en: I added it to the cart in advance to buy the moment the sale starts.

entries.nuance: 온라인 쇼핑에서는 거의 항상 '담다' 동사를 써요 ('장바구니에 담다'). '넣다'도 통하지만 앱 버튼에는 '담기'라고 쓰여 있어요. 실제 마트의 바구니와 인터넷 카트 둘 다 같은 단어라 일상에서 정말 자주 들립니다.

Saying 장바구니에 사다 — 사다 is for the final purchase; you 담다 (add) to a cart, then 결제 (check out)
Confusing it with 바구니 alone — 바구니 is just any basket, 장바구니 specifically implies shopping

entries.explanation: "delivery / shipping (of an ordered item)" is 배송 (baesong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배송이 빠르다 ("the shipping is fast"). Watch the particle attached to 배송 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. the menu label for tracking your parcel

examples.romanization: jumunhan ji iteul dwaenneunde ajik baesong an wasseoyo.
examples.en: It's been two days since I ordered but the delivery still hasn't come.
examples.note: 배송이 오다/안 오다 is everyday spoken usage

examples.ko: 여기 배송이 진짜 빨라서 자주 시켜요.
examples.romanization: yeogi baesongi jinjja ppallaseo jaju sikyeoyo.
examples.en: Shipping here is really fast so I order often.
examples.note: 배송 빠르다 is the key selling point in Korea

examples.ko: 배송 조회해 보니까 지금 터미널에 있대요.
examples.romanization: baesong johoehae bonikka jigeum teomineore itdaeyo.
examples.en: I checked the tracking and it says it's at the terminal now.

entries.nuance: '배송'은 파는 사람 입장의 '보내는' 과정 전체를 가리키고, '택배'는 그걸 운반하는 서비스/물건을 뜻해요. 한국 온라인 쇼핑에서 '배송 빠르다'는 거의 칭찬의 기본값이라 후기에 정말 많이 나옵니다. 회화에서는 '배송이 왔다/안 왔다'처럼 자연스럽게 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배달 instead of 배송 for shopping parcels — 배달 is for food/restaurant delivery, 배송 is for ordered products

entries.nuance: 내성적이다 is the neutral, textbook word for 'introverted' and is totally fine to say about yourself in interviews or intros. It describes drawing energy inward, not being unfriendly — Koreans don't read it as a flaw. For 'shy/timid' specifically, 소심하다 carries a more negative edge.

examples.romanization: siheom giganira yojeum jom yeminhae. mian.
examples.en: It's exam season so I'm a bit on edge lately. Sorry.
examples.note: Pre-emptive apology to a friend; very natural

examples.ko: 저는 잠귀가 예민해서 작은 소리에도 깨요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jamgwiga yeminhaeseo jageun soriedo kkaeyo.
examples.en: I'm a light sleeper, so even small sounds wake me up.
examples.note: 잠귀가 예민하다 = sensitive to sound while sleeping

examples.ko: 그 얘기는 좀 예민한 주제라서 조심해서 말해야 해요.
examples.romanization: geu yaegineun jom yeminhan jujeraseo josimhaeseo malhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: That's a sensitive topic, so you have to speak carefully about it.

entries.nuance: 예민하다 covers two things: a person being emotionally on-edge/touchy (often from stress), and physical sensitivity (skin, stomach, sleep). About someone's mood it can sound mildly critical, so people often say it about themselves to warn others. For a deeply sensitive, easily-hurt heart in a kinder sense, 섬세하다 sounds gentler.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't use it to mean 'smart/sharp'; that's 예리하다

entries.explanation: "blunt, curt, gruff (cold-seeming manner)" is 무뚝뚝하다 (muttukttukada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무뚝뚝하게 말하다 ("speak curtly"). Watch the particle attached to 무뚝뚝하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

examples.romanization: uri appaneun muttukttukajiman sogeun jeongmal ttatteutae.
examples.en: My dad is gruff but really warm on the inside.

examples.ko: 사장님이 무뚝뚝하게 대답해서 화난 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi muttukttukage daedapaeseo hwanan jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The boss answered so curtly that I thought he was angry.

examples.ko: 경상도 사람들은 무뚝뚝하다는 말을 자주 들어요.
examples.romanization: gyeongsangdo saramdeureun muttukttukadaneun mareul jaju deureoyo.
examples.en: People from Gyeongsang-do often get called blunt.

entries.nuance: 무뚝뚝하다 describes a curt, unexpressive manner — short answers, no small talk, a flat face — without necessarily meaning the person is mean. It's frequently paired with 'but warm inside' (속은 따뜻하다), especially about dads and older men. Don't confuse it with 차갑다 (cold-hearted), which implies actual coldness, not just a gruff style.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't drop a syllable and write 무뚝하다 — the word doubles up: 무뚝뚝하다
Using it to mean 'rude'; it's about manner/affect, not 무례하다 (rude)

usagePhrases.en: has a warm way of speaking

usagePhrases.note: 다정다감 is a common four-syllable expansion

examples.ko: 남자친구가 너무 다정해서 친구들이 다 부러워해요.

examples.ko: 선생님이 다정하게 말해 줘서 긴장이 풀렸어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi dajeonghage malhae jwoseo ginjangi pullyeosseoyo.

The owner of that cafe is always so warm.

entries.nuance: 다정하다 means warm, tender, and affectionate toward others — it's about emotional warmth and sweet treatment, a notch more intimate than 친절하다 (kind/polite, often to strangers or customers). It's a go-to compliment for partners, close friends, and warm teachers. The expanded form 다정다감하다 sounds slightly more literary but is common in praise.

Using 다정하다 for polite service — staff being nice to customers is 친절하다, not 다정하다
Don't pair it with strangers oddly; 다정하다 implies real warmth, so it sounds off for a one-time formal interaction

entries.explanation: 까칠하다 (kkachilhada) means "prickly, snippy, hard to please". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성격이 까칠하다 ("have a prickly personality"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 까칠하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Mildly negative, but often said affectionately
까칠하게 굴다 = behave in a prickly way

examples.ko: 우리 팀장님 평소엔 괜찮은데 마감 때만 까칠해져요.
examples.romanization: uri timjangnim pyeongsoen gwaenchaneunde magam ttaeman kkachilhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Our team lead is usually fine but gets prickly only around deadlines.

examples.ko: 왜 이렇게 까칠해? 무슨 일 있어?
examples.romanization: wae ireoke kkachilhae? museun il isseo?
examples.en: Why are you so snippy? Is something wrong?

examples.ko: 그 사람 까칠해 보여도 알고 보면 착해.
examples.romanization: geu saram kkachilhae boyeodo algo bomyeon chakae.
examples.en: He seems prickly, but once you really know him he's nice.
examples.note: 알고 보면 = when you actually get to know

entries.nuance: 까칠하다 literally means 'rough to the touch' and figuratively describes someone snippy, easily irritated, or hard to please. It's lighter and more playful than calling someone outright mean — friends tease each other with it. Originally about texture (dry skin, stubble), so you may also hear 피부가 까칠하다 for rough skin.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a serious insult — it's relatively mild; for genuinely mean use 못됐다

entries.nuance: 차분하다 means calm, composed, and steady — a person who doesn't get rattled, or a quiet, settled mood. entries.shortExplanation: 반창고 means "adhesive bandage / band-aid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반창고 (banchanggo) means "adhesive bandage / band-aid". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반창고 주세요 ("Please give me a band-aid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반창고 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 장 is the counter for flat/sheet items

examples.en: I cut my hand so I put on a band-aid.

examples.ko: 반창고 한 장만 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: banchanggo han jangman jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Could you give me just one band-aid?

examples.ko: 물집 잡혔는데 반창고 붙이는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: muljip japyeonneunde banchanggo buchineun ge naayo.
examples.en: I got a blister, so it's better to put on a band-aid.
examples.note: 물집(이) 잡히다 = to get a blister

entries.nuance: 반창고 is the standard word for an adhesive bandage; many Koreans also say the brand name 대일밴드 or just 밴드. The verb is 붙이다, and you count them with 장. Completely neutral, used by everyone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 반창고 (small adhesive strip) with 붕대 (a roll of gauze bandage)
Using 바르다 instead of 붙이다 — band-aids are stuck on

entries.explanation: "bandage / gauze wrap" is 붕대 (bungdae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 붕대 주세요 ("Please give me a bandage"). examples.note: 발목을 삐다 = to sprain one's ankle

entries.nuance: 붕대 is the rolled gauze bandage you wind around a sprain or larger wound, and the verb is 감다 (wrap), not 붙이다. Use it for ankles, wrists, and big cuts, whereas 반창고 is for small everyday nicks. Neutral register.

Using 붕대 붙이다 — a bandage is wrapped (감다), not stuck on
Confusing 붕대 with 반창고; 붕대 is the long roll, 반창고 is the small strip

entries.shortExplanation: 소독약 means "antiseptic / disinfectant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 소독약 (sodogyak) = "antiseptic / disinfectant". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 소독약 주세요 ("Please give me some antiseptic") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 소독약, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 소독약 주세요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 소독약.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 바르다 for putting it on the skin

usagePhrases.en: I cleaned the wound with antiseptic

examples.ko: 상처에 소독약 먼저 바르고 연고 바르세요.
examples.romanization: sangcheoe sodogyang meonjeo bareugo yeongo bareuseyo.
examples.en: Put antiseptic on the wound first, then apply ointment.
I cleaned the spot where I fell with antiseptic.
It stings a bit when I put on the antiseptic.

entries.nuance: 소독약 is the everyday term for wound antiseptics like 포비돈(povidone) or 과산화수소(hydrogen peroxide); pharmacists know it instantly. You 바르다 or 닦다 it onto a cut, and people often comment that it 따가워요 (stings). Neutral, practical vocabulary for any home first-aid kit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 소독약 먹다 — antiseptic is for external use, never swallowed
Confusing 소독약 (for wounds) with 소독제 (general disinfectant for surfaces/hands)

entries.explanation: 체온계 (cheongye) means "thermometer (for body temperature)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 체온계 있어요? ("Do you have a thermometer?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 체온계 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Asking at a pharmacy or at home

examples.en: When I measured my fever with a thermometer, it was 38.5 degrees.
examples.note: 열을 재다 = to take one's temperature

examples.en: I didn't have a thermometer at home so I bought one at the pharmacy.

examples.ko: 아기 체온계는 귀에 대는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: agi cheongyeneun gwie daeneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: For a baby, the ear thermometer is convenient.
examples.note: 귀에 대다 = to put against the ear

entries.nuance: 체온계 is specifically the device for measuring body temperature, and the verb pairing is 열을 재다 (take temperature). Since COVID, digital and 귀 (ear) types are everywhere, and you can buy one at any 약국. Neutral register.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 체온계 (body temperature) with 온도계 (general thermometer for air/water)
Using 보다 instead of 재다 — you 재다 (measure) temperature, not 보다

entries.explanation: "stomach / gastric medicine" is 위장약 (wijangyak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 위장약 주세요 ("Please give me some stomach medicine"). usagePhrases.note: 속이 쓰리다 = to have a burning/sour stomach

usagePhrases.en: stomach medicine on an empty stomach

examples.ko: 요즘 속이 자주 쓰려서 위장약 먹고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum sogi jaju sseuryeoseo wijangyang meokgo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days my stomach often burns, so I'm taking stomach medicine.

examples.ko: 빈속에 커피 마시면 속이 안 좋아서 위장약 챙겨요.
examples.romanization: binsoge keopi masimyeon sogi an joaseo wijangyak chaenggyeoyo.
examples.en: Coffee on an empty stomach upsets my stomach, so I keep stomach medicine handy.
examples.note: 속이 안 좋다 = to feel queasy/upset

examples.ko: 술 마시기 전에 위장약 먹는 사람도 있어요.
examples.romanization: sul masigi jeone wijangyang meongneun saramdo isseoyo.
examples.en: Some people take stomach medicine before drinking.

entries.nuance: 위장약 is the broad term for stomach/gut medicine covering acid, burning (속쓰림), and gastritis, and is distinct from 소화제, which is just for digestion after overeating. Pharmacists will ask your symptom (속쓰림, 더부룩함, 통증) before choosing. Neutral, very practical for adults in Korea.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 위장약 and 소화제 interchangeably — 위장약 treats acid/pain, 소화제 helps digestion
Saying 위약 — the correct word is 위장약

entries.shortExplanation: 알약 means "pill / tablet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 알약 (aryak) = "pill / tablet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 알약 못 먹어요 ("I can't swallow pills") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 알약, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 알약 못 먹어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 알약.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Common to ask for liquid or powder instead
알 is the counter for round small things

examples.ko: 저는 알약을 잘 못 삼켜요. 물약으로 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun aryageul jal mot samkyeoyo. muryageuro juseyo.
examples.en: I can't swallow pills well. Please give me the liquid form.
examples.note: 물약 = liquid medicine; useful alternative request

examples.ko: 이 알약은 하루에 두 알씩 드세요.
examples.romanization: i aryageun harue du alssik deuseyo.
examples.en: Take two of these tablets a day.
examples.note: 두 알씩 = two pills each (time); 씩 = per/each

examples.ko: 알약이 너무 커서 반으로 잘라 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: aryagi neomu keoseo baneuro jalla meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: The pill was too big so I cut it in half and took it.
examples.note: 반으로 자르다 = to cut in half

entries.nuance: 알약 is the everyday word for a solid pill or tablet, contrasted with 가루약 (powder) and 물약 (liquid). Counting uses 알, and the verbs are 먹다 or, more precisely, 삼키다 (swallow). If swallowing is hard, it's normal to ask the pharmacist for 물약 or 가루약. Neutral register.

Confusing the counter: it's 한 알, not 한 개, for pills
Saying 약알 — the correct order is 알약

examples.romanization: gamgi momsare onmomi ssusyeoseo kkomjjakagi sireoyo.
examples.en: With this achy cold my whole body aches and I don't want to move.

My grandma says her knees ache whenever it rains.

entries.nuance: 쑤시다는 안쪽에서 욱신거리며 지끈지끈 아픈 통증을 뜻하며, 근육통·관절통·몸살을 묘사할 때 거의 필수다. 표면이 따끔한 '따갑다'와 달리 깊고 묵직한 통증이라는 점이 핵심이다. 형용사처럼 '쑤셔요'로 상태를 말하지만 동사 활용도 하니 '쑤신다'도 자연스럽다.

'쑤셔요'를 '쑤시어요'로 또박또박 쓰는 것 — 줄여서 '쑤셔요'가 자연스럽다.

entries.explanation: 막차 (makcha) = "last train / last bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막차를 놓쳤어요. ("I missed the last train.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I have to catch the last train.

examples.en: Let's hurry before the last train is gone.

entries.nuance: 막차 (literally 'last vehicle') is a huge deal in Korean nightlife since the subway stops around midnight and missing it means an expensive taxi. You'll constantly hear 막차 끊기다 (service ends) and 막차 놓치다 (miss it); checking the 막차 시간 before drinking is a real survival habit. Its opposite is 첫차.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 막차를 잃어버렸어요 (lost it); to miss a train is 막차를 놓치다.
막차 시간 is the departure time of the last train, not the arrival time, so leave early enough to actually board it.

entries.explanation: "delay (of a train, bus, flight)" is 연착 (yeonchak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기차가 연착됐어요. ("The train was delayed."). examples.en: It snowed a lot, so the train was delayed 30 minutes.
I was late to my appointment because of the delay.
The KTX was delayed, so I got a refund.

entries.nuance: 연착 is a delay in arrival or departure for trains, buses, or flights; you'll hear it in station announcements as 연착 안내. The usual verb forms are 연착되다 and 연착하다, and for long KTX/SRT delays you can sometimes get partial compensation (보상). It contrasts with arriving 정시에 (on time).

Don't use 늦다 alone for a vehicle running late; the proper transit word is 연착되다.
Don't confuse 연착 (a transport delay) with 지각 (a person being late, e.g. to work).

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 급행, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. entries.nuance: 급행 is express service (on lines like Seoul Subway Line 9 or the GTX) that skips smaller stations to save time; its opposite is 완행 or 일반 (local/all-stops). Don't board a 급행 without checking if it stops at your station; it skips many.

entries.shortExplanation: 점점 means "gradually, more and more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 점점 (jeomjeom) means "gradually, more and more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 날씨가 점점 추워져요 ("The weather is gradually getting colder"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 날씨가 점점 추워져요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 점점.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.en: The weather is gradually getting colder
usagePhrases.note: Pairs naturally with -아/어지다 verbs that show change over time
Common with progressive -고 있다 to stress an ongoing trend

usagePhrases.en: My Korean is improving more and more
usagePhrases.note: Everyday way to describe steady skill growth
점점 더 stacks for extra emphasis on the increase

examples.en: Prices keep gradually rising these days, so it's a burden.
examples.note: A very real complaint among residents about cost of living

examples.ko: 운동을 시작하니까 몸이 점점 가벼워지는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: undongeul sijakanikka momi jeomjeom gabyeowojineun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Since I started working out, my body feels gradually lighter.
examples.note: 점점 + change verb describing a positive trend

examples.en: As night fell, the crowd gradually thinned out.
examples.note: Describes a slow decrease over time

entries.nuance: 점점 describes a slow, steady change in one direction and almost always travels with a verb of change like 좋아지다, 추워지다, or 늘다. It is not used for sudden shifts. The variant 점점 더 adds emphasis, and 점차 is a more formal written cousin you'll see in news and notices.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 점점 with a static verb like 점점 있어요 instead of a change verb such as 점점 많아져요
Confusing it with 갑자기 (suddenly); 점점 is always gradual, never abrupt

lesson.canDo: Use 점점 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 점점. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 날씨가 점점 추워져요.
Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.
lesson.teacherNote: 점점 should be taught as a sentence ingredient. The student needs the common frame more than a dictionary definition.
lesson.pronunciationTip: 점점 is written jeomjeom. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.shortExplanation: 갑자기 means "suddenly, all of a sudden" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "suddenly, all of a sudden" is 갑자기 (gapjagi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갑자기 비가 왔어요 ("It suddenly started raining"). Watch the particle attached to 갑자기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 갑자기 비가 왔어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 갑자기.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Classic weather use; the change is abrupt and unexpected

usagePhrases.en: Why are you acting like this all of a sudden?
usagePhrases.note: Mild way to question an out-of-nowhere change in someone
Useful for describing a sudden physical symptom
Very common when you abruptly remember something

examples.ko: 회사에서 갑자기 회식하자고 해서 약속을 취소했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo gapjagi hoesikajago haeseo yaksogeul chwisohaesseoyo.
examples.en: Work suddenly called a team dinner, so I canceled my plans.
examples.note: 갑자기 + unexpected work demand, a relatable scenario

examples.en: My laptop, which was totally fine, suddenly shut off.

examples.ko: 친구가 갑자기 연락이 안 돼서 걱정했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga gapjagi yeollagi an dwaeseo geokjeonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend suddenly became unreachable, so I was worried.
examples.note: Sudden change in an expected pattern

entries.nuance: 갑자기 marks something abrupt and usually unplanned, often with a nuance of surprise or disruption. It is the direct opposite of 점점. Native speakers also use it conversationally to react to a sudden change in someone's mood or behavior, as in 갑자기 왜 이래요, which can sound slightly accusatory depending on tone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 갑짜기; the correct form is 갑자기
Using it for slow changes where 점점 is needed, e.g. 갑자기 추워져요 sounds wrong for a gradual cooldown

lesson.canDo: Use 갑자기 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 갑자기. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 갑자기 비가 왔어요.
Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.
lesson.teacherNote: 갑자기 should be taught as a sentence ingredient. The student needs the common frame more than a dictionary definition.
lesson.pronunciationTip: 갑자기 is written gapjagi. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.shortExplanation: 드디어 means "finally, at last" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 드디어 (deudieo) = "finally, at last". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 드디어 끝났어요 ("It's finally over") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 드디어, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 드디어 끝났어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 드디어.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Expresses relief after a long wait or effort
Used after a long or tiring trip
Celebrating a result that took real effort

examples.ko: 반년을 기다린 콘서트 표를 드디어 구했어요.
examples.romanization: bannyeoneul gidarin konseoteu pyoreul deudieo guhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I finally got the concert ticket I'd waited half a year for.
My visa finally came through, so I feel relieved.
examples.note: Very relevant to a foreign resident's life

examples.en: Overtime is over and I'm finally going home.
examples.note: Everyday relief after a hard day

entries.nuance: 드디어 carries a strong sense of relief or satisfaction after a long anticipation, so it pairs with results the speaker actually wanted. It differs from 결국 (eventually/in the end), which can be neutral or even negative. Use 드디어 when there is a payoff worth celebrating, not just any final outcome.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 드디어 for unwanted endings; 결국 fits a negative or neutral conclusion better
Treating it as 'finally' in the sense of listing steps (lastly); that meaning is 마지막으로, not 드디어

lesson.canDo: Use 드디어 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 드디어. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.

Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.

entries.shortExplanation: 역시 means "as expected, sure enough; also/too" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 역시 (yeoksi) means "as expected, sure enough; also/too". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 역시 맛있네요 ("As expected, it's delicious"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 역시 맛있네요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 역시.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Confirming that something lived up to its reputation

usagePhrases.en: It's you, as I figured / you're the best
usagePhrases.note: Warm praise meaning someone came through just like you knew
역시 can also mean 'also', similar to 또한

usagePhrases.en: It's not working, just as I feared

examples.en: This place's kimchi stew is the best, as expected.
examples.note: 역시 confirming a favorite spot stayed great

examples.ko: 역시 출근 시간이라 지하철이 사람으로 꽉 찼어요.
examples.romanization: yeoksi chulgeun siganira jihacheori sarameuro kkwak chasseoyo.
examples.en: Sure enough, it's rush hour, so the subway is packed.

examples.ko: 고민하다가 역시 원래 계획대로 하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: gominhadaga yeoksi wollae gyehoekdaero hagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: After agonizing, I decided to go with the original plan after all.
examples.note: 역시 marking a return to what felt right all along

entries.nuance: 역시 has two everyday senses: confirming that reality matched your expectation (sure enough), and a softer 'as I thought, X is great' that works as a compliment. As an interjection, 역시! on its own means 'I knew it / nailed it.' It can also mean 'also/too,' though that use is more formal and less common in casual speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Overusing the 'also' meaning in casual talk where 도 or 또한 is more natural
Expecting it to mean 'again'; that is 다시 or 또, not 역시

entries.shortExplanation: 오히려 means "rather, on the contrary, if anything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rather, on the contrary, if anything" is 오히려 (ohiryeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오히려 잘됐어요 ("Actually it worked out better that way"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Actually it worked out better that way
usagePhrases.note: Reframes a seeming setback as a good thing

usagePhrases.en: I apologized but instead they got angry
usagePhrases.note: Marks a reaction opposite to what you'd expect

usagePhrases.en: The expensive one is, if anything, worse
usagePhrases.note: Contradicts the assumption that pricier means better

usagePhrases.en: It's I who should be thanking you, rather
usagePhrases.note: Politely flips a thank-you back onto yourself

examples.ko: 지하철이 막힐 줄 알았는데 오히려 더 빨랐어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheori makil jul aranneunde ohiryeo deo ppallasseoyo.
examples.en: I thought the subway would be jammed, but it was actually faster.
examples.note: 오히려 introducing the opposite of an expectation

examples.ko: 쉬려고 누웠는데 오히려 잠이 안 와요.
examples.romanization: swiryeogo nuwonneunde ohiryeo jami an wayo.
examples.en: I lay down to rest, but instead I can't fall asleep.
examples.note: Outcome contrary to the intended effect

examples.ko: 혼날 줄 알았는데 사장님이 오히려 칭찬해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: honnal jul aranneunde sajangnimi ohiryeo chingchanhae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I expected to get in trouble, but the boss praised me instead.
examples.note: A surprising reversal in a workplace setting

entries.nuance: 오히려 signals that the result runs counter to what you or the listener would naturally assume, often to a surprising or ironic degree. It frequently follows a clause with -는데 or -지만 that sets up the contrast. Think of it as 'contrary to expectation' rather than a simple 'instead,' which adds the flavor of a flipped assumption.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a plain 'instead' for choosing between options; 대신에 fits that better
Forgetting the setup clause, so the contrast 오히려 needs has nothing to push against

studyFlow: Say the word first: 오히려. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.

entries.shortExplanation: 막상 means "when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막상 (maksang) = "when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막상 해 보니까 쉬웠어요 ("When I actually tried it, it was easy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막상, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 막상 해 보니까 쉬웠어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 막상.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.en: I wanted to switch jobs, but now that I'm actually about to quit, I hesitate.
examples.note: 막상 contrasting a wish with the reality of acting on it

examples.en: I was worried about the presentation, but once I actually started, it was fine.
examples.note: 막상 + 시작하니까 showing the gap between dread and reality

examples.ko: 월급날만 기다렸는데 막상 받으니까 카드값으로 다 나갔어요.
examples.romanization: wolgeumnalman gidaryeonneunde maksang badeunikka kadeugapseuro da nagasseoyo.
examples.en: I only waited for payday, but when I actually got paid, it all went to the credit card bill.
examples.note: 막상 marking a letdown when the awaited moment arrives

entries.nuance: 막상 sets up a contrast between what you expected, planned, or imagined and what actually happens once you face the real situation. It very often pairs with -(으)니까 or -(으)려니까 to mark that moment of confronting reality. The flavor is 'in theory I thought X, but actually Y,' so it shines when the real experience defies your prior assumption.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a plain 'actually/really' fact; that is 사실 or 정말, while 막상 specifically means 'when faced with the real moment'
Dropping the setup, so there is no expectation for 막상 to contradict; it needs a prior assumption or plan to push against

lesson.canDo: Use 막상 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 막상. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 막상 해 보니까 쉬웠어요.
Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.
lesson.teacherNote: 막상 should be taught as a sentence ingredient. The student needs the common frame more than a dictionary definition.
lesson.pronunciationTip: 막상 is written maksang. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.shortExplanation: 어차피 means "anyway, in any case, either way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 어차피 (eochapi) means "anyway, in any case, either way". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어차피 늦었어요 ("We're late anyway"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어차피 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Accepting a fixed reality as the basis for what follows

usagePhrases.en: It's something I have to do either way
usagePhrases.note: Frames a task as unavoidable regardless of choice
States a settled outcome that won't change

usagePhrases.en: It's the same in any case
usagePhrases.note: Dismisses a distinction as ultimately irrelevant

examples.romanization: eochapi jibe ganeun girinikka gachi gayo.
examples.en: I'm headed home anyway, so let's go together.

examples.ko: 어차피 환불도 안 되는데 그냥 써야죠.

examples.en: It's non-refundable anyway, so I'll just use it.
No matter how much I worry, the result won't change either way.
examples.note: 어차피 stressing that effort won't alter the outcome

entries.nuance: 어차피 sets up a premise that is already decided or unavoidable, so the speaker reasons from it: since X is fixed anyway, Y. It often carries a tone of resignation or pragmatic acceptance. It pairs naturally with -니까 or -는데 to connect the fixed fact to the conclusion the speaker draws from it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a simple 'anyway' that just changes topics; that conversational filler is 아무튼 or 어쨌든
Placing it where the outcome is still open; 어차피 assumes the result is already settled

lesson.canDo: Use 어차피 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.

entries.shortExplanation: 굳이 means "(not) particularly, go out of one's way to, deliberately" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Watch the particle attached to 굳이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

entries.nuance: 굳이 conveys 'going out of one's way' for something not strictly necessary, and it shines in negative or rhetorical sentences like 굳이 안 해도 돼 (no need to bother). Used positively, it implies someone insisted on doing something despite it being unneeded. Korean speakers in their 20s-30s also use it as a one-word reaction, 굳이?, meaning 'is that really necessary?'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it as plain 'definitely'; that is 꼭 or 반드시, whereas 굳이 implies unnecessary effort
Forgetting that its most natural home is negative sentences, e.g. 굳이 안 사도 돼요

entries.english: by nature, originally so much, inherently
entries.shortExplanation: 워낙 means "by nature, originally so much, inherently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 워낙 (wonak) = "by nature, originally so much, inherently". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 워낙 바빠서 ("Since (they're) so inherently busy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 워낙, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 워낙 바빠서. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 워낙.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Gives an underlying reason rooted in a stable trait

usagePhrases.en: It's an inherently very famous place
I just can't handle spicy food at all
Because there are just so many people (as usual)
usagePhrases.note: Explains a situation by an inherent, baseline condition

examples.ko: 그 식당은 워낙 줄이 길어서 예약하는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun wonak juri gireoseo yeyakaneun ge naayo.
examples.en: That restaurant inherently has such long lines that it's better to reserve.
examples.note: 워낙 giving the baseline reason for advice

examples.ko: 제 룸메이트는 워낙 조용해서 집에 있는지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: je rummeiteuneun wonak joyonghaeseo jibe inneunjido mollayo.
examples.en: My roommate is so quiet by nature that I can't even tell if they're home.
examples.note: 워낙 describing an inherent personality trait

examples.ko: 요즘 워낙 물가가 비싸서 외식을 줄였어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum wonang mulgaga bissaseo oesigeul juryeosseoyo.
examples.en: Prices are just so high these days that I've cut back on eating out.

entries.nuance: 워낙 emphasizes that something is the way it is by its fundamental nature or to an inherently high degree, often setting up a reason with -아서/어서. It is close to 'so much by nature' and feels more grounded than 너무, because it points to a stable, baseline truth rather than a momentary feeling. It frequently explains why a predictable outcome follows.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it for 너무 to mean a temporary 'too much'; 워낙 implies an inherent, ongoing degree
Using it without a follow-up reason or result; 워낙 usually leads into an explanation, not a standalone statement

examples.ko: 옆집에서 자꾸 시끄럽게 해서 스트레스를 받아요.
examples.romanization: yeopjibeseo jakku sikkeureopge haeseo seuteureseureul badayo.
examples.en: The neighbors keep being noisy, so it stresses me out.

entries.nuance: 자꾸 means something happens again and again, and it usually carries a slightly negative or exasperated nuance, as if the repetition is bothersome or beyond control. It differs from 자주 (often), which is a neutral frequency word; 자꾸 emphasizes persistence and is frequently used to gently complain. It pairs well with verbs of habit or recurring trouble.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as a neutral 'often'; for plain frequency use 자주, since 자꾸 implies pesky repetition
Using it for scheduled regular events like 자꾸 운동해요; 규칙적으로 or 자주 fits planned routines better

examples.en: Could you give me a glass of water?

examples.note: 차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'; 대 counts the vehicle.

examples.en: There are five computers in the office.

examples.ko: 에어컨 한 대를 더 설치하고 싶어요.

examples.en: I want to install one more air conditioner.
examples.note: 한 대를 더 = 'one more unit'; 대 fits appliances.

entries.nuance: 대 is the go-to counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, and air conditioners. It covers almost anything mechanical or electronic in the home or office, so a resident uses it constantly when talking about appliances. Pair it with native-Korean numbers.

Using 개 for cars or appliances instead of 대.
Counting people who ride in a car with 대 — people are 명, the vehicle is 대.

examples.en: That entire big building is all company offices.
examples.note: 한 채가 전부 = 'one whole building, all of it'; 전부 emphasizes scale.

entries.nuance: 채 counts entire dwellings and sizeable buildings — houses, traditional homes, and apartment buildings or units treated as whole properties. Counting rooms inside a home with 채 — rooms are 개 (방 한 개); the whole house is 채.

Native numbers before 송이: 한, 두, 세 송이.

Ask quantity of flowers with 몇 송이.

examples.en: Just one rose, please.
examples.note: 한 송이만 = 'just one bloom'; common at a flower shop.

examples.en: One bunch of grapes is 10,000 won.
examples.note: 송이 counts the grape cluster; typical fruit-stand pricing.

examples.en: I gave my girlfriend ten flowers as a gift.
examples.note: 열 송이를 marks the flowers; -한테 = 'to (a person)'.

entries.nuance: 송이 counts single blossoms and naturally clustered produce — a rose, a tulip, a bunch of grapes or bananas. For a wrapped bouquet you'd switch to 다발, but each separate stem or cluster is 송이. It takes native-Korean numbers and shows up whenever you buy flowers or fruit.

Using 개 for a single flower instead of the natural 송이.
Confusing 송이 (a single bloom/cluster) with 다발 (a bound bouquet).

examples.note: 두 줄 counts the gimbap rolls; 포장 = takeout packing.

examples.en: Please line up in a single line here.
examples.note: 한 줄로 = 'in one line'; common queue instruction.

examples.ko: 이 글을 두 줄로 요약해 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i geureul du jullo yoyakae bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I summarized this text in two lines.
examples.note: 두 줄로 = 'in two lines'; 줄 counts lines of writing.

entries.nuance: 줄 counts things arranged in a long line — a roll of gimbap, a row of seats, a queue of people, or lines of text. examples.en: I have two cats.
examples.note: 두 마리 counts the cats; 키우다 = to raise/keep a pet.

examples.en: Shall we order one whole chicken?

examples.en: I saw three birds in the park.
examples.note: 세 마리를 marks the birds as what was seen.

entries.nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, and even a whole cooked chicken at a fried-chicken place. Using 개 for animals instead of 마리.

examples.note: 세 끼를 counts the meals as the object of 먹다.

examples.romanization: bappaseo oneul han kkibakke mon meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was so busy I only ate one meal today.

entries.nuance: 군데 counts locations or spots — shops you visited, apartments you toured, or places on the body that hurt. It's especially handy with 몇 군데 ('how many places') and 여러 군데 ('several places') when comparing options or describing scattered pain. Use native-Korean numbers, and note 곳 is a close synonym that's slightly more formal.

Using 개 for places instead of the natural 군데 (or 곳).
Mixing up 군데 with 군대 (military/army) — different word entirely.

examples.en: Go straight up to the corner from here.

entries.nuance: 모퉁이 is the corner where a road or building bends, the spot you round on foot. For a four-way intersection of cars you want 사거리 instead, and 모퉁이 feels smaller and more pedestrian. Koreans give directions by chaining 모퉁이를 돌면... (once you turn the corner), so it is one of the most useful walking-direction words.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 모퉁이 for a big car intersection — that is 사거리 or 교차로
Saying 모서리 for a street corner; 모서리 is the sharp edge of an object like a table

entries.explanation: "the opposite side (right across, facing you)" is 맞은편 (majeunpyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 맞은편에 있다 ("to be on the opposite side"). entries.nuance: 맞은편 means the side directly facing you, as if the two spots stare at each other across a road or room. It is slightly more 'face-to-face' than 건너편, though in daily speech the two overlap heavily. Use it to pin a landmark: 약국 맞은편 (across from the pharmacy) tells someone exactly where to look.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 맞은편 with 옆 (next to); 맞은편 is across, not beside
Forgetting the location particle — say 맞은편에 있어요, not just 맞은편 있어요

entries.shortExplanation: 건너편 means "the other side (across the road or river)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 건너편 (geonneopyeon) = "the other side (across the road or river)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 길 건너편 ("across the street") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건너편, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.en: There's a big supermarket across the street.

examples.note: 으려면 = if you want to; pairs with crossing

examples.en: My friend waved from across the way.

entries.nuance: 건너편 is the side you reach by crossing something — a road, a river, the tracks — and it pairs naturally with 건너다 (to cross). It overlaps with 맞은편, but 건너편 emphasizes the act of crossing over to get there, while 맞은편 stresses simply facing you. For directions involving a crosswalk, 건너편 is the word locals reach for first.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 건너편 when the place is on your own side; it must be across something you cross
Mixing it up with 다음 (next); 건너편 is across, not the next one along

entries.explanation: 지름길 (jireumgil) means "shortcut". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지름길로 가다 ("to go by the shortcut"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 지름길 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.en: If you go this way, it's a shortcut.

examples.note: 질러가다 + 지름길 are a natural pair

entries.nuance: 지름길 is a shorter, faster route that skips the long way around, often through alleys or back streets a local would know. Figuratively it can also mean a 'fast track' to a goal (성공의 지름길 = the shortcut to success), so context decides. In navigation talk it pairs with 질러가다 (to cut across) and contrasts with 돌아가다 (to go the long way).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 지름낄 or 지름킬; the spelling is 지름길
Confusing it with 골목길 (alley) — an alley can be a shortcut, but 지름길 is specifically the shorter route

entries.explanation: "fork in the road / crossroads" is 갈림길 (gallimgil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갈림길에서 ("at the fork in the road"). Watch the particle attached to 갈림길 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.en: at the fork in the road

examples.en: At the fork, go to the left.

examples.note: figurative use; a big decision point

entries.nuance: 갈림길 is the point where one road splits into two or more, the moment you must choose a direction. Literally it guides walking or driving (갈림길에서 오른쪽), but Koreans use it just as often for life's big decision points (인생의 갈림길). The verb 갈리다 (to be divided) is the root, so the image is a path branching apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 갈림길 (a fork) with 사거리 (a four-way intersection); a fork splits, an intersection crosses
Spelling it 갈림낄 — the correct form is 갈림길

entries.nuance: 수능 (short for 대학수학능력시험) is the single national university entrance exam taken once a year in November, and it is a massive cultural event in Korea. As a resident you'll notice altered traffic, hushed neighborhoods, and even delayed flights on 수능 날. Use 보다 (to take/sit) with it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수능을 하다 — exams take 보다, not 하다.
Treating it as a generic 'final exam' — 수능 is specifically the once-a-year national college entrance test.

entries.nuance: 논술 refers to argumentative essay exams that test logical reasoning and writing, used as one university-admissions route alongside grades and the 수능. Confusing 논술 (argumentative essay) with 작문/에세이 (general composition).

entries.nuance: 입시 refers to the entire entrance-examination and admissions process, especially the high-stakes race into university, rather than one exam. Equating 입시 with a single test — it's the whole admissions process including 수능, 논술, and interviews.

examples.en: Studying steadily is better than cramming.
If you keep at Korean steadily, you improve quickly.

examples.romanization: geu haksaengeun kkujunhi chulseokaeseo seongjeogi ollasseoyo.

entries.nuance: 꾸준히 means doing something steadily and consistently over time without giving up, and it's the praise word Koreans use for sustainable effort. In any study or self-improvement talk it's the natural opposite of cramming or quitting. It modifies verbs like 공부하다, 연습하다, and 하다.

Using it as an adjective — it's an adverb; the adjective form is 꾸준하다.

feeling that wells up, slightly passive nuance
common phrase, e.g. 후회 없이 살자

examples.en: I'm very curious, so I love learning anything.
examples.note: 호기심이 많다 = to have lots of curiosity

examples.ko: 호기심에 한국 예능을 봤다가 푹 빠졌어요.
examples.romanization: hogisime hanguk yeneungeul bwatdaga puk ppajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I watched a Korean variety show out of curiosity and got totally hooked.

entries.nuance: 호기심 is curiosity, the pull to know or try something new, and 호기심이 많다 is a warm compliment about an open, eager personality. The phrase 호기심에 ('out of curiosity, on a whim') is super handy for explaining why you tried something. It pairs with 생기다/들다, not 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 호기심하다; use 호기심이 생기다/많다
Confusing it with 관심 (interest/attention); 호기심 is the itch to find out, 관심 is sustained interest or care

examples.ko: 다이어트 중인데 야식 먹어서 죄책감이 들어요.
examples.romanization: daieoteu junginde yasing meogeoseo joechaekgami deureoyo.
examples.en: I'm on a diet but ate a late-night snack, so I feel guilty.

examples.ko: 바쁘다고 부모님께 연락 못 해서 죄책감이 좀 있어요.
examples.romanization: bappeudago bumonimkke yeollang mo taeseo joechaekgami jom isseoyo.
examples.en: I feel a bit guilty for not contacting my parents, blaming being busy.
The lie I told stayed with me as guilt.
examples.note: 죄책감으로 남다 = to linger as guilt

entries.nuance: 죄책감 is the inward feeling of guilt over something you did, paired most naturally with 들다 (죄책감이 들어요). 20-30s use it lightly and often, even about diet slip-ups or skipping the gym, not only serious wrongs. Don't confuse it with 미안함 (the feeling of being sorry toward a person); 죄책감 is the internal weight on your conscience.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 죄책감하다; the noun pairs with 들다/느끼다, never 하다
Mixing it with 미안함; 미안함 is 'sorry toward someone,' 죄책감 is the inner guilt itself

examples.en: It was hard, but finishing the work gives me a sense of fulfillment.

examples.ko: 가르친 학생이 합격해서 정말 보람이 있었어요.
examples.romanization: gareuchin haksaengi hapgyeokaeseo jeongmal borami isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The student I taught passed, so it was truly rewarding.

examples.ko: 오늘은 할 일을 다 해서 보람찬 하루였어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun hal ireul da haeseo boramchan haruyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I got everything done today, so it was a fulfilling day.

entries.nuance: 보람 is the warm payoff feeling when your effort proves worthwhile, the reward of seeing hard work bear fruit. It's a deeply positive word Koreans use about jobs, study, volunteering, or parenting: 보람을 느끼다 (to feel fulfilled) and 보람차다 (rewarding). There's no clean one-word English match, which makes it a satisfying word to add to your everyday vocabulary.

Reducing it to 'reward' as in money/prize; 보람 is the inner sense of worthwhileness, not a material payout
Saying 보람하다; use 보람을 느끼다, 보람이 있다, or the adjective 보람차다

entries.explanation: 세금 (segeum) means "tax". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세금을 내다 ("to pay tax"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 is the standard verb for paying taxes, bills, fees
붙다 (to stick) is how Koreans say tax/fees are tacked onto a price
신고 = official declaration; 종합소득세 신고 is the yearly income-tax filing
환급 is the refund you get back, e.g. 연말정산 환급 at year-end

examples.en: Tax comes out of my paycheck automatically.
examples.note: 빠지다 here = to be deducted; common for 4대보험·세금

examples.en: Is tax included in this price?
examples.note: Useful when a quote looks suspiciously low; 부가세 별도 means VAT not included

examples.en: Freelancers have to file taxes themselves.
examples.note: Relevant for foreigners doing 3.3% 사업소득 work

entries.nuance: 세금 is the general word covering income tax, VAT, property tax and more. In daily life you mostly hear it about your paycheck (소득세 빠진다) or when checking if 부가세 is included in a price. For the once-a-year reckoning, people say 연말정산 (year-end settlement) rather than 세금 itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 세금을 사다 — you 내다 (pay) tax, never 사다.
Confusing 세금 (tax) with 요금 (a usage fee/fare); your phone bill is 요금, not 세금.

entries.explanation: "pension" is 연금 (yeongeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국민연금 ("national pension"). Watch the particle attached to 연금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: The mandatory state pension; foreigners on certain visas pay in too
받다 for the money you collect after retirement
가입하다 is the verb for joining/signing up for any scheme
개인 = personal; a voluntary retirement savings product from a bank or insurer

examples.en: National pension is taken out of my salary every month.
I also signed up for a private pension for my old age.
examples.note: 들다 (to sign up) is colloquial for joining insurance/pension; 노후 = later life

examples.en: From when can I start receiving the pension?
examples.note: Practical question about the payout age (currently rising past 60)

entries.nuance: 연금 usually means 국민연금, the compulsory national pension deducted from your pay. Some foreigners can claim a lump-sum refund (반환일시금) when they leave Korea, depending on their country's agreement. 개인연금/퇴직연금 are extra retirement products you choose yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 연금 (pension) and 연봉 (annual salary) — they look similar but mean very different things.
Using 연금 for any monthly payment; it specifically means retirement income, not a subscription or installment.

entries.shortExplanation: 물가 means "cost of living / prices" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 물가 (mulga) = "cost of living / prices". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 물가가 오르다 ("prices go up / inflation rises") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 물가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 물가가 오르다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 물가.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 오르다 is the default verb; 물가가 올랐어요 is everyday small talk

usagePhrases.en: the cost of living is high
usagePhrases.note: Koreans say 물가가 비싸다, treating overall prices as a thing that can be expensive
상승 = a rise; you'll see 물가 상승률 (inflation rate) in the news
안정되다 = to become stable; the opposite of runaway inflation

examples.ko: 요즘 물가가 너무 올라서 장 보기 무서워요.
examples.romanization: yojeum mulgaga neomu ollaseo jang bogi museowoyo.
examples.en: Prices have gone up so much lately that I'm scared to go grocery shopping.
examples.note: 장 보다 = to do grocery shopping; very common complaint among young residents

examples.en: Seoul is expensive but convenient to live in.
examples.note: Typical way to describe a city's cost of living

examples.en: My salary stays the same but only prices keep rising.
examples.note: 그대로 = unchanged; a relatable money gripe

entries.nuance: 물가 refers to the general price level of goods and services, not the price tag on one item (that's 가격 or 값). When friends complain about inflation, they say 물가가 올랐다 rather than naming specific prices. It is one of the most-used words in casual money conversations in Korea right now.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 물가가 비싸요 about a single product — use 가격/값 for one item, 물가 only for overall prices.
Writing 물까 or 물카 — it is 물가, and the 가 is pronounced tense (mulkka) but still spelled 가.
