entries.nuance: 환율 is the rate between the won and a foreign currency, central to anyone who sends money abroad or shops on overseas sites. Saying 환율이 올랐다 means the foreign currency got more expensive in won, so it costs you more to buy dollars. Apps like Wise or your bank's 환율 우대 (rate discount) come up a lot.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 환율 (exchange rate) with 환전 (the act of exchanging cash) — you 환전하다 at a rate, the rate itself is 환율.
Assuming 환율이 올랐다 is always good; for sending money home a higher won-per-dollar rate means you pay more.

내다 when you owe it, e.g. on a loan (대출 이자)
율 = rate; also 금리 in formal/news contexts

examples.note: 적금 = installment savings; -은 편이다 = relatively/on the higher side

examples.en: The loan interest goes out every month and it's a burden.
examples.note: 부담되다 = to feel like a financial burden, very common

examples.en: Rates went up lately so the interest increased.
examples.note: Distinguishes 금리 (the rate) from 이자 (the actual money)

entries.nuance: 이자 is the actual money — what your savings earn or what you owe on a loan. The rate itself is 이자율 or, more formally, 금리. Whether 이자 is good or bad depends entirely on which side you're on: 예금 이자 (deposit interest) is welcome, 대출 이자 (loan interest) hurts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이자 for the rate — the percentage is 이자율/금리; 이자 is the won amount.
Saying 이자를 받다 about a loan you owe — you 내다 (pay) loan interest; you 받다 (receive) interest only on your own deposits.

entries.nuance: 원금 is the original sum you put in or borrowed, separate from the 이자 (interest) on top. 원금 보장 (principal protected) vs. 원금 손실 가능 (principal may be lost) is the single most important distinction when a bank or app offers you an investment. Watch for it whenever 펀드 or 주식 are involved.

Confusing 원금 (principal) with 현금 (cash) — they sound a bit alike but are unrelated.
Thinking 원금 보장 means profit is guaranteed; it only means you won't lose your initial amount, not that you'll gain.

entries.nuance: 펀드 is a pooled investment product (mutual fund) you usually buy through a bank app or securities account. Unlike a 예금/적금, a 펀드 has no guaranteed return and your 원금 is at risk. Many 20-30s start with an 적립식 펀드 or jump to 주식/ETF on apps like 토스증권 or 키움.

Spelling it 펀트 — it is 펀드, from English 'fund'.
Assuming a 펀드 works like a savings account; it is not 원금 보장, so returns can be negative.

entries.nuance: 가계부 literally means household-account book, but today it almost always refers to a budgeting app that auto-syncs your cards and accounts. Confusing 가계부 (your personal budget) with 영수증 (receipt) or 명세서 (statement) — those are inputs to the 가계부.

entries.nuance: 비상금 is money set aside for emergencies — sudden medical bills, job loss, a broken phone. Financial-advice content for 20-30s constantly recommends building a 비상금 first.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 비상금 (emergency savings) with 용돈 (allowance/pocket money) — 용돈 is for everyday spending, 비상금 is untouched until an emergency.
Treating 비상금 as investment money; the point is that it stays safe and instantly accessible, not that it grows.

entries.nuance: 지출 means money going out — your spending or expenses — and is the natural opposite of 소득/수입. Budgeting talk constantly contrasts 수입 vs 지출, and the first advice is always 고정 지출 (fixed costs) 줄이기. It feels a touch more formal than just 돈 쓰다 but is completely normal in everyday money conversations.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 지출 (money going out) with 지급 (a payment being made/disbursed) — they look similar but 지급 is about issuing payment, often from an institution.
Pairing it as 소득과 지출 only; the very common everyday pairing is 수입과 지출.

entries.nuance: 절약 is the noun for thrift or economizing, turned into a verb with 하다 (절약하다). It applies to money, energy, and time alike, and carries a positive, virtuous tone — being good at 절약 is a compliment. It often appears alongside 아끼다 (to use sparingly) and is the goal behind keeping a 가계부.

usagePhrases.note: What you file at a police station or station office when you lose something.
Verb form; more formal/written than 잃어버리다 in spoken use.
물 here means 'object'; 분실물 센터 = lost & found center.
Very common combo — put the noun before 분실.

examples.en: I lost my wallet on the subway.
examples.note: 분실하다 sounds appropriately formal when reporting.

examples.en: I'd like to file a lost-item report.
examples.note: -(으)려고 하는데요 softly opens a request at a counter.

examples.en: What floor is the lost & found on?
examples.note: Useful at big stations and department stores.

entries.nuance: 분실 is the noun the system uses on signs and forms; in casual speech people still say 잃어버렸어요. Use 분실 when talking to officials, writing a report, or reading signage like 분실물 보관소. It implies you misplaced your own item, not that someone took it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 분실 (you lost it) with 도난 (it was stolen) — police treat them very differently.
분실 is a noun; to make it a verb add 하다 (분실하다), don't just say 분실해요 about a person.

usagePhrases.note: Filed when an item is taken by someone, unlike 분실.
당하다 marks you as the victim of the action.
Often seen in notices warning residents.
방지 = prevention; common on locks and tags.

examples.en: My bike got stolen.
examples.note: 도난당하다 is the natural verb when you're the victim.

examples.en: I came to the police to report a theft.
examples.note: Pair 도난 with 신고 at the station.

examples.ko: 요즘 이 동네에 택배 도난이 많대요.
examples.romanization: yojeum i dongnee taekbae donani mantaeyo.
examples.en: They say there's a lot of parcel theft in this neighborhood lately.

entries.nuance: 도난 specifically means someone took your property, so police open a criminal case rather than just logging a lost item. Use 도난당하다 to say you were the victim; saying plain 도난했어요 wrongly sounds like you did the stealing. It is more formal than the everyday 훔쳐 갔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Never say 도난했어요 to mean 'I was robbed' — that reads as 'I committed theft'; use 도난당했어요.
도난 (stolen) is not 분실 (misplaced); using the wrong one changes whether police investigate.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common compound — write it as one word.
나다 is the natural intransitive verb for accidents.
내다 marks you as the one at fault.
현장 = the spot where it happened.

examples.en: There was just a traffic accident up ahead.
examples.note: 사고가 나다 = an accident occurs, no one blamed yet.

examples.en: I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
examples.note: 112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance.

entries.nuance: 사고 covers car crashes, workplace mishaps, and any sudden harmful event. The key contrast is 사고가 나다 (it happened) versus 사고를 내다 (you caused it) — Koreans listen closely to which you use. For a fender-bender people often add 접촉사고 (minor collision).

Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the second admits liability.
사고 is the event; the injured person is a 피해자, not a 사고.

usagePhrases.note: Used for accidents, disputes, and out-of-court deals.
The amount paid to settle, esp. after an accident.
서 = written document you both sign.
보다 here means 'to work out' an agreement.

examples.en: I reached a settlement with the other party.
examples.note: 합의를 보다 is the everyday phrasing.

examples.en: I received one million won as a settlement.
We filled out the settlement agreement at the police station.
examples.note: Often signed before charges are dropped.

entries.nuance: 합의 is huge in Korean accident and minor-crime culture: reaching 합의 with the victim often reduces or drops a case. It implies both sides agreed, usually with money (합의금) changing hands. Don't confuse it with a casual 'agreement' on plans — that's more like 약속 or 동의.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
합의 (legal/financial settlement) is not 동의 (agreeing with an opinion) — keep them separate.
Saying 합의했어요 implies a deal is final; if you're still negotiating, say 합의 중이에요.

entries.explanation: "fine (criminal penalty)" is 벌금 (beolgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌금을 내다 ("to pay a fine"). 형 = a type of criminal sentence.

entries.nuance: 벌금 is a criminal-court fine for an actual offense, so it goes on a different track than 과태료 (an administrative penalty for minor rule-breaking). Koreans distinguish them sharply: a 벌금 means you were found to have committed a crime. Always pair it with 내다 (to pay), not 주다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 벌금 (criminal fine) with 과태료 (admin penalty like illegal parking) — they have different legal weight.
Use 벌금을 내다, not 벌금을 주다; 주다 sounds like you're giving money away as a gift.

entries.nuance: 처벌 is the legal penalty itself — fines, sentences — and pairs with crimes and serious violations. A culturally important phrase is 처벌을 원하지 않는다 (I don't wish them punished), which a 피해자 can state to soften a case. Use 처벌받다 when you're the one penalized, 처벌하다 for the authority acting.

Don't say 처벌했어요 about yourself when you mean you were punished — that's 처벌받았어요.
처벌 (legal punishment) is not 벌금 (a fine); a 벌금 is one form of 처벌, not the whole concept.

쌓다 (to stack up) = build over time, very common collocation
진정한 (genuine) is the set adjective you'll hear in dramas and toasts
금이 가다 = a crack forms; idiomatic for a damaged relationship

examples.ko: 10년 우정인데 돈 문제로 이렇게 멀어질 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: 10nyeon ujeonginde don munjero ireoke meoreojil jul mollasseo.
examples.en: We've been friends for 10 years; I never thought money would push us apart like this.
examples.note: 멀어지다 = grow distant; banmal between close friends

examples.ko: 힘들 때 곁에 있어 주는 게 진짜 우정이죠.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae gyeote isseo juneun ge jinjja ujeongijyo.
examples.en: Being by your side when times are hard is real friendship.
examples.note: 곁에 있어 주다 = stay by one's side; polite reflective tone

examples.en: The bond between you two is really tight.
examples.note: 끈끈하다 = sticky/tight, a warm compliment about closeness

entries.nuance: 우정 is the abstract concept of friendship (the bond itself), not a friend — the person is 친구. You build it over time with 쌓다 and describe it as deep (깊다) or tight (끈끈하다). It carries a slightly weighty, sincere feeling, so Koreans use it for meaningful long-term bonds rather than casual acquaintances.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 우정 to mean 'a friend' — the person is 친구; 우정 is the relationship
Saying 우정을 만들다 (make a friendship); the idiomatic verb is 쌓다 (build up) or 나누다 (share)

쌓다 again — trust is built up over time
잃다 = lose; what happens after a betrayal or broken promise

examples.en: Lie once and trust collapses.
examples.note: Common life lesson tone; 무너지다 stresses total breakdown

examples.ko: 저 사람은 말한 건 꼭 지켜서 신뢰가 가.
examples.romanization: jeo sarameun malhan geon kkok jikyeoseo silloega ga.
examples.en: That person always keeps their word, so I trust them.
Building trust at work takes time.
examples.note: Practical workplace reality; -(으)려면 = if you want to

entries.nuance: 신뢰 is trust as a noun, more formal and considered than the verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). You say 신뢰가 가다 ('trust flows') when someone earns your confidence, and 신뢰가 무너지다 when it breaks. Confusing 신뢰 (earned, reasoned trust) with 믿음 (belief/faith), which can be more emotional or religious

usagePhrases.note: 의리가 있다 = the standard way to praise someone's loyalty
지키다 = uphold; staying loyal through hard times

usagePhrases.en: to be disloyal / a fair-weather friend

examples.ko: 야, 친구끼리 이러면 의리 없는 거지.
examples.romanization: ya, chingukkiri ireomyeon uiri eopsneun geoji.
examples.en: Hey, doing this to a friend is just disloyal.

examples.ko: 우리 형은 의리 하나는 진짜 끝내줘.
examples.romanization: uri hyeongeun uiri hananeun jinjja kkeunnaejwo.
examples.en: If there's one thing my older brother has, it's loyalty.
examples.note: 끝내주다 = be awesome; 하나는 highlights one standout trait

examples.en: I helped them to the end out of loyalty.
examples.note: 끝까지 = to the very end; -때문에 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 의리 is a deeply Korean value: staying faithful to friends, family, or your crew even when it costs you. It's tied to not abandoning people and repaying what you owe emotionally. You'll hear it constantly among friends ('의리 없냐?') and in films about brotherhood. It's warmer and more personal than formal 충성 (allegiance).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it as plain 'loyalty' to a company/country — that's 충성; 의리 is loyalty to people you have a bond with
Forgetting it's often used bare in speech: '의리 없어' rather than always '의리가 없어'

entries.explanation: 갈등 (galdeung) means "conflict, friction (between people)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 갈등이 생기다 ("for a conflict to arise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 갈등 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 갈등이 생기다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 갈등.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = come into being; the default verb for conflict starting
Common compound; also 부부 갈등 (marital), 노사 갈등 (labor-management)

examples.ko: 룸메이트랑 청소 문제로 갈등이 좀 있어요.
examples.romanization: rummeiteurang cheongso munjero galdeungi jom isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm having some friction with my roommate over cleaning.

examples.ko: 갈등이 생기면 바로 대화로 푸는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: galdeungi saenggimyeon baro daehwaro puneun ge joayo.
examples.en: When conflict comes up, it's best to resolve it right away by talking.
The conflict within the team is deepening.

entries.nuance: 갈등 covers interpersonal friction and inner dilemmas alike, but in daily life it usually means tension or clashing between people. It's more neutral and 'situational' than 싸움 (a fight/quarrel) — you can have 갈등 without ever raising your voice. You 풀다 (untie) it, not 'win' it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 갈등 for a loud argument — that moment is 싸움 or 다툼; 갈등 is the underlying tension
Saying 갈등을 이기다 (win the conflict); you 풀다 (resolve) or 해결하다 it, you don't win it

usagePhrases.note: 풀다 = untie; exactly the verb you need to apologize
Verb form; 오해했어요 = I misunderstood / I got it wrong
오해하지 마 = super common reassurance among friends

examples.ko: 아, 그거 오해예요. 그런 뜻 아니었어요.
examples.romanization: a, geugeo ohaeyeyo. geureon tteut anieosseoyo.
examples.en: Ah, that's a misunderstanding. I didn't mean it that way.
examples.note: 그런 뜻 아니었어요 = I didn't mean it like that; defusing tension

examples.ko: 오해하지 마, 너 욕한 거 아니야.
examples.romanization: ohaehaji ma, neo yokan geo aniya.
examples.en: Don't get the wrong idea, I wasn't badmouthing you.
examples.note: Reassuring a friend in banmal; 욕하다 = badmouth/curse

examples.ko: 빨리 만나서 오해를 푸는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: ppalli mannaseo ohaereul puneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: We'd better meet soon and clear up the misunderstanding.
examples.note: -는 게 좋겠어요 = it'd be best to; gentle suggestion

entries.nuance: 오해 is a misunderstanding where someone reads a situation or your intent wrong. The key phrase for fixing it is 오해를 풀다 (untie the misunderstanding). '오해하지 마' is one of the most useful relationship phrases you'll ever learn — it heads off conflict before it grows. Note 오해 (wrong understanding) vs 착각 (a mistaken impression, often about oneself).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오해를 고치다 (fix a misunderstanding); the idiom is 오해를 풀다 (untie it)
Mixing up 오해 (misreading someone/something) with 착각 (a personal delusion or mix-up)

뒤에서 = behind the back; the typical setting
남 = other people; 남 험담 = talking trash about others

examples.romanization: dareun saram heomdamhaneun geo byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: I don't really like badmouthing other people.
examples.note: 별로 안 좋아하다 = not really a fan of; polite distancing

examples.ko: 걔는 맨날 뒤에서 동료 험담만 해.
examples.romanization: gyaeneun maennal dwieseo dongnyo heomdamman hae.
examples.en: She does nothing but badmouth coworkers behind their backs.
examples.note: 맨날 = every single day; banmal complaint

examples.ko: 험담은 결국 돌고 돌아 본인한테 와요.
examples.romanization: heomdameun gyeolguk dolgo dora boninhante wayo.
examples.en: Badmouthing eventually goes around and comes back to you.
examples.note: 돌고 돌아 = going around and around; proverb-like warning

entries.nuance: 험담 is speaking ill of someone, with a clearly negative, malicious edge — it's not neutral gossip. entries.nuance: 눈치 is one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. 눈치가 빠르다 (quick eye) is high praise; 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism. 눈치를 보다 means reading someone's mood, often a superior's. Living in Korea, you'll use and need this word constantly.

entries.nuance: 인연 is the idea that some meetings are destined — it carries a soft, almost spiritual feeling rooted in Buddhist thought. It applies to romance, friendships, mentors, even chance encounters. '우리 인연인가 봐' is a sweet, slightly flirty line. Ending things is 인연을 끊다. It's warmer and more fateful than the plain 관계 (relationship).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 인연 as a neutral word for any 'relationship' — that's 관계; 인연 implies fate/destiny
Saying 인연을 만나다 (meet a fate); you say 인연이 있다 / 인연이 닿다 or 인연을 만들다

In Korean the particle or ending next to 배신 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. 하다 verb; 배신했어 = you betrayed me
-감 = sense/feeling; 배신감 드는 게 = the betrayed feeling that comes
Literally 'hit the back of the head'; vivid synonym for betraying

examples.note: 믿었던 = whom I had trusted; raw banmal

examples.en: Because of the sense of betrayal, I couldn't trust anyone for a while.
examples.note: 한동안 = for a while; 배신감 = feeling of betrayal

entries.nuance: 배신 is betrayal — breaking someone's trust or loyalty, a heavy and emotional word. You're usually on the receiving end with 배신을 당하다. The vivid idiom 뒤통수(를) 치다 ('hit the back of the head') is what people often say in casual speech for being backstabbed. 배신감 (the feeling) is just as commonly used as the act itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배신 for minor letdowns — it's strong, for real broken trust, not mild disappointment (실망)
Forgetting the passive: to say 'I was betrayed' use 배신당하다, not just 배신하다 (which means you did the betraying)

usagePhrases.en: to compromise / each give a little
usagePhrases.note: 서로 = each other; the spirit of meeting halfway

examples.en: I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.

examples.romanization: dul da jogeumssik yangbohamyeon geumbang haegyeoldwaeyo.

examples.note: 조금씩 = little by little; advice for resolving conflict

entries.nuance: 양보 is the act of yielding — giving up your seat, your turn, or your preference for someone else's sake. It's a prized social virtue in Korea, especially toward elders (자리를 양보하다 on the subway is everyday courtesy). In disagreements, 서로 양보하다 means meeting halfway. It's voluntary and gracious, not losing or being forced to give in (양보 ≠ 포기).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 양보 (graciously yielding to someone) with 포기 (giving up on a goal entirely)
Using it only for seats — it also covers yielding your turn, opinion, or right-of-way while driving (양보 운전)

Saying 화해를 만들다 (make a reconciliation); just use the verb 화해하다 or 화해를 하다

entries.nuance: 갈비 covers the rib cut and a whole family of dishes — grilled 갈비, marinated 양념갈비, and the soup 갈비탕. Because it can be beef or pork, locals always say 소갈비 or 돼지갈비 to be clear, and beef ribs read as a more special, costly meal.

Assuming 갈비 always means beef — at many BBQ spots it defaults to pork (돼지갈비).
Mixing up 갈비 (ribs) with 갈비탕 (rib soup); one is grilled, one is a soup dish.

entries.nuance: 등심 is the go-to grilling cut at beef-focused restaurants, prized for being relatively lean yet tender. You'll constantly see it next to 안심 and the upgraded 꽃등심 (ribeye) on menus, so recognizing the cut names helps you order beef confidently.

examples.en: Mackerel gives off a bit of a smell when grilled.
examples.note: Oily fish like 고등어 are aromatic while cooking.

entries.nuance: 고등어 (mackerel) is an everyday, affordable fish that anchors home-style meals as 고등어구이 or 고등어조림. Because it's an oily fish, locals talk about it being 비리다 (fishy) if not fresh, and it's often sold by the 손 (a pair), which is a useful counter to recognize at the market.

entries.nuance: 연어 (salmon) has become hugely popular in Korea, especially raw as 연어회 or 연어 초밥 and in 연어 덮밥 rice bowls. Unlike many native fish, it's a trendy, mild option newcomers often gravitate to, so it's worth knowing alongside the more traditional 회 fish.

entries.explanation: 건조기 (geonjogi) means "clothes dryer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 건조기 ("dryer"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 건조기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Short for 의류 건조기; in everyday speech 건조기 almost always means the clothes dryer, not a food dehydrator.
돌리다 (lit. spin/turn) is the standard verb for running any rotating appliance: 세탁기 돌리다, 건조기 돌리다.
넣다 = put in; 빨래를 건조기에 넣다 is the natural way to say load the dryer.
꺼내다 = take out; pairs with 넣다 for loading/unloading.

examples.ko: 빨래 다 됐으면 건조기에 넣어 줘.
examples.romanization: ppallae da dwaesseumyeon geonjogie neoeo jwo.
examples.en: If the laundry's done, put it in the dryer.
examples.note: 빨래 다 됐다 = the laundry's finished (washing); casual 줘 for a roommate or partner.

examples.ko: 우리 집은 건조기가 없어서 빨래를 베란다에 널어요.
examples.romanization: uri jibeun geonjogiga eopseoseo ppallaereul berandae neoreoyo.
examples.en: We don't have a dryer, so we hang the laundry on the balcony.
examples.note: Very common situation in Korean apartments; 널다 = to hang out to dry.

examples.en: When you run the dryer, the towels get really fluffy.
examples.note: 보송보송하다 = soft and fluffy/dry; a typical selling point Koreans mention about dryers.

entries.nuance: 한국에서 건조기는 비교적 최근에 보편화된 가전이라 없는 집도 많아요. 그래서 '건조기 있어요?'는 자취방이나 월세 집을 구할 때 실제로 자주 묻는 질문이에요. 식품 건조기와 헷갈릴 수 있지만 일상 대화에서는 거의 항상 의류 건조기를 뜻합니다.

drills.note: Short for 의류 건조기; in everyday speech 건조기 almost always means the clothes dryer, not a food dehydrator.
돌리다 (lit. spin/turn) is the standard verb for running any rotating appliance: 세탁기 돌리다, 건조기 돌리다.

usagePhrases.note: Essential in Korean winters when 난방 (heating) makes indoor air very dry.
틀다 is the go-to verb for appliances that put out air/sound/water (가습기, 에어컨, 선풍기, 음악).
물(을) 채우다 = fill with water; daily maintenance task.
세척 = washing/cleaning; 가습기 세척 is stressed a lot in Korea for hygiene reasons.

examples.en: It's so dry in winter that I sleep with the humidifier on.
examples.note: 건조하다 = to be dry (air/skin); a very common winter complaint.

examples.ko: 가습기 물 좀 채워 줄래? 거의 다 떨어졌어.
examples.romanization: gaseupgi mul jom chaewo jullae? geoui da tteoreojyeosseo.
examples.en: Can you refill the humidifier? It's almost empty.
examples.note: 물이 떨어지다 = to run out of water; 줄래? is a soft casual request.

examples.ko: 가습기는 자주 안 닦으면 세균이 생겨요.
examples.romanization: gaseupgineun jaju an dakkeumyeon segyuni saenggyeoyo.
examples.en: If you don't clean the humidifier often, bacteria grow in it.
examples.note: 세균이 생기다 = bacteria form; reflects real concern after Korea's humidifier-disinfectant scandal.

entries.nuance: 가습기는 한국 겨울 필수품이에요. 아파트 난방이 강해서 공기가 많이 건조해지거든요. 과거 '가습기 살균제 사건' 때문에 한국 사람들은 가습기 청소와 위생에 특히 민감하니, 세척 이야기가 자연스럽게 나옵니다.

Don't confuse 가습기 (adds moisture) with 제습기 (removes moisture) — they're opposites.
Using 켜다 isn't wrong, but 틀다 sounds more natural with 가습기 in casual speech.

entries.shortExplanation: 공기청정기 means "air purifier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공기청정기 (gonggicheongjeonggi) = "air purifier". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공기청정기 ("air purifier") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공기청정기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Often shortened to 공청기 in casual speech; a near-must-have because of 미세먼지 (fine dust).
틀다 again for air-output appliances; 켜다 also fine.
필터(를) 갈다 = replace the filter; 갈다 = to replace/change a consumable part.
심하다 = severe; the usual reason people run a 공기청정기.

examples.ko: 미세먼지 심한 날엔 공기청정기를 하루 종일 틀어 놔요.
examples.romanization: misemeonji simhan naren gonggicheongjeonggireul haru jongil teureo nwayo.
examples.en: On days with bad fine dust, I leave the air purifier on all day.
examples.note: 틀어 놓다 = leave (it) turned on; 하루 종일 = all day long.

examples.ko: 공기청정기 필터 갈 때 됐나 봐. 빨간불 들어왔어.
examples.romanization: gonggicheongjeonggi pilteo gal ttae dwaenna bwa. ppalganbul deureowasseo.
examples.en: Looks like it's time to change the air purifier filter. The red light came on.
examples.note: 빨간불(이) 들어오다 = the red light comes on; 갈 때 되다 = time to replace.

examples.ko: 요즘 집집마다 공기청정기 하나씩은 다 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jipjimmada gonggicheongjeonggi hanassigeun da isseoyo.
examples.en: These days pretty much every household has at least one air purifier.
examples.note: 집집마다 = every household; 하나씩은 = at least one each.

entries.nuance: 한국은 봄철 미세먼지·황사 때문에 공기청정기가 거의 생활필수품이 됐어요. 자취하는 20-30대도 작은 모델 하나쯤은 두는 경우가 많습니다. 필터 교체 알림(빨간불)과 미세먼지 농도 표시등 이야기가 일상에서 자주 나와요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
청정기 alone is ambiguous; say 공기청정기 (or casual 공청기) to mean an air purifier specifically.
Don't confuse it with 정수기 (water purifier) — 공기 vs 물; the 청정/정수 parts sound similar to beginners.

entries.shortExplanation: 정수기 means "water purifier / water dispenser" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정수기 (jeongsugi) means "water purifier / water dispenser". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정수기 ("water purifier"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정수기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A countertop/standing unit dispensing filtered cold and hot water; extremely common in Korean homes and offices.
렌탈(rental) is huge in Korea — many people rent a 정수기 with monthly fees and visits from a 코디 (service rep) rather than buying.
정수기 dispenses 온수(hot), 냉수(cold), and 정수(room-temp filtered) water.
Pairs with 온수; you choose by pressing the corresponding button.

examples.ko: 정수기에서 온수 받아서 컵라면 끓여 먹었어.
examples.romanization: jeongsugieseo onsu badaseo keomnamyeon kkeuryeo meogeosseo.
examples.en: I got hot water from the purifier and made a cup ramyeon.
examples.note: 물(을) 받다 = to dispense/get water into a container; 컵라면 = cup ramyeon.

examples.ko: 우리 회사 정수기는 냉수가 진짜 시원해요.
examples.romanization: uri hoesa jeongsugineun naengsuga jinjja siwonhaeyo.
examples.en: The water purifier at my office has really cold water.
examples.note: Office 정수기 are standard; 시원하다 = refreshingly cold.

examples.ko: 정수기 렌탈하면 코디가 정기적으로 필터 갈아 줘요.
examples.romanization: jeongsugi rentalhamyeon kodiga jeonggijeogeuro pilteo gara jwoyo.
examples.en: If you rent a water purifier, a service rep changes the filters regularly.
examples.note: 코디 = the brand's visiting service rep; 정기적으로 = regularly. A distinctly Korean rental-service detail.

entries.nuance: 한국에서는 정수기를 '사는' 것보다 '렌탈'하는 문화가 강해요. 코웨이·SK매직 같은 회사에서 매달 요금을 내고 코디 방문 관리를 받죠. 온수가 바로 나와서 차나 컵라면을 끓일 때도 자주 씁니다. 외국인에게는 렌탈 개념이 낯설 수 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 정수기 (water) with 공기청정기 (air) — 정수/청정 sound alike.
정수기 물 = filtered drinking water, whereas 생수 is bottled water you buy; they're different sources.

entries.explanation: "dishwasher" is 식기세척기 (sikgisecheokgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식기세척기 ("dishwasher"). usagePhrases.note: Often shortened to 식세기 in everyday speech, especially online and among younger people.
돌리다 for the wash cycle, same as with washing machine/dryer.
The chore a 식기세척기 replaces; 설거지(를) 하다 = to wash dishes by hand.
식기세척기 전용 세제 = dishwasher-specific detergent; you can't use regular dish soap.

examples.ko: 식세기 산 뒤로 설거지 스트레스가 확 줄었어요.
examples.romanization: siksegi san dwiro seolgeoji seuteureseuga hwak jureosseoyo.
examples.en: Ever since I bought a dishwasher, my stress over dishes dropped a lot.
examples.note: Casual 식세기; 산 뒤로 = ever since buying (clearer than 사고 나서, which collides with 사고 'accident'); 확 = sharply.

examples.ko: 그릇 식기세척기에 넣기 전에 음식물은 좀 털어 내.
examples.romanization: geureut sikgisecheokgie neoki jeone eumsingmureun jom teoreo nae.
examples.en: Scrape off the food scraps before putting the dishes in the dishwasher.
examples.note: 털어 내다 = to shake/scrape off; casual command 내 ending.

examples.ko: 식기세척기에는 꼭 전용 세제를 써야 돼요.
examples.romanization: sikgisecheokgieneun kkok jeonyong sejereul sseoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: You have to use dedicated detergent in a dishwasher.
examples.note: 꼭 = definitely/must; common warning to new owners.

entries.nuance: 식기세척기(줄여서 '식세기')는 한국 신혼부부와 1인 가구 사이에서 인기가 빠르게 늘고 있는 가전이에요. 손 설거지를 줄여 주는 효도/자취 필수템으로 자주 언급됩니다. 일반 주방세제 대신 전용 세제를 써야 한다는 점을 모르는 사람이 많아 대화 소재가 됩니다.

examples.ko: 요즘 원룸은 가스 대신 인덕션이 많아요.

examples.ko: 인덕션은 냄비를 아무거나 못 써. 전용이어야 돼.
examples.romanization: indeoksyeoneun naembireul amugeona mot sseo. jeonyongieoya dwae.
examples.en: You can't use just any pot on induction. It has to be induction-compatible.
examples.note: 아무거나 못 쓰다 = can't use just anything; common gotcha for new users.

examples.ko: 인덕션이라 불 조절이 빨라서 라면 끓이기 편해요.
examples.romanization: indeoksyeonira bul jojeori ppallaseo ramyeon kkeurigi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Since it's induction, the heat changes fast, so it's easy to cook ramyeon.
examples.note: Koreans still say 불 조절 even without a flame; 끓이다 = to boil.

entries.nuance: 인덕션은 화재 위험이 적고 청소가 쉬워서 한국 신축 아파트·원룸 기본 옵션이 되고 있어요. 다만 자석이 붙는 '인덕션 전용' 냄비라야 작동해서, 이사 후 기존 냄비를 못 쓰는 경우가 흔합니다. 가스레인지와 비교하는 대화가 자취·신혼 맥락에서 자주 나와요.

usagePhrases.note: A heated mat you lay on the floor or bed; a winter staple, cheaper to run than cranking the 보일러.
켜다 for a simple on/off device with a power switch/dial.
온도(를) 조절하다 = adjust the temperature; 전기장판 usually has a dial controller.
저온 화상 = a burn from prolonged contact with mild heat; a real risk people warn about with 전기장판.

examples.ko: 보일러 틀기 아까워서 전기장판만 켜고 자.
examples.romanization: boilleo teulgi akkawoseo jeongijangpanman kyeogo ja.
examples.en: It feels wasteful to run the heating, so I just sleep with the electric blanket on.
examples.note: 아깝다 = to feel wasteful/reluctant to spend; a very relatable money-saving move.

examples.ko: 전기장판 너무 뜨겁게 틀고 자면 저온 화상 입을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeongijangpan neomu tteugeopge teulgo jamyeon jeoon hwasang ibeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you sleep with the electric blanket turned up too high, you can get a low-temperature burn.
examples.note: 화상(을) 입다 = to get burned; common safety warning.

examples.ko: 겨울엔 전기장판 위에 이불 깔고 뒹굴뒹굴해요.
examples.romanization: gyeouren jeongijangpan wie ibul kkalgo dwingguldwinggulhaeyo.
examples.en: In winter I lay a blanket on the electric pad and just lounge around.
examples.note: 뒹굴뒹굴하다 = to roll around/laze; cozy winter image many Koreans relate to.

entries.nuance: 전기장판은 한국 겨울의 가성비 난방템이에요. 가스보일러를 돌리면 가스비가 많이 나오니까, 자취생이나 절약하는 사람들은 전기장판으로 몸만 따뜻하게 데우는 경우가 많죠. 비슷한 제품으로 물을 데우는 '온수매트'도 있는데, 저온 화상 주의 이야기가 자주 함께 나옵니다.

전기장판 (electric coil mat) vs 온수매트 (hot-water mat) are different products — the latter circulates warm water and is marketed as safer.
Leaving it on high all night risks 저온 화상; warn rather than assuming it's harmless because the heat feels mild.

entries.shortExplanation: 제습기 means "dehumidifier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dehumidifier" is 제습기 (jeseupgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 제습기 ("dehumidifier"). Watch the particle attached to 제습기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: Pulls moisture out of the air; in heavy demand during Korea's humid 장마 (rainy season) and summer.
돌리다 commonly used; 틀다 also fine.
물통(을) 비우다 = empty the (collected) water tank; the main upkeep task.
습하다 describes the muggy air that makes you reach for the 제습기.

examples.ko: 장마철엔 집이 너무 습해서 제습기를 계속 돌려요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren jibi neomu seupaeseo jeseupgireul gyesok dollyeoyo.
examples.en: During the rainy season the house gets so damp that I keep the dehumidifier running.

examples.ko: 제습기 물통 꽉 찼어. 비워야 돼.
examples.romanization: jeseupgi multong kkwak chasseo. biwoya dwae.
examples.en: The dehumidifier's tank is full. It needs emptying.
examples.note: 꽉 차다 = to be completely full; 비우다 = to empty.

examples.ko: 제습기 틀어 놓으니까 빨래도 빨리 마르네.
examples.romanization: jeseupgi teureo noeunikka ppallaedo ppalli mareune.
examples.en: With the dehumidifier on, the laundry dries faster too.
examples.note: 마르다 = to dry; 틀어 놓다 = leave running. A common practical use.

entries.nuance: 한국 여름은 장마와 높은 습도 때문에 제습기 수요가 급증해요. 곰팡이 예방과 실내 건조에 쓰이고, 건조기가 없는 집에서는 빨래 말리는 용도로도 자주 사용됩니다. 가습기와 정반대 기능이라는 점을 기억하면 헷갈리지 않아요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
제습기 (removes moisture) is the opposite of 가습기 (adds moisture) — the 제/가 prefix flips the meaning.
You must empty the 물통 regularly; if you forget, it auto-stops when full, which beginners mistake for a malfunction.

examples.ko: 나갈 때 가스 잠갔는지 꼭 확인해.
examples.romanization: nagal ttae gaseu jamganneunji kko kwaginhae.
examples.en: Make sure to check whether you turned off the gas when you leave.
examples.note: 잠그다 = to lock/shut off (a valve); a near-universal Korean safety reminder.

examples.ko: 우리 집은 아직 가스레인지라 냄비 아무거나 다 써요.
examples.romanization: uri jibeun ajik gaseureinjira naembi amugeona da sseoyo.
examples.en: Our place still has a gas range, so I can use any pot at all.
examples.note: Contrasts with 인덕션's pot restriction; 아무거나 = anything.

examples.ko: 가스레인지 불 너무 세니까 좀 줄여.
examples.romanization: gaseureinji bul neomu senikka jom juryeo.
examples.en: The gas flame is too strong, so turn it down a bit.
examples.note: 불이 세다 = the flame is strong; 줄이다 = to reduce. Casual 줄여 command.

entries.nuance: 가스레인지는 한국의 전통적인 조리 기구로, 구축 아파트나 오래된 집에 많아요. 화재·가스 누출 위험 때문에 '외출 전 가스 잠그기'가 생활화돼 있죠. 최근 신축에서는 인덕션으로 대체되는 추세라 두 단어를 비교하는 대화가 흔합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't forget 가스 잠그다 before leaving — it's the expected safety phrasing, not just 가스레인지 끄다.

Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Almost always an electric 전기밥솥; arguably the single most essential appliance in a Korean kitchen.
밥(을) 하다 = to make rice/a meal; 밥솥에 밥하다 is the everyday phrase.
보온 = warming mode; the 밥솥 keeps rice warm for hours after cooking.
압력밥솥 = the pressure type (e.g. Cuckoo) that makes notably stickier, glossier rice.

examples.ko: 밥솥에 밥 해 놨으니까 데워서 먹어.
examples.romanization: bapsote ba pae nwasseunikka dewoseo meogeo.
examples.en: I've cooked rice in the rice cooker, so heat it up and eat.
examples.note: 해 놓다 = have done (in advance); 데우다 = to warm up. Very common family note.

examples.ko: 밥솥 보온으로 오래 두면 밥이 누레져요.
examples.romanization: bapsot booneuro orae dumyeon babi nurejyeoyo.
examples.en: If you leave rice on warm in the cooker too long, it turns yellowish.
examples.note: 누렇다 → 누레지다 (ㅎ-irregular, dark-vowel class, like 누레요); a real complaint about long keep-warm.

examples.en: If you live alone, a rice cooker is truly a must-have.
examples.note: 자취하다 = to live on one's own; 필수 = essential.

entries.nuance: 밥솥(전기밥솥)은 한국 가정의 핵심 가전이에요. 쿠쿠·쿠첸 같은 브랜드의 압력밥솥이 유명하고, 갓 지은 밥을 보온으로 오래 유지하는 기능이 중요하죠. 자취를 시작하는 외국인이 가장 먼저 사게 되는 가전 중 하나라 실용성이 매우 높습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
솥 alone means a traditional cast pot; for the everyday electric appliance say 밥솥 (or 전기밥솥).
Pronounce/write the final consonant correctly: it's 밥솥 (ㅌ batchim), often mis-typed as 밥속.

entries.shortExplanation: 멀티탭 means "power strip / multi-outlet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "power strip / multi-outlet" is 멀티탭 (meoltitaep). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 멀티탭 ("power strip"). Watch the particle attached to 멀티탭 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 멀티탭. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 멀티탭.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Konglish from 'multi-tap'; the strip with multiple outlets and often individual on/off switches.
콘센트 = the wall socket; a 멀티탭 plugs into a 콘센트 to give you more sockets.
플러그를 꽂다 = to plug in; 멀티탭에 꽂다 = plug into the power strip.
문어발(식) = plugging too many things into one strip; warned against as a fire hazard.

examples.ko: 콘센트가 부족해서 멀티탭 하나 더 샀어요.
examples.romanization: konsenteuga bujokaeseo meoltitae pana deo sasseoyo.
examples.en: There weren't enough outlets, so I bought another power strip.
examples.note: 부족하다 = to be insufficient; classic studio-apartment problem.

examples.ko: 충전기 멀티탭에 꽂아 놨어. 저기 스위치 켜면 돼.
examples.romanization: chungjeongi meoltitaebe kkoja nwasseo. jeogi seuwichi kyeomyeon dwae.
examples.en: I plugged the charger into the power strip. Just flip that switch.
examples.note: 꽂아 놓다 = have it plugged in; many 멀티탭 have per-socket switches.

examples.en: It's dangerous to plug everything into one power strip octopus-style.
examples.note: 문어발 = overloading one strip; a standard fire-safety warning.

entries.nuance: 한국 원룸·자취방은 콘센트가 부족한 경우가 많아서 멀티탭이 거의 필수예요. 개별 스위치로 대기전력을 차단해 전기세를 아끼기도 하죠. '문어발식 콘센트'는 화재 위험으로 자주 경고되니, 안전 맥락에서 잘 나오는 단어입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
멀티탭 (the strip) vs 콘센트 (the wall socket) are different things; learners often call the strip a 콘센트.
It's Konglish — native English 'power strip', but in Korea you must say 멀티탭 to be understood.

entries.shortExplanation: 리모컨 means "remote control" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 리모컨 (rimokeon) = "remote control". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 리모컨 ("remote control") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 리모컨, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 리모컨. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 리모컨.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Konglish shortening of 'remote control'; used for TV, 에어컨, etc. (e.g. 에어컨 리모컨).
건전지(를) 갈다 = change the (AA/AAA) batteries that a 리모컨 runs on.
채널(을) 돌리다 = flip channels with the TV remote; 돌리다 lingers from the dial era.
볼륨(을) 키우다/줄이다 = raise/lower the volume via the remote.

examples.ko: 리모컨 어디 갔어? 소파 밑에 있나 봐.
examples.romanization: rimokeon eodi gasseo? sopa mite inna bwa.
examples.en: Where did the remote go? It might be under the couch.
examples.note: 어디 갔어? = where did it go?; the universal lost-remote line.

examples.ko: 리모컨 건전지 다 됐나 봐. 채널이 안 돌아가.
examples.romanization: rimokeon geonjeonji da dwaenna bwa. chaeneori an doraga.
examples.en: Looks like the remote's batteries died. The channels won't change.
examples.note: 건전지 다 되다 = batteries are dead; 안 돌아가다 = won't change/respond.

examples.ko: 에어컨 리모컨으로 온도 좀 낮춰 줄래?
examples.romanization: eeokeol limokeoneuro ondo jom natchwo jullae?
examples.en: Can you lower the temperature with the AC remote?
examples.note: 에어컨 리모컨 = AC remote; 낮추다 = to lower; 줄래? soft request.

entries.nuance: 리모컨은 TV뿐 아니라 에어컨, 셋톱박스 등 거의 모든 가전에 딸려 와서 집집마다 여러 개가 굴러다녀요. 그래서 '리모컨 어디 갔어?'는 한국 가정의 단골 대사죠. 건전지 교체와 채널·볼륨 조절 표현이 함께 쓰입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Standard form is 리모컨; 리모콘 is a frequent misspelling.
It runs on 건전지 (dry-cell batteries), not 충전 — don't say 리모컨 충전하다 for a normal AA/AAA remote.

entries.shortExplanation: 손목 means "wrist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 손목 (sonmok) means "wrist". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손목이 아파요 ("My wrist hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 손목 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 손목이 아파요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 손목.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Go-to line at the clinic or pharmacy
Written as one word — 손목 (wrist) + 시계 (watch)
시큰거리다 describes a dull joint ache

examples.ko: 마우스를 오래 써서 손목이 너무 아파요.
examples.romanization: mauseureul orae sseoseo sonmogi neomu apayo.
examples.en: My wrist really hurts from using the mouse too long.
I sprained my wrist catching myself when I fell.
examples.note: 짚다 = to brace/prop with your hand

examples.ko: 손목에 무리가 가지 않게 보호대를 차세요.
examples.romanization: sonmoge muriga gaji anke bohodaereul chaseyo.
examples.en: Wear a brace so you don't strain your wrist.
examples.note: 무리가 가다 = to put strain on

entries.nuance: 손목 is the joint where the hand (손) meets the arm. Korean stacks 손 + 목, so think 'hand-neck.' Office workers use it constantly to describe RSI-type pain from keyboards and phones, so it is genuinely useful at the doctor.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 손목 (wrist) with 목 (neck) — 목 alone means your neck/throat.
It's a body part, not the watch itself; the watch is 손목시계.

entries.explanation: "ankle" is 발목 (balmok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 발목을 삐었어요 ("I sprained my ankle"). Watch the particle attached to 발목 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common ankle complaint

examples.en: I sprained my ankle on the stairs and walked with a limp.
My ankle is so swollen my shoe won't fit.

examples.ko: 등산 갈 때는 발목을 잡아주는 신발을 신으세요.
examples.romanization: deungsan gal ttaeneun balmogeul jabajuneun sinbareul sineuseyo.
examples.en: Wear shoes that support your ankle when you go hiking.

entries.nuance: 발목 is 발 (foot) + 목 (neck), the joint above your foot. Ankle sprains are extremely common, so 발목을 삐다 is a phrase you'll hear and use at orthopedic clinics (정형외과) all the time. It also shows up when talking about pant length.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 발 아파요 when you specifically twisted the ankle — use 발목 to be precise.
Remember 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 / 부었어요, not 붓어요.

examples.romanization: teniseureul chin dwiro palkkumchiga gyesok apayo.
examples.en: My elbow has been hurting ever since I played tennis.
examples.note: 'Tennis elbow' is a real diagnosis here too

examples.en: I bumped into the next person's elbow on the crowded subway.

entries.nuance: 팔꿈치 is the elbow joint. The spelling trips people up — it's 팔(arm) + 꿈치, written as one word with the double consonant ㄲ. You'll need it for joint pain, for describing crowded subway jostling, and for posture.

A frequent misspelling is 팔꿉치 or 팔굼치 — the correct form is 팔꿈치.
Don't drop the 팔 and just say 꿈치; the full word is 팔꿈치.

entries.explanation: 발가락 (balgarak) means "toe". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발가락을 찧었어요 ("I stubbed my toe"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 발가락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. entries.nuance: 발가락 means toe (발 foot + 가락 digit), parallel to 손가락 (finger). Use 엄지발가락 for the big toe and 새끼발가락 for the pinky toe. It's practical for shoe-fitting and for the very common foot issues like 무좀.

entries.shortExplanation: 허벅지 means "thigh" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "thigh" is 허벅지 (heobeokji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 허벅지가 굵다 ("to have thick thighs"). Watch the particle attached to 허벅지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

examples.en: My thighs are so sore after doing squats.
The jeans are tight around the thighs.
My thighs go numb if I sit too long.

entries.nuance: 허벅지 is the thick upper part of the leg, the thigh. It comes up constantly at the gym (스쿼트, 런지) and when clothes don't fit right. For the inner thigh say 허벅지 안쪽, and for the back of the thigh 허벅지 뒤.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 허벅지 (thigh) with 종아리 (calf) — the calf is the lower leg.
허벅지 is informal-neutral; in a medical setting you might also hear 대퇴부, but 허벅지 is what people actually say.

entries.explanation: 종아리 (jongari) = "calf (lower leg)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 종아리가 뭉쳤어요 ("My calf is knotted up") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 종아리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 종아리가 뭉쳤어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 종아리.

usagePhrases.note: 쥐가 나다 = to get a cramp
Common after a long day standing

examples.en: My calves got really tight from wearing high heels.
I woke up because I got a cramp in my calf.
My calves are all swollen from walking a lot.

entries.nuance: 종아리 is the back muscle of the lower leg, the calf. You'll hear it for cramps (쥐가 나다), for tightness after standing or walking, and at massage shops. 종아리 알 refers specifically to the bulge of the calf muscle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 종아리 (calf) and 정강이 (shin); the shin is the hard front bone.
쥐가 나다 (to cramp) is idiomatic — don't translate 쥐 (mouse) literally.

entries.explanation: 정강이 (jeonggangi) means "shin". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정강이를 부딪혔어요 ("I banged my shin"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정강이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 침대 모서리에 정강이를 부딪혀서 멍이 들었어요.
examples.romanization: chimdae moseorie jeonggangireul budityeoseo meongi deureosseoyo.
examples.en: I banged my shin on the corner of the bed and got a bruise.
I got kicked in the shin by the opposing player during soccer.

examples.ko: 정강이는 살이 없어서 부딪히면 정말 아파요.
examples.romanization: jeonggangineun sari eopseoseo buditimyeon jeongmal apayo.
examples.en: The shin has no padding, so it really hurts when you hit it.
examples.note: 살이 없다 = to have no flesh/padding

entries.nuance: 정강이 is the hard bony front of the lower leg, the shin — the opposite side from 종아리 (calf). Because it's all bone with little cushioning, hitting it on furniture is a sharp, memorable pain everyone relates to. The bone itself is 정강이뼈.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 정강이 (front shin) with 종아리 (back calf).
When you got hit, use the passive 차이다/부딪히다 (got kicked/bumped), not the active form.

examples.en: I hit the back of my head on the shelf corner and got a bump.
examples.note: 혹이 나다 = to get a lump

examples.en: I got stabbed in the back by a friend I trusted.

examples.ko: 한국 사람들은 뒤통수가 예쁜 걸 신경 써요.
examples.romanization: hanguk saramdeureun dwitongsuga yeppeun geol singyeong sseoyo.
examples.en: Koreans care about having a nicely shaped back of the head.

entries.nuance: 뒤통수 literally means the back of the head (뒤 back + 통수). Beyond the physical sense, 뒤통수를 치다/맞다 is an extremely common idiom for betraying or being betrayed — worth knowing both meanings. Koreans also genuinely comment on whether someone's 뒤통수 is round or flat (납작하다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't take 뒤통수를 맞았어요 literally if the context is social — it usually means 'I got betrayed.'
It's casual; in formal/medical speech you'd say 뒷머리 or 후두부 instead.

I braced my fall with my palms.

entries.nuance: 손바닥 is the palm, the inner surface of the hand (손 hand + 바닥 floor/flat surface). The opposite, the back of the hand, is 손등. 손바닥만 하다 ('palm-sized') is a handy idiom for describing something very small, like a cramped apartment.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 손바닥 (palm) with 손등 (back of the hand).
손바닥만 하다 is figurative for 'tiny' — not a literal measurement.

entries.nuance: 발바닥 is the sole, the bottom flat surface of the foot (발 foot + 바닥 flat surface), mirroring 손바닥. It comes up after long days of walking, with blisters (물집), and at foot-massage or 지압 shops, which are popular in Korea.

Don't confuse 발바닥 (sole) with 발등 (top of the foot).
물집이 잡히다 / 물집이 생기다 (to form a blister) is the natural collocation — not 물집을 만들다.

Watch the particle attached to 겨드랑이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

examples.romanization: yeoreumen gyeodeurangie ttami neomu mani nayo.
examples.en: My armpits sweat way too much in summer.

examples.ko: 땀 냄새 때문에 겨드랑이에 데오드란트를 발라요.
examples.romanization: ttam naemsae ttaemune gyeodeurangie deodeuranteureul ballayo.
examples.en: I put deodorant on my armpits because of sweat odor.
I felt a lump in my armpit so I went to the hospital.

entries.nuance: 겨드랑이 is the armpit/underarm. It's very practical in Korea's hot, humid summers when talking about sweat (땀) and odor (냄새), and it also comes up with deodorant, hair removal (제모), and noticing lumps. The spelling with -랑이 is worth memorizing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A common misspelling is 겨드랑 or 겨드량이 — the standard form is 겨드랑이.
For 'I sweat,' use 땀이 나다 (sweat comes out), not 땀을 하다.

entries.explanation: 엉덩이 (eongdeongi) = "buttocks; hip area / bottom". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 엉덩이가 아파요 ("My bottom hurts") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 엉덩이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.ko: 딱딱한 의자에 오래 앉아서 엉덩이가 아파요.
examples.romanization: ttakttakan uijae orae anjaseo eongdeongiga apayo.
examples.en: My bottom hurts from sitting on a hard chair too long.

examples.ko: 공부 잘하려면 엉덩이를 오래 붙이고 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gongbu jalharyeomyeon eongdeongireul orae buchigo isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: To study well you have to keep your butt in the chair a long time.
examples.note: 엉덩이를 붙이다 = to sit and persevere

examples.ko: 요즘 엉덩이 운동으로 스쿼트를 하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum eongdeongi undongeuro seukwoteureul hago isseoyo.
examples.en: I've been doing squats as a glute workout lately.

entries.nuance: 엉덩이 is the buttocks/bottom and the general hip-seat area. It's an everyday, non-vulgar word used for sitting-related soreness, for fitness (엉덩이 운동), and in idioms like 엉덩이가 무겁다 (a homebody / slow to move) and 엉덩이를 붙이다 (to settle in and stick with a task).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
엉덩이 is neutral and fine in normal conversation; 궁둥이 is more casual/childish for the same area — stick with 엉덩이.
Don't confuse it with 허리 (waist/lower back); back pain is 허리, seat soreness is 엉덩이.

entries.explanation: 구청 (gucheong) means "district (gu) office". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 구청에 가다 ("go to the district office"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 구청 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 구청 is the gu-level admin office; covers a whole district like 마포구, 강남구

usagePhrases.en: get issued at the district office
usagePhrases.note: for documents like 건축물대장 or 토지대장 you go to the 구청, while a simple 등본 is fine at the 동사무소
민원실 is the help-desk floor where you take a number and wait
관할 means the office responsible for your address; matters when filing complaints

examples.en: You register a business at the tax office, not the district office.
examples.note: common mix-up; 구청 handles residency/buildings, 세무서 handles taxes

examples.ko: 전입신고는 가까운 동사무소나 구청에서 하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeonipsingoneun gakkaun dongsamusona gucheongeseo hamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can file your move-in report at a nearby community office or the district office.
examples.note: 동사무소 is usually closer and enough for this

examples.en: I booked online on the district office website before going.
examples.note: many 구청 now take online reservations to cut waiting

entries.nuance: 구청 is the borough-level government office serving an entire 구 (district), one tier above the neighborhood 동사무소. As a resident you mainly visit it for ID documents, building/property paperwork, and parking or noise complaints. For everyday certificates, the closer 동사무소 is usually enough.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 구청 with 시청: 시청 (city hall) governs the whole city, 구청 governs one district within it.
Going to 구청 for taxes; income and business taxes are handled at the 세무서, not the 구청.

usagePhrases.en: get (a document) issued at the dong office
usagePhrases.note: 떼다 is the natural verb for pulling a certificate like 주민등록등본

examples.en: When you move, file your move-in report at the dong office within 14 days.
examples.note: 전입신고 is legally required; late filing can mean a small fine

examples.en: These days the dong office is officially called an administrative welfare center.
examples.note: the modern name is 행정복지센터, but everyone still says 동사무소

examples.en: I printed my residence certificate right from the unmanned kiosk at the dong office.
examples.note: the self-service kiosk avoids waiting in line

entries.nuance: 동사무소 is the neighborhood-level office where residents handle the most common errands: move-in reports, residence and family certificates, and ID-related paperwork. Its official name changed to 주민센터 and then 행정복지센터, but spoken Korean still overwhelmingly uses 동사무소. It is almost always closer and faster than the district 구청.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming the kiosk needs a fee for everything; a 등본 print is cheap or free, but you still need your ID to use it.
Saying 동사무소 for the whole district; it only covers one 동 (neighborhood), not the entire 구.

entries.nuance: 등기소 is the registry office that keeps official records of property ownership and company registrations. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 등기소 (property registry) with 등기우편 (registered mail at the post office); they are unrelated despite sharing 등기.

entries.nuance: 출입국사무소 is the immigration office, the single most important government office for a foreign resident: it issues the 외국인등록증 (ARC), processes visa extensions and changes, and records address updates. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reporting an address change only at the 동사무소; foreign residents must also report it to the 출입국사무소.
Showing up without a reservation; most immigration offices now require booking and may turn away walk-ins.

entries.nuance: 우편함 is the mailbox where letters and official notices are delivered, typically a locked unit in an apartment lobby. entries.nuance: 관공서 is the general term covering all government and public offices, the kind of place you go for official paperwork, from the 구청 to the 세무서. entries.nuance: 무척 means 'very' but carries a warm, emotional flavor, so it fits feelings, people, and personal reactions more than dry facts. Koreans often choose it over 아주 when they want to sound sincere rather than clinical. In very casual texting people lean on 너무 or 진짜 instead, but 무척 sounds nicely heartfelt in speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 무척 with a negative like 'not very' — for that you want 그다지 안 / 별로 안, not 무척 안.
Treating it as slang; 무척 is fully standard and slightly soft/literary, so it never sounds rude or too casual.

entries.nuance: 굉장히 is one of the most reachable strong intensifiers in everyday Korean and sounds natural in both casual and polite speech. It leans toward describing impressiveness, scale, or intensity, so it shines with adjectives like 크다, 많다, 맛있다. It is a notch stronger and more vivid than 아주, but still completely standard for work emails and conversation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 굉장이 — the correct spelling is 굉장히 with 히.
Overusing it on tiny things; saying 굉장히 for a minor matter can sound like exaggeration, where 꽤 or 좀 would fit better.

entries.nuance: 상당히 means a notable, measured degree and carries a slightly formal, composed tone, so it fits reviews, reports, and adult conversation well. Compared with the more emotional 무척 or casual 되게, it sounds objective and a bit understated, as if you are reporting a fact. It is a favorite in written feedback and workplace speech where you want to sound thoughtful.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it in very casual chat with friends, where it can sound stiff — 되게 or 엄청 are more natural there.
Confusing the adverb 상당히 with the adnominal 상당한; you need 상당한 directly before a noun (상당한 노력), not 상당히.

entries.nuance: 제법 means 'fairly' but with the special nuance that something turned out better or more than you expected, often with a touch of admiration. Telling someone 제법 잘하네요 is a compliment, while a flat 잘하네요 is more neutral. Because it implies surprise, avoid it about things you always expected to be good — there it can sound faintly condescending.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제법 toward a clearly skilled senior or expert, where the 'surprisingly good' nuance can feel patronizing.
Treating it as a plain synonym for 아주; 제법 specifically signals 'more than expected,' not just a high degree.

entries.nuance: 다소 means 'somewhat / a little' but belongs to formal written and broadcast Korean, so you see it in notices, weather reports, and customer messages rather than chat with friends. It softens a statement politely, much like English 'somewhat,' and pairs often with mildly negative words (지연, 부족, 아쉽다). In casual speech Koreans say 좀 or 약간 instead, so reserve 다소 for polished contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다소 in casual conversation with friends, where it sounds oddly stiff — use 좀 instead.
Pairing it with very strong words; 다소 implies a small-to-moderate degree, so 다소 엄청 is contradictory.

entries.nuance: 살짝 means 'slightly' but with a light, gentle, often cute feeling, used for small actions, mild tastes, and softened emotions. It is extremely common in casual speech and cooking, where it suggests doing something briefly or to a small degree. Compared with the neutral 약간, 살짝 feels more vivid and conversational, almost like 'just a touch.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Forgetting it also modifies actions (살짝 만지다 = touch lightly), not just adjectives — it is not purely a 'somewhat' word.

entries.explanation: 도무지 (domuji) means "(not) at all, simply (can't)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도무지 모르겠어요 ("I simply have no idea"). entries.nuance: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and must be used with a negative, expressing total impossibility plus a feeling of frustration. It is close to 도저히 but leans slightly more toward 'I cannot grasp/understand,' often about confusion. Because it demands negation, it never appears in positive sentences — 도무지 좋아요 is impossible.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도무지 in a positive sentence; it only works with negation (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다).
Confusing it with 도대체 (what on earth); 도대체 questions, while 도무지 emphasizes inability.

entries.shortExplanation: 훨씬 means "much, far (more) — comparative" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "much, far (more) — comparative" is 훨씬 (hwolssin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 훨씬 더 좋아요 ("It's much better"). Watch the particle attached to 훨씬 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 훨씬 더 좋아요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 훨씬.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Almost always used with comparisons; often before 더
Stresses a big gap between two things
버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 = much faster than the bus
나아요 = better; common when comparing conditions

examples.en: The subway is much faster than a taxi.
examples.note: Classic A보다 B 훨씬 comparison structure

examples.en: After taking the medicine, I feel much better.
examples.note: 괜찮아지다 = to get better; comparing before/after

examples.ko: 이 집이 전에 살던 곳보다 훨씬 넓어요.
examples.romanization: i jibi jeone saldeon gotboda hwolssin neolbeoyo.
examples.en: This place is far more spacious than where I lived before.

entries.nuance: 훨씬 is the go-to word for emphasizing a large gap in comparisons, equivalent to 'much/far more.' It pairs naturally with 더 and with the 보다 comparative structure, and it implies the difference is significant, not slight. Unlike plain intensifiers, 훨씬 almost always needs something to compare against, even if that comparison is just implied by context.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 훨씬 with no comparison at all; saying 훨씬 좋아요 out of nowhere sounds incomplete — there must be an implied 'than X.'
Replacing 아주/너무 with 훨씬 for a simple high degree; 훨씬 is specifically comparative, not a general 'very.'

entries.explanation: 되게 (doege) = "really, so (casual spoken)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 되게 맛있어요 ("It's so good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 되게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 되게 맛있어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 되게.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Super common in casual speech, like spoken 'really'
Everyday complaint about distance or effort
Mainly spoken; in writing people prefer 정말/아주

examples.ko: 여기 분위기 되게 좋다, 자주 오자.
examples.romanization: yeogi bunwigi doege jota, jaju oja.
examples.en: This place has a really nice vibe, let's come often.
That movie was so fun, I recommend it.
The roads are really jammed today.
examples.note: 막히다 = to be congested; everyday gripe

entries.nuance: 되게 is a very common casual intensifier meaning 'really/so,' almost exclusively used in spoken Korean among friends and peers. It feels lively and natural in conversation but looks out of place in formal writing or business emails, where 아주 or 정말 fit better. Younger people use it constantly, so recognizing 되게 is key to following everyday speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 되게 in formal documents or emails, where it sounds too casual — use 정말/아주 instead.
Spelling it 됬게 or 돼게; the correct form is 되게.

entries.explanation: 엄청 (eomcheong) means "super, a ton, tremendously". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 엄청 많아요 ("There's a ton"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 엄청 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Strong, casual; great for amounts and intensity
Common spoken intensifier among all ages
Adjective form: 효과가 엄청나요 = the effect is huge

examples.en: It's the weekend so the mart is super crowded.

examples.ko: 이번 시험 공부를 엄청 했는데 떨려요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheom gongbureul eomcheong haenneunde tteollyeoyo.
examples.en: I studied a ton for this exam but I'm nervous.
The delivery came incredibly fast.
examples.note: Pairs with 빨리; common food-delivery comment

entries.nuance: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' stressing a large amount or high intensity. It is slightly more colloquial than 굉장히 and is extremely frequent in everyday speech and texting. It works for quantity (엄청 많다) and intensity (엄청 덥다) alike, and the related 엄청나다 lets you use it as a full adjective.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 엄청 in formal writing where it reads as too casual; choose 매우/대단히 there.
Saying 엄청 with tiny degrees; like other strong intensifiers it implies a genuinely large amount, not 'a little.'

entries.explanation: "even more, a level more" is 한층 (hancheung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한층 더 좋아졌어요 ("It's gotten even better"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Often paired with 더; implies stepping up a level
Common in product or service descriptions
Formal-ish, used for improvement and progress

examples.en: After updating the app, it became even more convenient.
examples.note: Natural when reviewing an app or service

examples.ko: 연습을 꾸준히 했더니 실력이 한층 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: yeonseubeul kkujunhi haetdeoni sillyeogi hancheung neureosseoyo.

examples.note: 한층 stresses a clear step up

examples.en: Now that it's autumn, the foliage is even more beautiful.
examples.note: 단풍 = autumn leaves; slightly literary tone

entries.nuance: 한층 means 'even more / a level higher,' picturing improvement as climbing one more step from an already-good state. It is a bit more polished and written-sounding than 더, so it fits reviews, descriptions, and thoughtful speech. It almost always implies a positive upgrade and frequently appears as 한층 더 for extra emphasis.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 한층 for a first-time degree with no prior baseline; it implies going 'one level further' from an existing state.
Treating it as fully casual; in chatty 반말 a simple 더 or 훨씬 usually sounds more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 부쩍 means "markedly, noticeably (more)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부쩍 (bujjeok) = "markedly, noticeably (more)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부쩍 늘었어요 ("It increased noticeably") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부쩍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 부쩍 늘었어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 부쩍.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Implies a sudden, visible rise over a short time
Notes a marked change in someone's appearance
부쩍 자주 보이네요 = I see you around a lot more lately

examples.en: I've been noticeably more tired lately, so I sleep early.
examples.note: 요즘 + 부쩍 is a very natural pairing

examples.ko: 환절기라 그런지 감기 환자가 부쩍 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira geureonji gamgi hwanjaga bujjeong neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe because of the season change, cold patients have increased markedly.

examples.ko: 조카가 못 본 사이에 부쩍 컸어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga mot bon saie bujjeok keosseoyo.
examples.en: My niece/nephew has grown so much since I last saw them.
examples.note: 못 본 사이에 = while I wasn't seeing them

entries.nuance: 부쩍 describes a marked, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short period, often 'suddenly a lot more.' It pairs most naturally with verbs of change like 늘다, 줄다, 커지다, 추워지다, and with 요즘 to mean 'lately, noticeably.' Unlike steady-change words such as 점점, 부쩍 stresses that the jump is striking and easy to notice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 부쩍 with static adjectives (부쩍 예쁘다 sounds odd); it wants verbs of change like 예뻐졌다.
Confusing it with the gradual 점점/차츰; 부쩍 implies a sharp, noticeable jump, not slow change.

entries.nuance: 찝찝하다 is that nagging, not-quite-resolved discomfort — a conversation that ended badly, a decision you're not sure about, or even a slightly unclean feeling. It's milder than guilt or anxiety; it's the residue that sticks with you. Very common in casual speech; the spelling 찜찜하다 is also accepted but 찝찝하다 is more frequent online.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse it with 불안하다 (anxious about the future) — 찝찝하다 is about an unresolved feeling lingering from something that already happened.
Avoid it in formal writing or business contexts; it reads as casual and a little slangy.

entries.nuance: 벅차다 has two flavors: the heart-swelling kind (overcome with joy, pride, gratitude) and the practical kind (a workload or responsibility that's too much for you). With 가슴이 it's almost always the emotional, positive sense. Listen to context to tell which one a speaker means.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't assume 벅차다 is always positive — '일이 벅차다' means a task is overwhelming in a stressful, can't-cope way.
It is not the same as 바쁘다 (busy); 벅차다 implies the amount exceeds your capacity, not just that you have a lot to do.

entries.nuance: 허전하다 is the quiet emptiness left behind when something or someone is missing — a friend moves away, a routine ends, or you just feel a vague void. It's gentler and more wistful than 외롭다 (lonely); it can attach to a place, a body part (느낌), or your heart. Often paired with 마음이 or 뭔가.

entries.nuance: 홀가분하다 is the lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a big project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use it for momentary relief — 홀가분하다 implies a lasting burden has finally been set down for good.
It's close to 후련하다 but not identical: 후련하다 = the cathartic release; 홀가분하다 = the resulting freedom and lightness.

Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서먹해요 ("things feel awkward (between us)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서먹하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; describes the relationship's distance
attributive form; 사이 = the relationship between people
adverb form, e.g. 서먹하게 인사하다 to greet stiffly

examples.en: Meeting after so long, things feel a little awkward.
examples.note: distance that builds up after time apart

examples.en: We're on the same team, but it's still awkward between us.
The two of them grew distant after the fight.

entries.nuance: 서먹하다 describes the awkward, not-yet-comfortable distance between people who aren't close — new coworkers, friends after a long gap, or two people after an argument. It's about interpersonal coolness, not personal embarrassment. The reduplicated 서먹서먹하다 is very common and a touch more vivid.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use it for self-conscious embarrassment — that's 어색하다/멋쩍다. 서먹하다 is specifically the distance between two parties.
It needs a relationship context; you can't be 서먹하다 by yourself — it's always 'between' people (둘이 서먹하다).
