entries.shortExplanation: 못마땅하다 means "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" is 못마땅하다 (monmattanghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 못마땅해요 ("I'm displeased / I disapprove"). Watch the particle attached to 못마땅하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 못마땅해요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 못마땅하다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; expresses disapproval of something
attributive form; very common with 표정/얼굴/눈빛
adverb form, e.g. 못마땅하게 쳐다보다 to glare disapprovingly

examples.en: The manager was displeased with my report.
examples.note: use 못마땅해하다 when describing someone else's displeasure

examples.en: What are you so unhappy about?
examples.note: casual; said when someone is clearly grumbling

examples.en: Mom had a disapproving look about my decision.

entries.nuance: 못마땅하다 means something doesn't sit right with you — you disapprove or find it unsatisfactory. It's often shown through facial expression (못마땅한 표정) rather than stated outright, and frequently involves a senior person reacting to a junior's choices. When describing a third person's feeling, use 못마땅해하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
When the displeased one is someone else, you must say 못마땅해하다 — Korean adjectives of feeling need -아/어하다 for third-person description.
Don't confuse it with 화나다 (angry); 못마땅하다 is quieter disapproval or dissatisfaction, not active anger.

examples.note: noticing someone else's sour mood; -아/어 보이다 = looks

examples.en: That tone rubbed me the wrong way.
examples.note: past tense; reacting to something mildly offensive

entries.nuance: 언짢다 describes being in a displeased, slightly offended, sour mood — the way you feel when something rubs you wrong but you're not full-on angry. It's a notch more personal and mood-focused than 못마땅하다, and it appears constantly in polite apologies ('기분 언짢으셨다면'). Remember the silent ㄶ batchim in pronunciation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write it 언잖다 — the correct spelling is 언짢다 with ㄶ, even though the ㅎ is not clearly pronounced.
It's milder than 화나다; use 언짢다 for a soured mood or mild offense, not for real anger.

entries.explanation: 흐뭇하다 (heumutada) means "warmly pleased; contented (often watching others)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 흐뭇해요 ("I feel warmly pleased"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 흐뭇하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.en: Watching the kids play, I feel so warm inside.
examples.note: the classic context: contentment watching others

examples.en: My junior has grown so capable — it makes me proud and happy.
examples.note: warm pride at someone else's growth

examples.en: He gave a contented smile.
examples.note: describing the gentle smile this feeling produces

entries.nuance: 흐뭇하다 is a warm, gentle contentment — the soft satisfaction of watching something turn out well, especially others doing well (kids playing, a junior succeeding). It's tender and a little proud, not excited or thrilled. It pairs naturally with 미소 (smile) and 바라보다 (look on), since it's often a feeling you wear on your face.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use it for your own exciting achievements — 흐뭇하다 is calm, warm satisfaction, often directed at others or at a pleasing outcome.
When describing someone else's contentment, use 흐뭇해하다 (e.g. 부모님이 흐뭇해하셨어요).

examples.en: Reading my parents' letter, I got all choked up.

examples.note: casual ending; that nose-tingling pre-tears feeling

entries.nuance: 뭉클하다 is the sudden lump-in-your-throat, heart-swelling feeling of being deeply moved — a heartfelt letter, a reunion, a touching scene. It's warmer and more tender than just 감동하다 (to be impressed/moved); 뭉클 captures the physical welling-up sensation. Pair it with 가슴이 or the very evocative 코끝이.

Don't use it for intellectual admiration — 뭉클하다 is the emotional, almost-teary physical reaction, not 'impressive'.
It describes a momentary surge, not a lasting state; you feel 뭉클하다 in a touching instant, then it passes.

entries.explanation: 멋쩍다 (meotjjeokda) = "self-conscious; sheepish; awkwardly embarrassed". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 멋쩍어요 ("I feel sheepish/awkward") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 멋쩍다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. entries.nuance: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or stuck with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. Don't spell it 멋적다 — the standard spelling is 멋쩍다.
It's about your own sheepishness, unlike 서먹하다 which is the distance between two people; don't swap them.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 안방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 안 (inner) + 방 (room); the biggest/main bedroom, usually for the couple or whoever leads the household
location marker 에 for 'where something is'
the en-suite bathroom attached to 안방, a big selling point in Korean apartments
common when roommates or family decide who gets 안방

examples.ko: 저는 안방 쓰고, 동생은 작은방 써요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun anbang sseugo, dongsaengeun jageunbang sseoyo.
examples.en: I use the master bedroom and my younger sibling uses the small room.
examples.note: 작은방 (small room) is the natural pair word for 안방

examples.en: It's convenient because the master bedroom has an attached bathroom.
examples.note: 딸려 있다 = 'comes attached'; very common phrase in apartment listings

examples.ko: 집 보러 갔는데 안방이 생각보다 넓더라고요.
examples.romanization: jip boreo ganneunde anbangi saenggakboda neolbdeoragoyo.
examples.en: I went to see the place and the master bedroom was bigger than I expected.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a personal observation; natural when describing a viewing

entries.nuance: 안방 isn't just any large room, it's culturally the 'main' bedroom of the home, traditionally where the head of the household sleeps. When flat-hunting or splitting rooms with a roommate, 안방 vs 작은방 is the standard way Koreans divide bedrooms, and 안방 usually has the en-suite bathroom.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling any bedroom 안방. Only the main/largest one is 안방; the others are 작은방 or just 방.
Confusing 안방 with 거실 (living room). 안방 is a private bedroom, not the shared living area.

usagePhrases.en: the washing machine is in the utility room
usagePhrases.note: the washer is almost always here, not in a bathroom
it gets cluttered fast, so cleaning it is a real chore

examples.en: I keep the washing machine and the kimchi fridge in the utility room.
examples.note: 김치냉장고 in the 다용도실 is extremely typical of Korean homes

examples.ko: 다용도실에 짐을 너무 쌓아 놔서 발 디딜 데가 없어요.
examples.romanization: dayongdosire jimeul neomu ssaa nwaseo bal didil dega eopseoyo.
examples.en: I've piled up so much stuff in the utility room that there's no room to step.
examples.note: 발 디딜 데가 없다 = idiom for 'no space to step', very natural here

examples.ko: 이 집은 다용도실이 따로 있어서 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: i jibeun dayongdosiri ttaro isseoseo maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: I like this place because it has a separate utility room.
examples.note: 다용도실이 따로 있다 is a common plus point when choosing an apartment

entries.nuance: Almost every Korean apartment (아파트) has a 다용도실, a small enclosed space off the kitchen, often behind the 베란다, where the washing machine, kimchi fridge, cleaning supplies, and recycling live. Listings proudly mention it. If you live here, you'll use this word constantly when talking about laundry or storage.

Mixing up 다용도실 (utility room) with 창고 (storage/warehouse). 다용도실 is an active work/storage space inside the home.

entries.explanation: 신발장 (sinbaljang) = "shoe cabinet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신발장 ("shoe cabinet") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신발장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 신발장. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 신발장.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 신발 (shoes) + 장 (cabinet); the built-in cabinet at the entrance where you store shoes

usagePhrases.en: to put into the shoe cabinet
usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = to put in; what you do after taking your shoes off
a constant complaint, especially for people with many shoes
정리 = tidying; a frequent small chore at the 현관

examples.en: Please take off your shoes and put them in the shoe cabinet.
examples.note: Said to guests; taking shoes off indoors is mandatory in Korean homes

examples.ko: 신발장이 꽉 차서 새 운동화 둘 데가 없어요.
examples.romanization: sinbaljangi kkwak chaseo sae undonghwa dul dega eopseoyo.
examples.en: The shoe cabinet is full, so there's nowhere to put my new sneakers.
examples.note: 꽉 차다 = to be packed full; very natural daily speech

examples.ko: 택배는 신발장 위에 올려 두시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: taekbaeneun sinbaljang wie ollyeo dusimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just leave the delivery on top of the shoe cabinet.
examples.note: Common instruction to a delivery driver; 위에 올려 두다 = leave on top

entries.nuance: The 신발장 sits right at the 현관 (entryway) and is part of daily ritual: shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. Most apartments have a built-in one. It's also a handy surface, people often drop keys, masks, or deliveries on top of it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 신발 박스 or 신발 상자 (a shoe box). The furniture piece is 신발장.
Forgetting the shoe-removal rule. You don't just walk in, you put shoes in the 신발장 first.

usagePhrases.note: a single flat board mounted on a wall or inside a cabinet for putting things on

usagePhrases.en: to set up on a shelf
usagePhrases.note: 올려 두다 = to place up (and leave); typical action with a shelf
달다 = to mount/install; what you do with a drill or adhesive
벽 (wall) + 선반; popular in small apartments to save floor space

examples.en: Just set the books on the shelf.
examples.note: 그냥 ('just') softens the instruction, very natural casual tone

examples.ko: 화장실에 선반 하나 달았더니 훨씬 깔끔해졌어요.
examples.romanization: hwajangsire seonban hana daratdeoni hwolssin kkalkkeumhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After I put up one shelf in the bathroom, it got much tidier.
examples.note: -았더니 shows result of an action; common when describing a small home upgrade

examples.ko: 선반이 높아서 발판 없이는 손이 안 닿아요.
examples.romanization: seonbani nopaseo balpan eopsineun soni an daayo.
examples.en: The shelf is so high I can't reach it without a step stool.
examples.note: 손이 안 닿다 = can't reach; everyday expression

entries.nuance: 선반 is a single shelf board, not a whole bookcase (that's 책장). In tiny Korean officetels and one-rooms, wall-mounted 선반 are a go-to space saver, sold cheaply at 다이소 and IKEA. You'll hear it for kitchen, bathroom, and entryway storage alike.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 선반 for a full bookshelf unit. A standing bookcase is 책장; 선반 is just one shelf/ledge.
Confusing 선반 (shelf) with 서랍 (drawer). A 선반 is open; a 서랍 slides out.

usagePhrases.en: on top of the TV stand
usagePhrases.note: where the TV and remote usually go
a common furniture purchase when moving in

usagePhrases.en: the drawer of the TV stand
usagePhrases.note: 거실장 often has drawers for remotes and cables

examples.en: I put the TV on top of the living-room cabinet.
examples.note: 티비 (casual for TV) + 올려놓다 = to set on top; everyday phrasing

examples.en: When I moved, I got myself a new TV stand.
examples.note: 장만하다 = to acquire/get (a bigger purchase); natural for furniture

examples.ko: 리모컨은 거실장 서랍 안에 있을 거예요.
examples.romanization: rimokeoneun geosiljang seorap ane isseul geoyeyo.
examples.en: The remote is probably in the drawer of the TV stand.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a guess; a very real daily situation

entries.nuance: 거실장 is the low, wide cabinet that anchors a Korean living room, the TV goes on top and remotes, cables, and odds-and-ends hide in its drawers and doors. Confusing 거실장 with 거실 (the living room itself). 거실장 is the furniture; 거실 is the room.

entries.nuance: 방석 is the flat sit-on cushion central to Korea's floor-sitting culture, you'll see stacks of them for guests, at floor-seating restaurants, and on hard dining chairs. entries.explanation: 장염 (jangyeom) means "enteritis, stomach flu (gut infection/inflammation)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 장염에 걸리다 ("to get enteritis / a stomach bug"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 장염 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. entries.nuance: 장염은 장에 염증이 생겨 복통·구토·설사가 함께 오는 흔한 병으로, 영어의 'stomach flu'에 가깝다. 병이라서 '장염이 나다'가 아니라 '장염에 걸리다'로 쓰는 것이 자연스럽다. 단순히 체한 '배탈'보다 더 심하고 며칠 가는 상태를 가리키며, 병원에서는 '급성 장염'이라는 진단명을 자주 듣는다.

entries.shortExplanation: 비염 means "rhinitis (chronic stuffy/runny nose, often allergic)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rhinitis (chronic stuffy/runny nose, often allergic)" is 비염 (biyeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비염이 있다 ("to have rhinitis"). Watch the particle attached to 비염 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. examples.en: I have allergic rhinitis, so my nose gets stuffy every spring.

examples.en: My grandmother has diabetes, so she can't eat sweets.

entries.nuance: 골절은 뼈가 부러지거나 금이 간 것을 가리키는 한자어로, 병원·정형외과에서는 '골절'을, 일상 대화에서는 '뼈가 부러지다'를 더 많이 쓴다. '골절이 되다, 골절상을 입다'처럼 표현하며 치료로 '깁스를 하다'가 자주 따라온다. 단순히 삐끗한 '염좌'와 달리 뼈 자체가 손상된 더 심한 상태다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
염좌(삔 것)와 혼동하는 것 — 골절은 뼈가 부러진 것, 염좌는 인대·근육이 늘어나거나 삔 것이라 다르다.
'골절을 하다'라고 하는 것 — '골절이 되다, 뼈가 부러지다, 골절상을 입다'가 자연스럽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 충치 means "cavity, tooth decay" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 충치 (chungchi) means "cavity, tooth decay". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 충치가 생기다 ("to get a cavity"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 충치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

examples.romanization: dan geol mani meogeotdeoni chungchiga saenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ate a lot of sweets and got a cavity.

examples.ko: 충치 때문에 찬물을 마실 때 이가 시려요.
examples.romanization: chungchi ttaemune chanmureul masil ttae iga siryeoyo.
examples.en: Because of the cavity, my tooth aches when I drink cold water.

examples.romanization: oneul chigwaeseo chungchi du gaereul ttaewosseoyo.
examples.en: I got two cavities filled at the dentist today.

entries.nuance: 충치는 이가 썩어 구멍이 생기는 것으로, 치과에서 가장 자주 쓰는 단어다. '충치가 생기다/있다'로 상태를 말하고, 치료는 구어로 '충치를 때우다'(메우다)라고 아주 흔하게 표현한다. 시린 증상은 '이가 시리다', 아픈 것은 '이가 아프다'로 함께 쓰면 치과에서 자연스럽게 통한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

치료를 '충치를 고치다'로만 쓰는 것 — 구어에서는 '충치를 때우다'가 훨씬 자연스럽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 염좌 means "sprain (twisted/strained ligament)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sprain (twisted/strained ligament)" is 염좌 (yeomjwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 발목 염좌 ("ankle sprain"). Watch the particle attached to 염좌 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 발목 염좌. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 염좌.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.en: I twisted my ankle playing soccer, and the hospital said it's a sprain.
It's not a fracture, just a simple sprain, so I'm relieved.

examples.romanization: yeomjwail ttaen eoreumjjimjillo bugireul ppaeneun ge joayo.
examples.en: For a sprain, it's good to reduce swelling with an ice pack.

entries.nuance: 염좌는 인대나 근육이 삐거나 늘어난 것을 가리키는 한자어로, 진단서·정형외과에서는 '발목 염좌'처럼 쓰지만 일상 대화에서는 '발목을 삐다'를 훨씬 많이 쓴다. 뼈가 부러진 '골절'보다 가벼운 부상이라 '단순 염좌'라고 안심하듯 말하기도 한다. 치료는 보통 '부기를 빼다, 얼음찜질을 하다'와 함께 표현한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
골절과 혼동하는 것 — 염좌는 인대·근육이 삔 것, 골절은 뼈가 부러진 것이라 심각도와 부위가 다르다.

entries.shortExplanation: 방광염 means "cystitis, bladder infection (a common UTI)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 방광염 (banggwangyeom) = "cystitis, bladder infection (a common UTI)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방광염에 걸리다 ("to get a bladder infection") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방광염, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 방광염에 걸리다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 방광염.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 오줌이 자주 마렵고 소변볼 때 따가워서 병원 갔더니 방광염이래요.
examples.romanization: ojumi jaju maryeopgo sobyeonbol ttae ttagawoseo byeongwon gatdeoni banggwangyeomiraeyo.
examples.en: I kept needing to pee and it stung, so I went to the doctor and it's cystitis.

examples.ko: 물을 적게 마시고 참았더니 방광염에 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: mureul jeokge masigo chamatdeoni banggwangyeome geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't drink enough water and held it in, so I got a bladder infection.

examples.ko: 방광염은 물을 많이 마시고 항생제를 먹으면 금방 나아요.
examples.romanization: banggwangyeomeun mureul mani masigo hangsaengjereul meogeumyeon geumbang naayo.
examples.en: Cystitis gets better quickly with lots of water and antibiotics.

entries.nuance: 방광염은 방광에 염증·감염이 생겨 소변이 자주 마렵고 소변볼 때 따갑거나 아픈 병으로, 흔히 말하는 요로감염(UTI)의 대표적인 형태다. 특히 물을 적게 마시거나 소변을 오래 참으면 잘 생기고 여성에게 더 흔하다. 병이라 '방광염에 걸리다'로 쓰고, 자주 반복되면 '재발하다'라고 한다. 다소 민망해도 병원에서는 그대로 말하면 정확히 통한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
단순히 '오줌소태'로만 알고 정확한 병명을 못 쓰는 것 — 병원에서는 '방광염'이라고 해야 진단·처방이 명확해진다.
'방광염이 아프다'라고 하는 것 — 병명이라 '방광염에 걸리다, 방광염 때문에 아프다'처럼 써야 자연스럽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 프라이팬 means "frying pan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 프라이팬 (peuraipaen) means "frying pan". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 프라이팬 ("frying pan"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 프라이팬 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday word for a flat pan. '후라이팬' is heard but '프라이팬' is the standard spelling.
Use 에 (location) + a cooking verb like 굽다, 부치다, 볶다.
코팅 = the non-stick coating; people worry about it peeling (벗겨지다).

usagePhrases.en: I'm thinking of buying a frying pan
usagePhrases.note: Counter 개 or just 하나 works when buying one.

examples.en: I put oil in the pan and started with a fried egg.
examples.note: 기름(을) 두르다 = to coat the pan with oil, a set phrase.

examples.ko: 이 프라이팬 코팅 다 벗겨져서 새로 사야 돼요.
examples.romanization: i peuraipaen koting da beotgyeojyeoseo saero saya dwaeyo.
examples.en: The coating on this pan is all peeled off, so I have to buy a new one.

examples.ko: 코팅 프라이팬은 센 불에서 예열하면 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: koting peuraipaeneun sen bureseo yeyeolhamyeon an joayo.
examples.en: It's not good to preheat a non-stick pan on high heat.
examples.note: 센 불 = high heat; common cooking caution.

entries.nuance: 프라이팬은 바닥이 평평한 팬을 가리키고, 깊은 냄비와는 다릅니다. 한국 가정집에서는 대부분 코팅(논스틱) 프라이팬을 쓰기 때문에 '코팅이 벗겨졌다'는 표현을 자주 듣게 됩니다. 1인 가구라면 작은 프라이팬 하나만 있어도 계란프라이나 간단한 볶음 요리는 충분히 할 수 있습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing '후라이팬'; the textbook-standard spelling is '프라이팬'.
Confusing it with 냄비 (a deeper pot) — 프라이팬 is the shallow, flat one for frying.

entries.explanation: "rice scoop / paddle" is 주걱 (jugeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주걱 ("rice paddle/scoop"). Watch the particle attached to 주걱 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 주걱. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 주걱.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: The flat paddle for scooping rice; usually plastic and comes with rice cookers.
밥 + 주걱; the most common full form, used interchangeably with 주걱.

usagePhrases.en: to scoop rice with a paddle
usagePhrases.note: 밥을 푸다 = to dish out rice, the verb that pairs with 주걱.

usagePhrases.en: Can you pass me the rice scoop?
usagePhrases.note: Casual request at the dinner table.

examples.ko: 밥솥에서 밥 좀 주걱으로 떠 줄래?
examples.romanization: bapsoteseo bap jom jugeogeuro tteo jullae?
examples.en: Can you scoop some rice from the cooker with the paddle?
examples.note: (으)로 marks the tool; 뜨다/푸다 both work for serving rice.

examples.ko: 주걱에 물 살짝 묻히면 밥이 안 들러붙어요.
examples.romanization: jugeoge mul saljjang mutimyeon babi an deulleobuteoyo.
examples.en: If you wet the paddle a little, the rice won't stick to it.
examples.note: Practical kitchen tip; 들러붙다 = to stick.

examples.ko: 새 밥솥 사니까 주걱이랑 계량컵이 같이 왔어요.
examples.romanization: sae bapsot sanikka jugeogirang gyeryangkeobi gachi wasseoyo.
examples.en: When I bought a new rice cooker, a paddle and measuring cup came with it.

entries.nuance: 주걱은 밥을 풀 때 쓰는 납작한 도구로, 보통 밥솥을 사면 함께 들어 있습니다. '밥주걱'이라고 풀어서 말해도 똑같은 뜻이고 둘 다 자연스럽습니다. 국이나 찌개를 뜰 때 쓰는 둥근 국자와는 모양과 용도가 완전히 다르니 구분해서 쓰세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 주걱 for soup — for liquids you need 국자, not the flat 주걱.
Pairing it with 담다 only; the natural verb for serving rice is 푸다 or 뜨다.

lesson.canDo: Use 주걱 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 주걱. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 주걱.
Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.
lesson.teacherNote: 주걱 should be taught as a sentence ingredient. The student needs the common frame more than a dictionary definition.
lesson.pronunciationTip: 주걱 is written jugeok. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.shortExplanation: 집게 means "tongs" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 집게 (jipge) = "tongs". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 집게 ("tongs") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 집게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 집게. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 집게.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: General word for tongs; at a BBQ place it's the metal tongs for flipping meat.
집다 (to pick up) is the root verb; 집게 is literally 'the thing that picks up'.
Common at 고깃집; ask 집게 좀 주세요 if yours is dirty.
Same word 집게 also means clothespin — context tells which.

examples.ko: 고기 탈 것 같은데 집게로 좀 뒤집어 주세요.
examples.romanization: gogi tal geot gateunde jipgero jom dwijibeo juseyo.
examples.en: The meat looks like it might burn — please flip it with the tongs.
examples.note: Typical line at a Korean BBQ table.

examples.ko: 집게랑 가위 좀 새 걸로 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: jipgerang gawi jom sae geollo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you give us clean tongs and scissors?
examples.note: 새 거 = a new/clean one; standard request at 고깃집.

examples.ko: 뜨거우니까 손으로 잡지 말고 집게 쓰세요.
examples.romanization: tteugeounikka soneuro japji malgo jipge sseuseyo.
examples.en: It's hot, so use the tongs instead of grabbing it by hand.

entries.nuance: 집게는 한국에서 고기를 구울 때 빠질 수 없는 도구라 식당에서 '집게 주세요'라고 자주 말하게 됩니다. 같은 단어가 빨래를 너는 집게(클립)도 뜻하니 상황으로 구분해야 합니다. 고깃집에서는 보통 집게와 가위(자르는 가위)를 세트로 쓴다는 점도 알아 두면 좋습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling tongs 핀셋 — 핀셋 is tiny tweezers; kitchen/BBQ tongs are 집게.
Forgetting that 집게 also means clothespin, which can cause confusion out of context.

entries.shortExplanation: 수저 means "spoon and chopsticks (set); spoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수저 (sujeo) means "spoon and chopsticks (set); spoon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수저 ("spoon and chopsticks set"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수저 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 수저. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 수저.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Collective word for 숟가락 + 젓가락; also loosely means 'spoon'.

usagePhrases.en: Can you set out the spoons and chopsticks?
usagePhrases.note: 수저(를) 놓다 = to set the table with utensils.
The container on a restaurant table holding 수저; very common at eateries.
A boxed set, common as a gift (e.g., wedding 집들이 gifts).

examples.ko: 밥 먹게 수저 좀 놓아 줘.
examples.romanization: bam meokge sujeo jom noa jwo.
examples.en: Set out the utensils so we can eat.
examples.note: 수저 놓다 is the set phrase for laying the table.

examples.ko: 식당 가면 수저통에서 수저 꺼내서 놓으면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sikdang gamyeon sujeotongeseo sujeo kkeonaeseo noeumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: At restaurants, just take the utensils out of the caddy and set them down.
I got a cutlery set as a housewarming gift.

entries.nuance: 수저는 숟가락과 젓가락을 한꺼번에 가리키는 말이라, 식탁을 차릴 때 '수저 놓아 줘'처럼 매우 자주 씁니다. 한국 식당 테이블에는 보통 '수저통'이 놓여 있어서 직접 꺼내 쓰는 문화가 익숙해야 합니다. 좁은 의미로 그냥 '숟가락'을 뜻하기도 하니 문맥을 보세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 수저 means only chopsticks — it covers the spoon(+chopsticks), not just 젓가락.
Saying 수저를 차리다 — the table is 차리다, but utensils are 놓다.

entries.shortExplanation: 텀블러 means "tumbler / reusable cup" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tumbler / reusable cup" is 텀블러 (teombeulleo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 텀블러 ("reusable tumbler"). Watch the particle attached to 텀블러 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: An insulated reusable cup; carrying one is very common among young Koreans.
Cafés give a discount (텀블러 할인) when you bring one.
Usually a few hundred won off; ask 텀블러 할인 돼요?
보온 = keeps heat; 보냉 = keeps cold.

examples.ko: 텀블러 가져왔는데 여기에 담아 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: teombeulleo gajyeowanneunde yeogie dama jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I brought my tumbler — could you put it in here?
examples.note: Polite café request; 담다 = to pour/put into.

examples.ko: 요즘 카페에서 텀블러 쓰면 할인해 줘요.
examples.romanization: yojeum kapeeseo teombeulleo sseumyeon harinhae jwoyo.
examples.en: These days cafés give a discount if you use a tumbler.

examples.ko: 이 텀블러는 보온이 잘 돼서 아침에 넣은 커피가 점심까지 따뜻해요.
examples.romanization: i teombeulleoneun booni jal dwaeseo achime neoeun keopiga jeomsimkkaji ttatteutaeyo.
examples.en: This tumbler insulates well, so coffee I put in at morning stays warm till lunch.

entries.nuance: 텀블러는 보온·보냉이 되는 휴대용 컵으로, 한국의 2030 세대가 일회용 컵 대신 들고 다니는 필수품처럼 자리 잡았습니다. 카페에서 '텀블러 할인 돼요?'라고 물으면 작은 금액이지만 할인을 받을 수 있어 실용적입니다. 단순한 일회용 컵이나 머그컵과 달리 뚜껑이 있고 들고 다니는 용도라는 점이 핵심입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 컵 for it — 컵 is generic; an insulated carry cup is specifically 텀블러.
Asking 텀블러 있어요? at a café expecting a discount — the phrase is 텀블러 할인 돼요?

entries.explanation: 뚜껑 (ttukkeong) = "lid / cover". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 뚜껑 ("lid, cover, cap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 뚜껑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: Covers pots, containers, bottles — any kind of lid.
덮다 = to cover; the natural pair-verb for 뚜껑.
열다 for opening; 닫다 also works for screw-on caps.
Specify with the noun + 뚜껑 when needed (병뚜껑 = bottle cap).

examples.ko: 국 끓을 때 뚜껑 덮어 놓으면 더 빨리 끓어요.
examples.romanization: guk kkeureul ttae ttukkeong deopeo noeumyeon deo ppalli kkeureoyo.
examples.en: If you keep the lid on while the soup boils, it boils faster.
This side-dish container's lid won't close.
It's hot, so be careful when you take the lid off.

entries.nuance: 뚜껑은 냄비, 반찬통, 병 등 무엇이든 위를 덮는 부분을 가리키는 폭넓은 말입니다. 덮을 때는 '덮다', 열 때는 '열다'를 쓰며, 꽉 잠그는 병뚜껑에는 '닫다/잠그다'도 자연스럽습니다. 어떤 뚜껑인지 분명히 하려면 '냄비 뚜껑', '병뚜껑'처럼 앞에 대상을 붙여 말합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 문 (door) or 마개 indiscriminately — a general lid/cover is 뚜껑.
Saying 뚜껑을 닫다 for a flat pot lid; for resting a lid on top, 덮다 is more natural.

usagePhrases.en: to store away in a container

examples.romanization: nameun banchaneun milpyeyonggie damaseo naengjanggoe neoeo duseyo.

examples.note: 담아서 = and then... ; 넣어 두다 = store away.

examples.ko: 밀폐용기 뚜껑이랑 몸통이 짝이 안 맞아요.

examples.ko: 국물 있는 건 밀폐 잘 되는 통에 담아야 안 새요.
examples.romanization: gungmul inneun geon milpye jal doeneun tonge damaya an saeyo.
examples.en: Soupy food should go in a well-sealing container so it doesn't leak.

entries.nuance: 밀폐용기는 냉장고에 음식을 보관할 때 쓰는 뚜껑 달린 통으로, 일상 대화에서는 '반찬통'이라고 더 자주 부릅니다. '밀폐'는 공기가 새지 않게 꽉 닫힌다는 뜻이라 국물 있는 음식을 옮길 때 특히 중요합니다. 자취하거나 도시락을 싸는 2030 세대에게는 사실상 필수품입니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 앞치마 means "apron" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 앞치마 (apchima) = "apron". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 앞치마 ("apron") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 앞치마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Worn to protect clothes while cooking or cleaning.
두르다 = to wrap around; the idiomatic verb for aprons.
입다 is also commonly heard, though 두르다 is more precise.

examples.en: Before cooking, I put on an apron first.
examples.note: 두르다 conjugates 둘렀어요; 부터 = starting with.

examples.ko: 김치 담글 때 옷에 안 묻게 앞치마 꼭 하세요.
examples.romanization: gimchi damgeul ttae ose an mutge apchima kko kaseyo.
examples.en: When making kimchi, wear an apron so it doesn't get on your clothes.
examples.note: 묻다 = to get smeared on; 앞치마(를) 하다 also works colloquially.

examples.en: I put my phone in the apron pocket.

entries.nuance: 앞치마는 요리하거나 청소할 때 옷이 더러워지지 않게 앞에 두르는 천입니다. 가장 자연스러운 동사는 '두르다'이지만 일상에서는 '입다'나 '하다'도 흔히 씁니다. 특히 김치를 담그거나 기름 튀는 요리를 할 때 옷을 보호하려고 자주 사용합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using only 입다 — the most idiomatic verb for an apron is 두르다.
Confusing 앞치마 with 수건/행주; the apron is worn on the body, not a wiping cloth.

entries.shortExplanation: 숙박 means "lodging, overnight stay" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 숙박 (sukbak) means "lodging, overnight stay". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 숙박 ("lodging / overnight stay"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 숙박 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Formal word for staying overnight somewhere; you'll see it on booking sites and signs.
비 = fee/cost; the price you pay for the night.
하다 verb form; more formal than just 자다 (to sleep).
Standard way to count a trip's length; read as '일박 이일'.

examples.en: Where are you staying?
examples.note: Common question when chatting about a trip; 어디서 = where (at).

examples.en: The lodging is pricier than I expected.
examples.note: -네요 adds a mild 'oh' reaction; natural in conversation.

examples.en: It's the weekend so the rooms are almost all booked.
examples.note: 다 찼어요 = all filled up; 거의 = almost.

entries.nuance: 숙박 is the umbrella term that covers any kind of overnight stay, from a hotel to a guesthouse. It feels official and shows up on reservation apps, receipts, and signs, whereas in casual speech people often just say where they're sleeping (호텔에서 자요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 숙박 (the act of staying) with 숙소 (the place itself).
숙박하다 is for staying the night, not for a daytime visit — use 가다/들르다 for that.

entries.explanation: "guesthouse" is 게스트하우스 (geseuteuhauseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 게스트하우스 ("guesthouse"). Watch the particle attached to 게스트하우스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Budget lodging with shared spaces; very popular with young travelers in Korea.
Common shortened form among 20-30s; 게스트하우스 → 게하.
A shared room with bunk beds, the cheapest option at a guesthouse.
Read '일인실'; a private room if you don't want a shared dorm.

examples.ko: 저는 여행할 때 보통 게스트하우스에 묵어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun yeohaenghal ttae botong geseuteuhauseue mugeoyo.
examples.en: When I travel I usually stay at a guesthouse.
examples.note: 묵다 = to stay/lodge, slightly more formal than 자다.

examples.en: I made a lot of friends at the guesthouse.
examples.note: 사귀다 = to make (friends); 게하 is the casual short form.

examples.en: This guesthouse has free breakfast.
examples.note: 조식 = breakfast (lodging context); 무료 = free of charge.

entries.nuance: 게스트하우스 are a staple of cheap travel in Korea, especially in Jeju and Busan, and they're known as places to meet other travelers at shared dinners or parties. Young people almost always shorten it to 게하 in speech and texts, so recognizing the slang is essential.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
게스트하우스 is written as one long loanword — don't split it as '게스트 하우스' in writing.
Don't assume every room is shared; many offer 1인실 or 2인실 private rooms too.

examples.en: If you check out late there's an extra fee.

usagePhrases.note: Busy travel periods like summer vacation and holidays when prices spike.
극 = extreme; the very busiest stretch (e.g., late July to mid-August).
오르다 = to rise; what happens to lodging in 성수기.
꽉 차다 = packed full; rooms sell out in 성수기.

It's peak season so plane tickets are hard to get.
examples.note: 구하다 = to obtain; -기가 힘들다 = is hard to do.

examples.en: It's better to go avoiding peak season.
examples.note: 피하다 = to avoid; -는 게 좋다 = it's good to.

entries.nuance: 성수기 covers the high-demand travel windows — summer (여름휴가), Chuseok, Seollal, and ski season — when lodging and flights cost far more and sell out fast. Residents plan around it constantly, often saying they want to 성수기를 피하다 (avoid peak season) to save money and crowds.

성수기 is the opposite of 비수기 (off-season) — don't mix them up.

야경 is specifically the scene at night; daytime scenery is just 경치 or 전망.
Don't confuse 야경 (night view) with 야간 (nighttime, the time period).

entries.shortExplanation: 일출 means "sunrise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sunrise" is 일출 (ilchul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일출 ("sunrise"). Watch the particle attached to 일출 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: The sun coming up; a big deal especially on New Year's Day.
Pure-Korean synonym for 일출; 해돋이 보러 가다 is very common.
Places like 정동진, 호미곶 known for 일출.
Watching the first sunrise of the year is a popular tradition.

examples.ko: 새해 첫날 일출 보러 동해에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: saehae cheonnal ilchul boreo donghaee gasseoyo.
examples.en: We went to the East Sea to see the New Year's sunrise.
examples.note: 첫날 = first day; 동해 = East Sea.

examples.en: I got up at 5 a.m. to watch the sunrise.
It was cloudy so we couldn't see the sunrise.
examples.note: 구름이 끼다 = to get cloudy; 못 봤어요 = couldn't see.

entries.nuance: 일출 (or the native 해돋이) is sunrise, and watching it carries real cultural weight — crowds head to the east coast to see the 새해 일출 (first sunrise of the year) and make wishes. It pairs with early-morning effort words like 새벽 and 일어나다, since catching it means getting up before dawn.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
일출 is the opposite of 일몰 (sunset) — keep the pair straight.
Both 일출 and 해돋이 mean sunrise; the native 해돋이 sounds warmer and is just as common in speech.

examples.note: -기로 유명하다 = famous for; 서해 = West Sea.

examples.note: 에 맞춰서 = timed to; 도착하다 = to arrive.

examples.ko: 노을이 너무 예뻐서 사진을 계속 찍었어요.
examples.romanization: noeuri neomu yeppeoseo sajineul gyesok jjigeosseoyo.
examples.en: The sunset glow was so pretty I kept taking photos.

entries.nuance: 일몰 is sunset, the counterpart to 일출, and Korea's west coast (서해) is the classic place to watch it sink into the sea. In everyday speech people often talk about the 노을 (the colorful afterglow) rather than the technical 일몰, especially when sharing photos of a pretty evening sky.

일몰 is sunset, not sunrise — its pair is 일출.

entries.nuance: 계곡 means both the V-shaped ravine and, in everyday speech, the cold stream inside it. Koreans treat 계곡 as the classic budget summer getaway, so you'll hear it constantly from June to August. It's distinct from 강 (a wide river); a 계곡 is the narrow, rocky mountain version.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 계곡 with 강 — 강 is a broad river, 계곡 is the rocky mountain stream/ravine.
Avoid spelling it 게곡; the correct vowel is ㅖ → 계곡.

entries.nuance: 폭포 is a neutral, everyday word for any waterfall, from a small drop in a 계곡 to a famous tourist one. entries.shortExplanation: 동굴 means "cave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동굴 (donggul) = "cave". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 동굴 ("cave") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동굴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 동굴. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 동굴.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Natural rock cave; also used figuratively for a cozy dark hideout
탐험 = exploration; common for tourist caves
안 = inside; 동굴 안은 시원해요 etc.
에 + 들어가다 for entering an enclosed space

examples.en: Inside the cave it's really cool even in summer.
examples.note: 안은 = inside (topic); caves stay cold year-round

examples.en: I checked out a lava cave in Jeju.
examples.note: 용암 = lava; Jeju's lava tubes are famous tourist spots

examples.en: The cave is dark, so you need a flashlight.

entries.nuance: 동굴 is the standard word for a natural cave, including Korea's famous limestone and Jeju lava caves that are popular day-trip spots. Locals also use it figuratively, as in 동굴 같은 방 (a cave-like room) for a dark cozy space. For tourism it's almost always paired with 구경하다 (to look around) or 탐험 (exploration).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 동굴, not 굴 alone, in most travel contexts — plain 굴 also means 'oyster,' which causes confusion.
For entering, say 동굴에 들어가다 (에), not 동굴로 들어가다 unless you mean direction/route.

lesson.canDo: Use 동굴 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 동굴. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 동굴.

lesson.pronunciationTip: 동굴 is written donggul. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.explanation: 절벽 (jeolbyeok) means "cliff". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 절벽 ("cliff"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 절벽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sheer rock face; also figurative for a dead end / crisis
끝 = edge/end; 절벽 끝에 서다 = stand at the edge
위 = top; views are described from 절벽 위
에서 marks the source of the fall

examples.ko: 절벽 위에서 보는 바다 풍경이 진짜 멋있어요.
examples.romanization: jeolbyeok wieseo boneun bada punggyeongi jinjja meosisseoyo.
examples.en: The ocean view from atop the cliff is really gorgeous.
examples.note: 풍경 = scenery; 위에서 = from on top

examples.ko: 위험하니까 절벽 끝에 너무 가까이 가지 마세요.
examples.romanization: wiheomhanikka jeolbyeok kkeute neomu gakkai gaji maseyo.
examples.en: It's dangerous, so don't go too close to the cliff edge.
examples.note: 가까이 = closely; safety warning at viewpoints

examples.en: These coastal cliffs are a famous photo spot.

entries.nuance: 절벽 is a steep cliff or sheer rock face, common along Korea's coastlines and hiking ridges where signs warn you to stay back. It also has a strong figurative use — 절벽 끝에 몰리다 means to be pushed to the brink. In travel talk it usually appears with 해안 (coastal) or as a scenic 명소.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 절벽 with 언덕 — 언덕 is a gentle hill, 절벽 is a vertical drop.
Spell it 절벽 (ㄹ batchim), not 절뼉 or 절벅.

entries.explanation: "tidal flat, mudflat" is 갯벌 (gaetbeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갯벌 ("tidal flat / mudflat"). Watch the particle attached to 갯벌 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: Coastal mud exposed at low tide; a west-coast specialty
체험 = hands-on experience; popular family activity

usagePhrases.en: dig for clams in the mudflat
usagePhrases.note: 캐다 = to dig up; classic mudflat activity
드러나다 = to be revealed, at low tide

examples.ko: 서해 갯벌에서 조개 캐는 체험을 했어요.
examples.romanization: seohae gaetbeoreseo jogae kaeneun cheheomeul haesseoyo.
examples.en: We did a clam-digging experience on the West Sea mudflats.
examples.note: 서해 = West Sea; signature west-coast activity

examples.en: At low tide the mudflat gets fully exposed.
examples.note: 썰물 = low tide; 쫙 = mimetic for spreading wide

examples.en: Mudflats are slippery, so wear rubber boots.

entries.nuance: 갯벌 is the muddy tidal flat exposed at low tide, a defining feature of Korea's West and South coasts and a popular hands-on 체험 for families and tourists. It's tied to tides, so you'll hear it with 썰물 (low tide) and activities like 조개 캐기 (clam digging). Korea's 갯벌 are even UNESCO-listed, so locals are proud of them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pronounce/spell it 갯벌 (sai-siot ㅅ batchim), not 개벌 or 갯펄 in standard writing.
갯벌 only exists at low tide spots — don't use it for a regular sandy 해변 (beach).

usagePhrases.note: Coastal light tower; a very common seaside photo landmark
Ports often have a red and a white one as a pair

examples.ko: 바닷가 등대 앞에서 사진 한 장 찍었어요.
examples.romanization: badatga deungdae apeseo sajin han jang jjigeosseoyo.
examples.en: I took a photo in front of the seaside lighthouse.
At night the lighthouse beam is visible from far away.
examples.note: 멀리까지 = all the way far; 보이다 = be visible

examples.ko: 빨간 등대 쪽으로 산책하면 노을이 예뻐요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan deungdae jjogeuro sanchaekamyeon noeuri yeppeoyo.
examples.en: If you stroll toward the red lighthouse, the sunset is pretty.

entries.nuance: 등대 is a lighthouse, and in Korea harbor breakwaters famously have a 빨간 등대 (red) and 하얀 등대 (white) marking the channel. They're prime spots for seaside walks, sunset photos, and dates, so the word comes up in casual coastal-trip talk. It also carries a warm figurative sense of a guiding light.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 등대 (lighthouse) with 등 (a lamp/light) or 등산 (hiking) — different words.
Say 등대 앞 / 등대 쪽 for location, not 등대에서 만나자 unless you literally mean meeting at its base.

entries.explanation: 항구 (hanggu) means "harbor, port". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 항구 ("harbor / port"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 항구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Where boats dock; think Busan, Sokcho, Tongyeong
도시 = city; Busan is the classic example

usagePhrases.en: a ship comes into the harbor
a raw-fish place near the harbor
usagePhrases.note: 횟집 = sashimi restaurant; ports = fresh seafood

examples.ko: 부산은 큰 항구 도시라서 회가 정말 신선해요.
examples.romanization: busaneun keun hanggu dosiraseo hoega jeongmal sinseonhaeyo.
examples.en: Busan is a big port city, so the sashimi is really fresh.
In the evening, ships come into the harbor one by one.

examples.ko: 항구 앞에서 갓 잡은 생선을 팔아요.
examples.romanization: hanggu apeseo gat jabeun saengseoneul parayo.
examples.en: They sell freshly caught fish right by the harbor.
examples.note: 갓 잡은 = freshly caught; 팔다 = to sell

entries.nuance: 항구 is a harbor or port, strongly associated with Korea's coastal seafood cities like Busan, Sokcho, and Tongyeong. It implies the whole working waterfront — docks, boats, fish markets — so it's a common travel-destination word, especially for 회 (sashimi) trips. 항구 도시 (port city) is a set phrase locals use with pride.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
항구 is the whole harbor; the specific docking pier is 부두 — keep the two distinct.
Don't confuse 항구 (harbor) with 공항 (airport), which reuses 항 but means something different.

usagePhrases.note: The built structure where ships tie up and load
여객선 = passenger ship; e.g. island ferries

examples.en: We looked at the sea while walking along the pier.

examples.ko: 섬에 가는 배는 저쪽 여객선 부두에서 타요.
examples.romanization: seome ganeun baeneun jeojjok yeogaekseon budueseo tayo.
examples.en: You catch the boat to the island at that passenger pier over there.
examples.note: 여객선 부두 = ferry pier; 타다 = to board

examples.en: A big ship is docked at the wharf.
examples.note: 정박해 있다 = is (in a state of) being docked

entries.nuance: 부두 is the specific built pier or wharf where boats tie up, as opposed to 항구, which is the whole harbor area around it. You'll need it most when catching island ferries (여객선 부두) or strolling a scenic waterfront. It's slightly more concrete and technical than 항구, but still everyday.

entries.explanation: 깜짝 (kkamjjak) means "with a start; suddenly (startled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 깜짝 놀라다 ("to be startled / get a shock"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 깜짝 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 깜짝 놀라다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 깜짝.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.en: to be startled / get a shock
usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing. 깜짝 almost always attaches to 놀라다.
Said out loud when something startles you. Extremely common spoken reaction.
깜짝 + noun means 'surprise ~'. Also 깜짝 파티 (surprise party), 깜짝 방문 (surprise visit).
Doubled form for repeated startling, e.g. from loud noises.

examples.en: You called me from behind so suddenly that I got startled.
examples.note: Classic 깜짝 놀라다 in past tense.

examples.en: You scared me, when did you come in?
I prepared a surprise party for my friend's birthday.

entries.nuance: 깜짝 captures the instant of being startled, not a slow surprise. By far its strongest collocation is 깜짝 놀라다, and the standalone exclamation 깜짝이야! is something you will hear (and say) constantly in Korea. As a noun-modifier it means 'surprise ~' like 깜짝 세일 or 깜짝 방문.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 깜짝 alone as a verb. It is an adverb, so you need a verb after it — 깜짝 놀라다, not 깜짝하다 (which is not a real word).
Confusing it with 갑자기 (suddenly). 갑자기 describes timing of any event; 깜짝 is specifically about the startle reaction.

examples.en: The results come out tomorrow, so I'm nervously on edge.

entries.nuance: 두근두근 is the sound-feeling of a racing heart and works for both happy excitement and anxious nerves. It is warmer and more personal than just saying 긴장돼요; Koreans use it for crushes, big days, and anticipation. You can use it adverbially (두근두근 떨려요) or as 두근두근하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for physical exertion. A pounding heart from running is usually 헐떡거리다 or just 숨차다, not 두근두근.
Forgetting it can be positive. It is not only fear; it heavily implies excitement and 설렘.

usagePhrases.note: The core collocation. Used for stars, clean surfaces, jewelry, eyes.
Adjective-like verb form. 청소했더니 바닥이 반짝반짝해요.
Describes bright, eager eyes, often a child's or someone excited.
Single 반짝 means 'brief flash', as in 반짝 세일 (a short, sudden sale).

examples.en: The stars are twinkling in the night sky.
After finishing the dishes, the bowls are sparkling clean.
The child waits for the present with sparkling eyes.

entries.nuance: 반짝반짝 evokes light bouncing off something repeatedly: stars, polished floors, jewelry, or bright eager eyes. It is the word in the Korean version of 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' (반짝반짝 작은 별). Note the single 반짝 separately means a brief one-off flash, which is why 반짝 세일 means a flash sale.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for steady, non-glittering brightness like a lamp. For plain brightness use 밝다, not 반짝반짝.
Mixing up 반짝 (brief flash / sparkle) with 번쩍 (a sudden big flash, like lightning) — 번쩍 is bigger and more startling.

entries.explanation: 주룩주룩 (jurukjuruk) means "pouring (rain) steadily; streaming down". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비가 주룩주룩 ("rain pouring down"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주룩주룩 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The default collocation. Steady, heavy streaming rain.
비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the full natural phrase.
Also used for tears running down the face.
For sweat streaming, e.g. in summer heat.

examples.ko: 아침부터 비가 주룩주룩 내려서 우산을 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: achimbuteo biga jurukjurung naeryeoseo usaneul chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It's been pouring since morning, so I grabbed an umbrella.

examples.ko: 슬픈 영화를 보다가 눈물이 주룩주룩 흘렀어요.
examples.romanization: seulpeun yeonghwareul bodaga nunmuri jurukjuru keulleosseoyo.
examples.en: While watching the sad movie, tears streamed down.

examples.ko: 한여름이라 조금만 걸어도 땀이 주룩주룩 나요.
examples.romanization: hanyeoreumira jogeumman georeodo ttami jurukjurung nayo.
examples.en: It's midsummer, so I sweat buckets even after walking a little.

entries.nuance: 주룩주룩 describes liquid running down in steady streams — most often heavy rain, but also tears and sweat. It is heavier and more continuous than a light drizzle. For Korea's rainy 장마 season this is the go-to word; you will see it in weather chat and texts constantly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for light rain. Drizzle is 부슬부슬 or 보슬보슬; 주룩주룩 is genuinely heavy, streaming rain.
Pairing it with 오다 awkwardly — 비가 주룩주룩 내리다/와요 are both fine, but 내리다 sounds the most natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 펑펑 means "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" is 펑펑 (peongpeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 펑펑 울다 ("to cry one's eyes out"). Watch the particle attached to 펑펑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 펑펑 울다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 펑펑.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Big, fast snowfall. 눈이 펑펑 와요.
To splurge / blow money. Slightly disapproving.
Single 펑 is the bursting/popping sound itself (balloon, firework).

examples.en: After breaking up, I cried my eyes out at home.

examples.ko: 밤새 눈이 펑펑 와서 길이 하얘졌어요.
examples.romanization: bamsae nuni peongpeong waseo giri hayaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It snowed heavily all night, so the roads turned white.

examples.ko: 월급 받자마자 돈을 펑펑 쓰면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: wolgeup batjamaja doneul peongpeong sseumyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You shouldn't blow your money the moment you get your paycheck.

entries.nuance: 펑펑 has three everyday senses tied by the idea of bursting out abundantly: crying hard (펑펑 울다), heavy snow (눈이 펑펑 와요), and splurging money (돈을 펑펑 쓰다). Context makes the meaning obvious. The single 펑 is the actual 'pop/bang' sound of something bursting.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 펑펑 for rain. Heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 쏟아지다; 펑펑 with weather specifically means snow.
Assuming 펑펑 울다 is mild. It implies serious, hard sobbing, not a few tears.

usagePhrases.note: Core usage. Moving quietly so as not to be noticed.
Approaching quietly, often to surprise someone or a pet.
Entering quietly, e.g. coming home late.

examples.ko: 아기가 자고 있어서 살금살금 걸어 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jago isseoseo salgeumsalgeum georeo nawasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby was sleeping, so I tiptoed out.
The cat crept up toward the bird.
I came home late, so I sneaked quietly to my room.

entries.nuance: 살금살금 describes moving deliberately and quietly to avoid being noticed — tiptoeing past a sleeping roommate, a cat stalking, sneaking home late. It carries a slightly playful, cautious feel. It pairs with verbs of motion like 걷다, 다가가다, 들어가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 슬금슬금, which implies sneaking away gradually/sheepishly (often to avoid blame). 살금살금 is more about quiet footsteps.
Using it for fast quiet movement. Stealthy-but-quick is 후다닥 or 잽싸게; 살금살금 is slow and careful.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 후다닥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: Springing up fast, e.g. when you oversleep.

usagePhrases.en: to get ready in a rush

examples.en: I overslept, so I got ready in a mad rush and left.

examples.ko: 배가 너무 고파서 밥을 후다닥 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: baega neomu gopaseo babeul hudadang meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was so hungry that I wolfed down my food.
I saw a cockroach and bolted.
examples.note: Sudden quick escape, a bit comic.

entries.nuance: 후다닥 conveys doing something in a fast, slightly frantic burst — jumping up, rushing to get ready, dashing off. It implies speed plus a bit of commotion or panic, unlike calm efficiency. Great for describing oversleeping mornings, which every newcomer will relate to.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for calm, smooth speed. Efficient quickness is 빨리 or 잽싸게; 후다닥 implies a flustered scramble.
Pairing it with slow, deliberate actions — it clashes with verbs like 천천히 or careful tasks.

entries.nuance: 촘촘하다 describes things spaced very closely with tiny gaps: comb teeth, mesh, weaving, stitches, or even a tightly packed schedule. The opposite is 성기다 or 듬성듬성하다 (sparse). It carries a sense of fineness and thoroughness, often positive.

Confusing with 빽빽하다; 빽빽하다 stresses crowdedness with no room, 촘촘하다 stresses fine, even spacing
Using it for large objects packed together; 촘촘하다 fits small, repeated units like teeth, threads, dots

examples.en: I have lots of meetings today, so my schedule is packed.

entries.nuance: 빡빡하다 covers two everyday meanings: physically tight/stiff (a drawer or screw that resists moving) and figuratively tight (a packed schedule or a barely-sufficient budget). commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing with 빡세다; 빡세다 (slang) means physically/mentally hard or grueling, while 빡빡하다 means tight with no slack
Using 좁다 for a tight schedule; 좁다 is narrow in space, 빡빡하다 is tight in time/money/resistance

entries.nuance: 매끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective for surfaces that feel smooth and frictionless: skin, paper, fabric, floors. Figuratively it describes a process or speech that flows without awkward bumps. Note the irregular forms: 매끄러워요, 매끄러운, 매끄러우니까.

entries.nuance: 끈적하다 (also 끈적거리다, 끈적이다) describes a sticky, tacky feel: spilled drinks, sweat on humid days, or gooey residue. For Korea's muggy summers it perfectly captures clammy skin. A heavier, syrupy stickiness can be 끈적끈적하다. The opposite clean/dry feel is 보송보송하다.

entries.nuance: 눅눅하다 describes things that have absorbed moisture and turned damp or soggy: crackers that lost their crunch, laundry that won't dry, a humid basement room. It is essential vocabulary for Korea's humid summers and 장마 (rainy season). The opposite crisp/dry feel is 바삭하다 or 보송보송하다.

Using 젖다 (to get wet) for soggy snacks; soggy-from-humidity is 눅눅해지다, not 젖다

entries.shortExplanation: 미리 means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 미리 (miri) means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 미리 예약했어요 ("I booked it in advance"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 미리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The single most useful collocation for residents making reservations

usagePhrases.en: Please let me know ahead of time
usagePhrases.note: Polite request to be given advance notice
Common when promising to prepare early
미리 + past regret about not knowing in time

examples.ko: 인기 식당은 미리 예약하지 않으면 자리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: ingi sikdangeun miri yeyakaji aneumyeon jariga eopseoyo.
examples.en: Popular restaurants have no seats unless you reserve in advance.
examples.note: 미리 + reservation, a constant reality of dining out in Korea

examples.ko: 월세 내는 날을 미리 알림으로 맞춰 놨어요.
examples.romanization: wolse naeneun nareul miri allimeuro matchwo nwasseoyo.
examples.en: I set a reminder in advance for the day rent is due.
examples.note: 미리 describing proactive planning a tenant relates to

examples.ko: 출근 전에 미리 지하철 시간을 확인해요.
examples.romanization: chulgeun jeone miri jihacheol siganeul hwaginhaeyo.
examples.en: I check the subway times in advance before heading to work.
examples.note: 미리 marking something done ahead of the main action

entries.nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're prepared, and it's one of the most practical adverbs for daily logistics like booking, paying, or checking. It focuses on the timing being early relative to a deadline or event, not just 'first.' It pairs naturally with verbs of preparation such as 예약하다, 준비하다, and 확인하다.

Confusing it with 우선/일단 (first of all); 미리 specifically means 'before the due time,' not 'firstly in a sequence'
Dropping it where the early timing matters, e.g. 예약했어요 alone loses the 'ahead of time' nuance that 미리 예약했어요 carries

entries.nuance: 우선 means 'first and foremost,' marking what should come before everything else in importance or order. It feels slightly more deliberate and prioritizing than 먼저, which is plain sequence, and it often pairs with -부터 to stress the starting point. The related noun 우선순위 (priority) is everywhere in work and life contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 미리 (in advance); 우선 is about order/priority, not doing something before a deadline
Overusing it for simple 'then/next' steps where 먼저 or 그다음에 is more natural

examples.note: 일단 prioritizing one action and deferring the rest

entries.nuance: 일단 means 'for now' or 'first, before sorting out the rest,' flagging a provisional first move while later details stay open. It's hugely common in casual speech as a way to defer decisions: 일단 ~하고 보자 means 'let's just do X first and see.' Unlike 우선 (priority) or 미리 (in advance), 일단 carries the flavor of 'tentatively, as a starting point.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating it exactly with 우선; 일단 leans 'provisionally for now,' while 우선 stresses priority/importance
Expecting it to mean 'in advance'; that nuance belongs to 미리, not 일단

entries.explanation: 곧 (got) means "soon, shortly, before long". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 곧 도착해요 ("I'll arrive soon"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 곧 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

Reassuring someone you're on your way
Announcing an event about to begin
Comforting that something will wrap up shortly

examples.ko: 거의 다 왔어요, 곧 도착하니까 조금만 기다려요.
examples.romanization: geoui da wasseoyo, got dochakanikka jogeumman gidaryeoyo.
examples.en: I'm almost there; I'll arrive soon, so wait just a bit.
examples.note: 곧 + 도착하다, the most relatable 'on my way' message

examples.en: I got a text saying the package will arrive soon.
examples.note: 곧 in a delivery notification context

examples.en: My vacation ends soon, so I'm sad about it.
examples.note: 곧 marking an imminent, near-future change

entries.nuance: 곧 means 'soon' in the near future, signaling that something will happen within a short time from now. It feels a bit cleaner and slightly more written or formal than the very casual 금방, though both work in speech. 곧 looks only forward in time, so it never describes the past, and it's a staple in 'almost there / starting soon' messages.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for the recent past ('a moment ago'); that is 방금 or 금방, while 곧 is strictly future
Confusing 곧 (soon) with 곳 (place); they sound similar but are unrelated words

Knowledge that was in place beforehand

examples.en: I tried to get a refund, but shipping had already started.

examples.ko: 그 소식은 이미 다들 알고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu sosigeun imi dadeul algo isseoyo.
examples.en: Everyone already knows that news.

entries.nuance: 이미 means 'already,' emphasizing that an action or state is completed and now fixed, often with a tone of 'there's no changing it.' It overlaps with 벌써 but is more neutral and factual, whereas 벌써 adds surprise that it happened so fast. 이미 is the natural choice when you're calmly noting that the deadline or moment has already passed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it freely with 벌써; 이미 is neutral about timing, while 벌써 carries 'so soon?!' surprise
Using it for the future; 이미 only describes things that are already done, never things about to happen

entries.nuance: 아까 refers to a short while earlier on the same day, somewhere between 'just now' and 'this morning' but always recent and within today. It's extremely common in casual speech to refer back to a recent moment, as in 아까 그거 (that thing from earlier). Unlike 방금 (a moment ago), 아까 can stretch to a few hours back, not just seconds.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for yesterday or longer ago; 아까 stays within today's recent past, use 어제/전에 for further back
Treating it the same as 방금; 방금 means seconds ago, while 아까 covers a broader 'earlier today'

entries.nuance: 그동안 means 'during that time / all this while,' referring to a stretch of time leading up to now or spanning a known gap. entries.nuance: 진작 means 'sooner / long ago,' almost always carrying regret or mild reproach that something wasn't done earlier than it was. It typically pairs with regret endings like -ㄹ걸, -았/었어야지, or -았/었으면, as in 진작 말하지 (you should've said so sooner). The variant 진작에 adds emphasis. It's about 'earlier than it actually happened,' colored by hindsight.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a neutral 'before' like 전에; 진작 always carries the 'should have, sooner' regret nuance
Pairing it with plain statements instead of regret forms; it wants endings like -ㄹ걸 or -았어야지 to land naturally

entries.shortExplanation: 고속버스 means "express (intercity) bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고속버스 (gosokbeoseu) means "express (intercity) bus". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고속버스 타고 가요 ("I'm going by express bus"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고속버스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 고속버스 타고 가요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 고속버스.

우등 = 3 wide seats per row, more legroom and pricier; worth knowing when booking

examples.ko: 부산 갈 때 KTX보다 고속버스가 훨씬 싸요.
examples.romanization: busan gal ttae KTXboda gosokbeoseuga hwolssin ssayo.
examples.en: When going to Busan, the express bus is much cheaper than the KTX.
examples.note: common cost trade-off residents weigh; 보다 compares the two

examples.en: It's the weekend, so the express bus tickets are all sold out.
examples.note: 매진되다 = to sell out; book early on holidays

examples.en: If you book the premium one, the seats are wide so it's comfortable.
examples.note: explains why people pay extra for 우등

entries.nuance: 고속버스 runs city-to-city on expressways with few or no stops, so people contrast it with the KTX (faster, pricier) and 시외버스 (more stops, smaller towns). For 20-30s on a budget it's the go-to for trips like Seoul-Busan when you don't mind the longer ride.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 고속버스 with 시외버스 — 고속버스 is nonstop expressway travel between major cities, while 시외버스 makes more stops and reaches smaller towns.
Saying 고속버스역 — buses use 터미널, not 역 (역 is for trains and subways).

entries.shortExplanation: 시외버스 means "intercity bus (with stops)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "intercity bus (with stops)" is 시외버스 (sioebeoseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시외버스 타다 ("to take an intercity bus"). Watch the particle attached to 시외버스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: used for trips to smaller cities or towns a 고속버스 doesn't reach
often shares a building with the 고속버스 terminal but a separate ticket window

examples.ko: 그 동네는 KTX가 안 가서 시외버스를 타야 돼요.
examples.romanization: geu dongneneun KTXga an gaseo sioebeoseureul taya dwaeyo.
examples.en: The KTX doesn't go to that town, so you have to take the intercity bus.
examples.note: typical reason to use 시외버스; 안 가다 = doesn't go there

examples.ko: 시외버스는 정류장에 자주 서서 시간이 더 걸려요.
examples.romanization: sioebeoseuneun jeongnyujange jaju seoseo sigani deo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: The intercity bus stops at stations often, so it takes more time.
examples.note: 서다 here = to stop; explains the trade-off vs 고속버스

examples.en: The last intercity bus is at 8, so we have to hurry.
examples.note: 막차 (last bus) is a key word; rural lines end early

entries.nuance: 시외버스 covers shorter regional routes and makes stops, so it reaches places the 고속버스 skips. Residents traveling to a friend's hometown or a small coastal town often have no choice but 시외버스, and schedules thin out fast in the evening.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 시외버스 and 고속버스 as the same thing — they leave from different windows and serve different routes.
Assuming frequent departures — rural 시외버스 lines may run only a few times a day, so always check the 시간표.

entries.shortExplanation: KTX means "KTX (high-speed train)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: KTX (KTX) = "KTX (high-speed train)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: KTX 타다 ("to take the KTX") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside KTX, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize KTX 타다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near KTX.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: read aloud as '케이티엑스'; the standard high-speed rail in Korea
done on the 코레일톡 (Korail Talk) app or at the station

자유석 = no assigned seat, cheaper; sit in any open seat in the 자유석 cars, unlike 입석 (standing)

examples.ko: 서울에서 부산까지 KTX로 두 시간 반 걸려요.
examples.romanization: seoureseo busankkaji KTXro du sigan ban geollyeoyo.
examples.en: From Seoul to Busan it takes two and a half hours by KTX.
examples.note: the classic speed selling point; KTX로 = by KTX

examples.ko: KTX 표가 비싸지만 빠르니까 자주 타요.
examples.romanization: KTX pyoga bissajiman ppareunikka jaju tayo.
examples.en: KTX tickets are expensive but since they're fast I take it often.

examples.ko: 주말에는 KTX 입석밖에 없을 때도 있어요.
examples.romanization: jumareneun KTX ipseokbakke eopseul ttaedo isseoyo.
examples.en: On weekends there are sometimes only KTX standing tickets left.
examples.note: 입석 = standing ticket; reality of holiday travel

entries.nuance: KTX is the fast, premium option people compare against 고속버스 and the cheaper 무궁화호/ITX trains. For a 20-30s resident it's the obvious pick when you value time over money, but holiday tickets vanish quickly, leaving only 자유석 or 입석.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading KTX as English letters — Koreans say 케이티엑스, so pronounce each letter in Korean.
Booking on the wrong app — KTX is Korail, so use 코레일톡, not the SRT app (SRT is a separate high-speed operator).

examples.note: everyday city scene; 가져다주다 = bring (to someone)

examples.romanization: seukuteoneun jobeun golmokdo jal danyeoseo pyeonhaeyo.

examples.romanization: bi ol ttae seukuteo tamyeon neomu wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: Riding a scooter when it rains is really dangerous.

entries.nuance: 스쿠터 specifically means the small automatic step-through motorbike, the kind delivery riders use, whereas 오토바이 is the broader word for any motorcycle. For a city resident the word comes up constantly because of food delivery and because scooter-share apps exist.

Using 스쿠터 for an electric kick-scooter — that's a 전동킥보드; 스쿠터 has a seat and an engine.
Assuming no license is needed — even small scooters require at least a 원동기 license.

examples.en: If you ride the Namsan cable car, the Seoul night view is really pretty.

examples.ko: 케이블카 왕복으로 끊는 게 더 싸요.
examples.romanization: keibeulka wangbogeuro kkeunhneun ge deo ssayo.

examples.ko: 바람이 너무 세서 케이블카 운행을 멈췄어요.

usagePhrases.note: the passenger/car ship to islands; also called 여객선
예매 = advance booking; island routes can fill up
차량 = vehicle; the kind you can drive your car onto
터미널 = terminal; the port building you board from

examples.en: To get to the island you have to take a ferry.
examples.note: core use case; -려면 = in order to

examples.ko: 파도가 높아서 오늘 페리가 다 결항됐어요.
examples.romanization: padoga nopaseo oneul periga da gyeolhangdwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The waves are high, so all the ferries were canceled today.
examples.note: 결항되다 = (a ship/flight) to be canceled; common in bad weather

examples.en: I loaded my car onto the ferry and went to Jeju.
examples.note: 싣다 = to load (cargo); the car-ferry option to Jeju

entries.nuance: 페리 is the word for a passenger or car ship to Korea's islands; in formal notices you'll also see 여객선. A resident planning a trip to 제주도, 울릉도, or a small island needs it, and should expect 결항 (cancellations) whenever the sea is rough.
