entries.explanation: 변기 (byeongi) means "toilet (bowl)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 변기 ("toilet bowl"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 변기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 변기. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 변기.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: The toilet fixture itself. The whole room is 화장실; the bowl is 변기.
막히다 = to get blocked; the single most useful phrase for renters.
물을 내리다 = to flush; 내리다 literally 'send down'.
Use 에 for the location you sit on.

examples.en: The toilet is clogged — do you have a plunger?
examples.note: 뚫어뻥 is the everyday word for a plunger.

examples.en: Is it okay to throw the toilet paper in the toilet?
examples.note: A real question in Korea, where plumbing usually does handle 휴지.

examples.ko: 나오기 전에 변기 물 꼭 내리세요.
examples.romanization: naogi jeone byeongi mul kkong naeriseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to flush before you come out.
examples.note: 물(을) 내리다 = to flush; 꼭 = without fail.

entries.nuance: 변기는 화장실 안에 있는 변기통 자체를 가리키고, 방 전체는 '화장실'이라고 부릅니다. 자취나 월세 생활에서 '변기가 막혔다', '변기 물이 안 내려간다' 같은 표현을 자주 쓰게 되니 꼭 알아 두세요. 물을 흘려보내는 동작은 '물을 내리다'라고 한다는 점도 함께 기억하면 좋습니다.

usagePhrases.note: Most Korean bathrooms use a handheld 샤워기 on a hose, not a fixed ceiling shower.

usagePhrases.en: to rinse off with the showerhead
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 marks the tool; 헹구다 = to rinse.

usagePhrases.en: no water comes out of the showerhead
usagePhrases.note: 물이 안 나오다 = water won't come out; a common malfunction.
갈다 = to replace; filter showerheads (필터 샤워기) are popular.

examples.en: The shower water suddenly turned cold.
examples.note: 차가워지다 = to become cold; boiler issues are common.

examples.en: I rinsed even the bathroom floor with the showerhead.
examples.note: 싹 = completely; handheld 샤워기 doubles as a cleaning tool.

examples.en: The water pressure was weak, so I changed the showerhead.
examples.note: 수압 = water pressure; 바꾸다 = to swap.

entries.nuance: 한국 욕실은 천장에 고정된 샤워 대신 호스에 달린 손잡이형 샤워기를 쓰는 집이 대부분입니다. 그래서 샤워기를 들고 몸을 씻는 것은 물론 욕실 바닥이나 변기 주변을 헹구는 청소 도구로도 자주 씁니다. 수압이 약하거나 물때가 끼면 '샤워기 헤드'만 따로 갈아 끼우는 경우도 많습니다.

usagePhrases.note: The tap at a sink or basin; 수도 = water supply, 꼭지 = knob/spout.
잠그다 = to shut/lock; the standard verb for closing a tap.
물이 새다 = water leaks; a frequent maintenance issue.

examples.note: 잠그다 conjugates to 잠가; a common water-saving reminder.

examples.en: The faucet is dripping (water leaks drip-drip).
The cold-water tap is really stiff to turn.

entries.nuance: 수도꼭지는 세면대나 싱크대에서 물을 틀고 잠그는 꼭지 부분을 말합니다. 동사는 켜고 끄는 가전과 달리 '틀다(열다)'와 '잠그다'를 쓰는 점이 중요합니다. 오래된 집에서는 수도꼭지에서 물이 새거나 손잡이가 뻑뻑해지는 일이 흔해서 수리 요청할 때 자주 등장하는 단어입니다.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 욕실화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Rubber slippers worn only in the wet bathroom; 욕실 + 화 (footwear).
갈아 신다 = to change footwear at the bathroom door.
미끄럽다 = slippery; worn soles are a fall risk.

examples.en: Put on the bathroom slippers when you go into the bathroom.
examples.note: Standard rule in many Korean homes.

examples.en: The soles of the bathroom slippers are worn, so I keep slipping.
examples.note: 닳다 = to wear down; 미끄러지다 = to slip.

examples.en: I bought a pair of bathroom slippers at Daiso.
examples.note: 켤레 = counter for pairs of footwear.

entries.nuance: 욕실화는 물기 있는 욕실에서만 신는 고무 슬리퍼로, 한국 집에서는 욕실 문 앞에 두고 들어갈 때 갈아 신는 경우가 많습니다. 신발을 세는 단위는 '켤레'를 쓰고, 바닥이 닳으면 미끄러워 넘어질 수 있어 주기적으로 바꿔 줍니다. 실내에서 신는 일반 슬리퍼와 달리 젖은 바닥 전용이라는 점이 특징입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting them with 개 — footwear pairs use the counter 켤레.
Wearing 욕실화 around the dry living space; they're meant for the wet bathroom only.

usagePhrases.note: The small cotton-tipped stick; 면 (cotton) + 봉 (stick).

usagePhrases.en: to clean one's ears with a swab
usagePhrases.note: 귀를 파다 = to dig/clean the ears; the most common use.
통 = the tub/container counter they're sold in.

usagePhrases.en: to dab onto a cotton swab
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = to put (liquid/medicine) onto the tip.

examples.en: After a shower I clean my ears with a cotton swab.
I dabbed disinfectant on a cotton swab and put it on the wound.

examples.ko: 면봉 다 썼으니까 한 통 더 사야겠어요.
examples.romanization: myeonbong da sseosseunikka han tong deo sayagesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm out of cotton swabs, so I should buy another tub.
examples.note: 한 통 = one container; 사야겠다 = I'd better buy.

entries.nuance: 면봉은 끝에 솜이 달린 작은 막대로, 보통 샤워 후 귀를 닦거나 화장을 정리할 때, 또는 상처에 약을 바를 때 씁니다. 보통 '한 통' 단위로 사며 욕실이나 화장대에 두고 씁니다. 영어 'Q-tip'에 해당하는 일상어로, 한국 어느 집에나 흔히 있는 물건입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it with 개만 — the package is usually counted as 통 (a tub).
Confusing 면봉 (cotton swab) with 솜 (cotton ball) or 화장솜 (cosmetic pad).

Watch the particle attached to 욕실매트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: The mat outside the shower to soak up water; also called 발매트.

usagePhrases.en: to lay down the bath mat
usagePhrases.note: 깔다 = to spread/lay out on the floor.
젖다 = to get wet/soaked; needs drying out.
빨다 = to launder; toss it in the washing machine.

examples.ko: 샤워하고 나오면 욕실매트가 발을 닦아 줘요.
examples.romanization: syawohago naomyeon yoksilmaeteuga bareul dakka jwoyo.
examples.en: When you step out of the shower, the bath mat dries your feet.
examples.note: 발(을) 닦다 = to dry the feet.

examples.en: If the bath mat stays damp, mold grows.
examples.note: 눅눅하다 = damp/clammy; 곰팡이가 피다 = mold forms.

examples.en: I wash the bath mat once a week.
examples.note: 일주일에 한 번 = once a week.

entries.nuance: 욕실매트는 샤워 후 욕실 밖이나 문 앞에 깔아 발의 물기를 닦는 매트로, '발매트'라고도 부릅니다. 젖은 채 두면 눅눅해지고 곰팡이가 잘 펴서 자주 말리거나 빨아 줘야 합니다. 빨래는 보통 세탁기에 돌리며, 미끄럼 방지가 되는 제품을 많이 씁니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 카펫 — a 카펫 is a room rug; the absorbent bathroom one is 욕실매트.
Leaving 깔다 out; the mat is laid down with 깔다, not 놓다 for a flat floor cover.

entries.explanation: 때수건 (ttaesugeon) = "exfoliating (scrub) towel / Italy towel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 때수건 ("scrubbing towel") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 때수건, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: 때 (dead skin/grime) + 수건; the rough mitt for scrubbing skin, a Korean staple.
(때를) 밀다 = to scrub off dead skin; the signature verb.
Done at the 목욕탕/찜질방 or at home; 때 = the grime that comes off.
까칠까칠하다 = rough-textured, which is the point.

examples.en: At the bathhouse I scrubbed my back with the scrub towel.

examples.ko: 때수건으로 너무 세게 밀면 피부가 따가워요.
examples.romanization: ttaesugeoneuro neomu sege milmyeon pibuga ttagawoyo.
examples.en: If you scrub too hard with the towel, your skin stings.

examples.ko: 외국인 친구한테 때수건 쓰는 법 알려 줬어요.
examples.romanization: oegugin chinguhante ttaesugeon sseuneun beop allyeo jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I taught my foreign friend how to use a scrub towel.
examples.note: A genuinely Korean cultural item worth knowing.

entries.nuance: 때수건은 까칠한 천으로 피부의 묵은 각질(때)을 밀어내는, 한국 목욕 문화의 상징 같은 물건입니다. 보통 '때를 민다'고 표현하고 목욕탕이나 찜질방에서, 또는 집에서 샤워할 때 씁니다. 너무 세게 밀면 피부가 상할 수 있어 외국인이라면 사용법을 알아 두면 좋습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 닦다 with it — the action is 때를 밀다 (to scrub off), not 닦다.
Treating it like a soft 수건; 때수건 is deliberately rough for exfoliating.

entries.explanation: 보라색 (borasaek) means "purple". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보라색 ("purple"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보라색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 보라색. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 보라색.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Standalone color noun; works as 'purple (one)' in shops
Color + noun = the most common modifier pattern

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the purple one, please
usagePhrases.note: Natural way to pick a color at a store

examples.en: Purple is my favorite color.
examples.note: 색 + 을/를 좋아해요 = stating a favorite

examples.en: Does this T-shirt also come in purple?
examples.note: Asking about color options while shopping

examples.en: Which is better, the purple or the pink?

entries.nuance: 보라색 covers the whole purple range, and 자주색 leans toward a deeper reddish-purple while 연보라색 is the pale lilac you'll see on cosmetics and stationery. In everyday speech most people just say 보라색 for anything purple, so you rarely need the more specific words unless you're matching paint or clothes precisely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping 색 and saying just 보라 — natural in casual speech but 보라색 is the safe full form when naming the color.
Confusing 보라색 (purple) with 파란색 (blue); they're separate colors in Korean, not shades of one word.

entries.explanation: "pink" is 분홍색 (bunhongsaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분홍색 ("pink"). Watch the particle attached to 분홍색 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard word for pink; 핑크 (loanword) is just as common

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a color other than pink?
usagePhrases.note: Asking for alternatives at a shop

examples.en: The cherry blossoms are pink, so they're really pretty.
examples.note: 이라서 = 'because it is', giving a reason

examples.en: I painted my daughter's room pink.
Red suits you better than pink.

entries.nuance: Koreans use 분홍색 and the English loanword 핑크 almost interchangeably, with 핑크 sounding a bit trendier in fashion and beauty contexts. There's no negative 'girly' baggage built into the word itself, though pastel 연분홍색 vs bright 형광 핑크 (neon pink) signal very different vibes.

Saying 검은색 for dark brown hair; Koreans distinguish 진갈색 (dark brown) from 검은색 (black).

entries.nuance: 남색 is the deep, almost ink-blue you see in school uniforms, suits, and denim, and many younger shoppers just say 네이비 in clothing contexts. It reads as more formal and 차분하다 (calm, composed) than bright 파란색, which is why it dominates business and uniform wear.

entries.nuance: 하늘색 is the soft, pale blue of a clear sky and is read as fresh, clean, and 시원하다 (cool/refreshing), which is why it's a summer-shirt and baby-clothes favorite. It contrasts sharply with deep 남색 (navy) and even with plain 파란색, which tends to mean a more saturated mid-blue.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling sky blue 파란색; Koreans clearly separate pale 하늘색 from stronger 파란색.
To describe the actual sky as clear, say 하늘이 맑아요 (sky + clear), not 하늘색이 맑아요 — 하늘색 is the color name, not the sky itself.

entries.nuance: 동그라미 is the casual, everyday word for a circle, while 원 is the formal/mathematical term you'd use in geometry class. In Korea a 동그라미 (O) means 'correct' and an X (가위표/엑스) means 'wrong', the reverse of the American check/cross habit, so this comes up constantly when grading or filling forms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 원 in casual speech where 동그라미 sounds more natural for an ordinary round shape.
Assuming a circle mark is neutral — in Korea 동그라미 specifically signals 'correct/yes'.

entries.nuance: 그러나 means 'however' and is the formal, written-feeling cousin of 하지만 and 그렇지만. You'll see it constantly in news articles, reports, essays, and official notices, but it sounds stiff in casual chat where 근데 or 하지만 fit better. It almost always starts a new sentence rather than joining clauses inside one.

Using it in casual speech where it sounds bookish; say 근데 or 하지만 with friends
Trying to glue two clauses together with it mid-sentence; 그러나 starts a fresh sentence, while -지만 attaches inside one

entries.nuance: 그러면 means 'then / in that case' and links a conclusion or next step to what was just said, like 'if that's the situation, then this.' In fast speech it's very often shortened to 그럼, which is identical in meaning. Don't confuse this logical 'then' with 그리고 ('and then' in a time sequence); 그러면 reacts to a condition, while 그리고 just lists the next event.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 그리고; 그러면 means 'in that case (conditional)', not 'and then (sequence)'
Forgetting that the casual contraction is 그럼, not 그러면, in everyday spoken Korean

entries.nuance: 따라서 means 'therefore / accordingly' and is the formal, logical 'so' you meet in reports, announcements, instructions, and academic writing. entries.nuance: 반면에 means 'on the other hand / whereas,' explicitly setting up a contrast between two sides, options, or qualities. You'll also see it attached to a clause as -는 반면(에), as in 비싼 반면에 ('while it's expensive').

Using it for a simple surprising contrast within one situation; 반면에 specifically compares two distinct sides, where 그런데 fits a single-topic twist

entries.nuance: 그럼에도 means 'even so / nevertheless,' signaling that what follows happens despite the obstacle just mentioned. It's most often heard in its full form 그럼에도 불구하고 ('in spite of that'), which adds weight and is common in speeches and writing. It carries a slightly elevated, determined tone, so it's stronger and more dramatic than a plain 그래도, which is the casual everyday equivalent.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for light, casual contrast where 그래도 fits better; 그럼에도 sounds formal and weighty
Writing the set phrase wrong as 그럼에도 불구하구; the correct form is 그럼에도 불구하고

entries.nuance: 한편 means 'meanwhile / on the other hand,' shifting attention to a parallel or contrasting situation, often used in news to switch topics ('한편, ...'). In the doubled form 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 it expresses two coexisting, mixed feelings ('part of me... but part of me...'). It's a bit more literary and reportorial than 반면에, and it can introduce a simultaneous scene rather than a strict A-versus-B comparison.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as a pure 'but'; 한편 shifts to a parallel scene or adds a coexisting angle, not a flat contradiction
Forgetting the mixed-feelings pattern 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는, which is its most useful conversational use

entries.nuance: 결국 means 'in the end / eventually,' summarizing the final outcome after a process, delay, or struggle. Unlike 드디어, which celebrates a happy long-awaited result, 결국 is neutral and often hints at resignation or an outcome that was perhaps inevitable. It frequently follows a clause with -지만 or -는데 that describes the lead-up, and 결국엔 is a common emphatic variant.

entries.nuance: 생맥주 (literally 'fresh/raw beer') is draft beer and a staple of Korean drinking spots, especially with fried chicken (치맥). It's ordered by glass size — 오백 (500cc) and 천 (1000cc) — and pitchers (피처) for groups. The clipped form 생맥 is very common in speech.

생맥주 is draft (on tap); bottled beer is 병맥주, canned is 캔맥주 — don't mix them up.
When ordering by size say 오백/천, not '500밀리리터'.

entries.nuance: 하이볼 is whiskey topped with sparkling water over ice, and it has become one of the trendiest drinks in Korea, popular at izakayas (이자카야), bars, and even as canned convenience-store versions. entries.explanation: "strong, rich, concentrated (of a drink/flavor)" is 진하다 (jinhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진하다 ("to be strong/rich"). Watch the particle attached to 진하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: for coffee, tea, broth, milk — concentrated flavor
진하게 = strongly; asking for an extra shot feel

examples.en: I like strong coffee.

examples.ko: 이 녹차는 너무 진해서 좀 써요.
examples.romanization: i nokchaneun neomu jinhaeseo jom sseoyo.

entries.nuance: 진하다 describes a deep, concentrated flavor — strong coffee, dark tea, rich broth, or creamy milk. For coffee it's the natural word for 'strong' (not 강하다). Its opposite is 연하다 (weak/light). Use 진하게 when asking a barista to make a drink stronger.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For a strong-tasting drink use 진하다, not 강하다 (강하다 is more for force/intensity in general).
For high-alcohol liquor, the word is 독하다, not 진하다 — 진하다 is about flavor concentration, not proof.

entries.explanation: 미지근하다 (mijigeunhada) = "to be lukewarm, tepid". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 미지근하다 ("to be lukewarm") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 미지근하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: neither hot nor cold; often a complaint about a drink
useful when you don't want it cold (e.g. taking medicine)

examples.en: The beer is lukewarm so it tastes bad.
Take the medicine with lukewarm water.
The americano had cooled off and was lukewarm.

entries.nuance: 미지근하다 means lukewarm/tepid — a drink that's lost its heat or never got cold. It often carries a mildly negative nuance (a beer or coffee that should be hot or cold but isn't). It's also genuinely useful for requesting 미지근한 물, which people prefer for taking medicine or for sensitive stomachs.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
미지근하다 = lukewarm; 따뜻하다 = pleasantly warm. A lukewarm drink that should be hot is 미지근하다 (a complaint), not 따뜻하다.
Don't use it for weather; it's mainly for liquids and objects, not air temperature (that's 포근하다/따뜻하다).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 신기하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: everyday word for 'wow, cool!' when something is new or surprising in a good way
반말, the reaction you blurt out staring at something new
polite, mild wonder at something you just learned or saw
신기하다 + 거(것); 신기한 거 봤어 = I saw something cool

examples.ko: 한국 지하철은 진짜 잘 돼 있어서 신기해요.
examples.romanization: hanguk jihacheoreun jinjja jal dwae isseoseo singihaeyo.
examples.en: The Korean subway is so well-organized, it's amazing.
examples.note: common reaction foreigners share with Korean friends

examples.en: Huh? This turns on automatically. That's cool.
examples.note: 혼잣말 muttered while poking at a gadget

examples.ko: 눈 처음 봤을 때 너무 신기했어.
examples.romanization: nun cheoeum bwasseul ttae neomu singihaesseo.
examples.en: When I saw snow for the first time it was so amazing.
examples.note: past tense 신기했어, recalling a first experience

entries.nuance: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected, like a smart gadget or your first snow. It carries a positive, almost childlike curiosity. Don't confuse it with 이상하다, which means weird in a slightly negative or off way.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for creepy/bad weirdness; that's 이상하다, not 신기하다 (신기하다 is positive wonder).
Writing 신기다 — the dictionary form keeps 하: 신기하다, 신기해요.

황홀하다 + ㄹ 정도로 = so beautiful that...

examples.en: The night view from Namsan was truly mesmerizing.
examples.note: 강조 with 진짜, sharing a date highlight

examples.en: Walking the cherry blossom path, it was just breathtaking.

examples.ko: 공연이 너무 황홀해서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: gongyeoni neomu hwangholhaeseo sigan ganeun jul mollasseo.
examples.en: The show was so enchanting I lost track of time.
examples.note: -아서 cause; pairs with 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어

entries.nuance: 황홀하다 describes beauty so intense it nearly sweeps you away, reserved for sunsets, night views, music, or a magical moment, not everyday 'pretty'. It feels literary and heightened, so dropping it on a so-so view sounds over the top. For ordinary 'pretty/nice' stick with 예쁘다 or 멋지다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Overusing it for mildly nice things; 황홀하다 is reserved for truly stunning, almost overwhelming beauty.
Confusing it with 행복하다 (happy); 황홀하다 is about being dazzled by beauty, not general happiness.

entries.explanation: 아찔하다 (ajjilhada) = "dizzying, heart-stopping, scary-close". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아찔하다 ("to be dizzying / heart-stopping") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아찔하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the rush when you almost got hurt or look down from a height
반말 reaction right after a near-miss
past tense, retelling a scary moment

usagePhrases.en: it's dizzying just to think about it
usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase for 'I shudder to imagine'

examples.en: A car cut in suddenly and it was really heart-stopping.
examples.note: near-accident on the road, very common

examples.en: When I looked down from the observatory it made me dizzy.
I almost lost my wallet. That was scary-close.

entries.nuance: 아찔하다 captures the dizzy, stomach-dropping jolt of a near-miss or a dangerous height, the physical wave of 'whew, that was close'. It's both literal dizziness and the emotional shock of almost-disaster, so Koreans use it constantly after close calls in traffic. Don't swap it for 무섭다 (scary), which is steady fear rather than that split-second lurch.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for ongoing fear; 아찔하다 is a momentary dizzy jolt, not sustained 무섭다.
Saying 아찔하다 for happy excitement; it implies danger or vertigo, not fun thrill (use 짜릿하다).

usagePhrases.en: this feels awkward / my stomach's off
to feel queasy in the stomach

usagePhrases.note: for a tense, awkward social atmosphere

examples.en: I overate, so my stomach feels a bit queasy.
examples.note: extremely common after a big meal

examples.ko: 그 자리가 너무 거북해서 일찍 나왔어.
examples.romanization: geu jariga neomu geobukaeseo iljjing nawasseo.

examples.note: V-기 거북하다 = awkward/uncomfortable to do (대답하기 거북하다)

entries.nuance: 거북하다 has two everyday uses: a queasy, heavy stomach (속이 거북하다) and an awkward, uneasy social feeling. Both share the idea of something not sitting right, physically or emotionally. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it only for physical inconvenience like a hard chair; that's 불편하다 (거북하다 is queasy/awkward).
Forgetting the stomach sense; 속이 거북하다 is a super common natural collocation.

usagePhrases.en: to feel let down by someone's coldness
usagePhrases.note: soft resentment when someone you care about is unkind or distant
반말, gentle reproach to a close person
-더라 recalling a moment you felt slighted

examples.ko: 힘들 때 연락 한 번 없어서 좀 야속했어.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae yeolla kan beon eopseoseo jom yasokaesseo.
examples.en: You didn't reach out once when I was struggling, it felt cold.
I know you were busy, but still, it felt heartless.
Even the weather is being cruel, it's raining.

entries.nuance: 야속하다 is the soft, wounded resentment you feel when someone close lets you down or seems cold, less anger than quiet hurt. It implies you expected warmth and didn't get it, so it carries affection underneath the complaint. It differs from 섭섭하다 (which is broader disappointment) by emphasizing the other side's seeming heartlessness.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for strangers; 야속하다 implies you expected kindness, so it fits close people or fate.
Treating it as strong anger; it's gentle, hurt reproach, not 화나다.

entries.nuance: 명절 is the word for Korea's two major lunar-calendar holidays, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (the harvest festival), when the whole country travels home to family. It carries a strong sense of family duty and reunion, so asking about someone's 명절 plans is a normal, slightly personal greeting. Smaller red-letter days like Children's Day are 공휴일, not 명절.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 명절 for every public holiday; a single day off like 광복절 is a 공휴일, while 명절 means the big lunar reunions.
Saying 명절 축하해요 sounds off — Koreans say 명절 잘 보내세요 (spend the holiday well), not 'congratulations'.

entries.nuance: 한가위 is the warm, native-Korean name for 추석, the autumn harvest festival held on the 15th of the eighth lunar month. You'll see it most in greetings and holiday cards, where 행복한 한가위 보내세요 sounds friendlier than the plain 추석. The famous saying 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라 expresses a wish that life were always as bountiful as this season.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
한가위 and 추석 mean the same holiday; 한가위 is just the softer native name, so don't treat them as two separate days.
It's spelled 한가위 (ending in 위), not 한가의 — the last syllable is 위, not 의.

entries.nuance: 연휴 means a run of consecutive days off, the practical thing Koreans actually plan around rather than a single holiday. When a 명절 or public holiday connects with a weekend it becomes a 황금연휴 (golden long weekend), and people often burn a vacation day on a 징검다리 (stepping-stone) workday to extend it. Flights and trains sell out fast, so locals book early.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
연휴 specifically means several days off in a row; for one single day off use 휴일, not 연휴.
Don't confuse 연휴 (consecutive days off) with 휴가 (your personal vacation/leave) — a 연휴 is on the calendar for everyone.

entries.nuance: 차례 is the simplified ancestral memorial rite performed on the morning of 설날 and 추석, where families set out food and bow to honor their ancestors. It differs from 제사, the rite held on the anniversary of a specific person's death. Many younger households now hold 차례 in a pared-down form or skip it to travel, which is increasingly accepted.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
차례 (holiday rite) and 제사 (death-anniversary rite) are not the same; use 제사 for the yearly memorial of a specific ancestor.
The verb is 차례를 지내다 (hold the rite), not 차례를 하다 — 지내다 is the fixed pairing.

usagePhrases.en: to make the New Year's bow

usagePhrases.note: The phrase you say while doing the 세배.

entries.nuance: 세배 is the deep, formal bow that younger people give to elders on 설날 to wish them a good year, said together with 새해 복 많이 받으세요. In return, elders offer words of advice and 세뱃돈 (New Year's cash), which children eagerly collect. Even as adults, you'll likely perform 세배 to parents and grandparents at the holiday gathering.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 세배 (the bow) with 세뱃돈 (the money received afterward) — they're related but different words.
세배 is the proper deep bow to elders, not a casual nod; performing it carelessly can read as disrespectful.

entries.explanation: 덕담 (deokdam) = "words of blessing / good wishes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 덕담 ("words of blessing") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: Kind, encouraging wishes elders give, especially at New Year.
하다 verb; what an elder does after receiving your 세배.
나누다 = to share; people trade 덕담 at the holiday table.
한마디 = a word/remark; 'say a few kind words' on a happy occasion.

examples.ko: 세배를 하면 어른들이 덕담을 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: sebaereul hamyeon eoreundeuri deokdameul hae juseyo.
examples.en: After you bow, the elders offer words of blessing.
examples.note: 해 주다 = to do (for someone); the elder's part of the 세배 exchange.

examples.en: For the new year I heard lots of wishes to stay healthy.
examples.note: -라는 = quoted wish ('be healthy'); typical New Year 덕담.

examples.ko: 결혼식에서 어른이 덕담 한마디 해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsigeseo eoreuni deokdam hanmadi hae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: At the wedding an elder said a few words of blessing.
examples.note: 덕담 isn't only for New Year; it fits any happy occasion.

entries.nuance: 덕담 means the warm, encouraging words of blessing that elders give younger people, most famously right after receiving a 세배 on 설날. The wishes are usually about health, success, or marriage, and accepting them gracefully is part of the ritual. Beyond New Year, 덕담 also covers the kind remarks an elder offers at weddings and other celebrations.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
덕담 is specifically positive, blessing-type talk for happy occasions — it's never used for advice that scolds or criticizes.
The verb is 덕담을 하다/나누다, not 덕담을 말하다; pair it with 하다 or 나누다 to sound natural.

Eating a bowl on New Year symbolically adds a year to your age.

examples.en: On Seollal morning we always eat tteokguk.

examples.en: Eating a bowl of tteokguk means you turn a year older.

entries.nuance: 떡국 is the soup of thinly sliced rice cakes in clear broth that Koreans eat on the morning of 설날. There's a long-running joke that finishing a bowl means you've officially gained a year, so people ask 떡국 몇 그릇 먹었어? to tease about age. A common, heartier variant is 떡만둣국, which adds dumplings to the same broth.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 떡국 (savory rice-cake soup) with 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice cakes) — different dishes despite both using 떡.
The New Year 'aging' line is a joke about 떡국; eating it doesn't really change your legal age, especially since the age-counting law changed.

entries.nuance: 송편 are small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut and steamed over pine needles, eaten at 추석. Families traditionally gather to shape them by hand using the verb 빚다, and there's a charming saying that making them neatly foretells a pretty daughter. The pine-needle steaming gives them their distinctive 솔잎 fragrance.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
송편 pairs with the verb 빚다 (to shape by hand), not 만들다 in the traditional phrasing — 송편을 빚다 sounds most natural.
송편 is the 추석 rice cake; don't confuse it with 떡국's rice cakes or generic 떡 — it's a specific shaped, filled variety.

usagePhrases.note: Visiting ancestors' graves to pay respects, especially at 추석.
가다 verb; the family outing to the gravesite during the holiday.
Cutting the overgrown grass on the mound, often done before 추석.
산소 = the burial mound you visit during 성묘.

examples.en: I went to visit the family graves with relatives for Chuseok.
examples.note: 다녀오다 = to go and come back; the typical holiday grave visit.

examples.en: Before the grave visit we first cleared the grass.
examples.note: -부터 = first of all; 벌초 usually precedes 성묘.

examples.ko: 요즘은 성묘 대신 납골당에 가는 사람도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun seongmyo daesin napgoldange ganeun saramdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many people go to a charnel house instead of tending graves.
examples.note: 납골당 = columbarium; reflects changing burial customs.

entries.nuance: 성묘 is the custom of visiting ancestors' graves to clean them and bow in respect, done above all at 추석 and 설날. It often follows 벌초, the chore of cutting back the grass on the 산소 (burial mound). As cremation has become the norm, more families now visit a 납골당 (columbarium) instead, but the word 성묘 still covers paying these respects.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
성묘 is going to the grave; 차례 is the food-table rite at home — they're separate parts of the holiday, not synonyms.
Don't confuse 성묘 (visiting/tending graves) with 벌초 (the specific task of cutting the grass) — 벌초 is one step within a 성묘 trip.

entries.explanation: 보름 (boreum) means "the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보름 ("the 15th (full-moon day)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보름 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The midpoint of a lunar month, when the moon is full.

usagePhrases.en: the first full moon of the year
usagePhrases.note: A traditional holiday on the 15th of the first lunar month.
달 = moon; the round moon seen on a 보름 night.
보름 also colloquially means a span of about 15 days.

examples.en: On the first full moon we crack and eat nuts (burum).
examples.note: 부럼 = nuts cracked for health; a 대보름 custom.

examples.ko: 오늘 밤 보름달이 정말 크고 밝아요.
examples.romanization: oneul bam boreumdari jeongmal keugo balgayo.
examples.en: Tonight's full moon is really big and bright.
examples.note: 보름달 = full moon; a natural everyday remark.

examples.ko: 여행 간 지 벌써 보름이 지났어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaeng gan ji beolsseo boreumi jinasseoyo.
examples.en: It's already been about half a month since the trip.
examples.note: 보름 here means roughly 15 days, a common colloquial use.

entries.nuance: 보름 literally marks the 15th day of the lunar month, the night of the full moon, and by extension is used casually to mean a span of about half a month. The big related holiday is 정월대보름, the first full moon of the year, when people crack 부럼 nuts and eat 오곡밥 for health and luck. In daily speech you'll most often hear it as 보름달 (full moon).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
보름 by itself is the 15th / full-moon day; the actual holiday is 정월대보름, so don't shorten the holiday's name to just 보름.
When 보름 means a duration it's roughly 15 days — don't read it as exactly two weeks (14 days).

entries.explanation: "the dog days of summer (hottest days)" is 복날 (bongnal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 복날 ("dog days (peak-summer days)"). 삼복 = the three bok days; the fiercest stretch of summer heat.

usagePhrases.en: eat samgyetang on a bok day
usagePhrases.note: The custom of eating hot ginseng-chicken soup to beat the heat.

examples.note: Eating 삼계탕 on 복날 causes famous lunchtime queues.

examples.en: Today's the first bok day — shall we go eat some restorative food?
During the peak-bok heat I don't even want to go outside.
examples.note: -기도 싫다 = don't even want to; describes the brutal heat.

entries.nuance: 복날 refers to the three hottest days of summer in the lunar calendar — 초복, 중복, and 말복 — collectively the time of 삼복더위, the fiercest heat. The custom is to eat a hot, restorative 보양식 like 삼계탕 to fight heat with heat, so famous soup restaurants get long lunchtime lines on these days. The dates appear on most Korean calendars.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
복날 isn't one fixed day; it's three separate days (초복, 중복, 말복) spread through summer, so use them by name when you mean a specific one.
Despite the heat, the 복날 custom is hot soup, not cold food — saying you'll eat 냉면 to 'celebrate' 복날 misses the point.

entries.nuance: 한복 is traditional Korean clothing, worn most often on 명절, at weddings, and at first-birthday parties, with the verb 입다. For young people and visitors it's also a popular activity to rent 한복 near palaces like Gyeongbokgung, since wearing it gets you free admission and great photos. A modernized 생활한복 is increasingly seen as everyday wear.

한복 takes 입다 (to wear/put on like clothes), not 쓰다 or 신다 — those are for hats and shoes respectively.
한복 isn't only a museum costume; treating it as purely old-fashioned ignores the trendy rental and 생활한복 culture among 20-30s.

entries.nuance: 복숭아 is one of Korea's most beloved summer fruits, and people genuinely split into two camps: 물복 (soft, juicy) versus 딱복 (firm, crunchy). It's also one of the more common food allergies here, so being able to say 복숭아 알레르기 있어요 can actually matter at a restaurant or a friend's house.

entries.nuance: 감 (persimmon) is a quintessential autumn fruit in Korea, sold as the crunchy 단감 or the soft, spoon-eaten 홍시, and dried into chewy 곶감 for winter. The key flavor word is 떫다 (astringent) — an unripe persimmon dries out your mouth, a sensation 20-30s here describe constantly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 감 by itself when you mean a specific type — at a market, specify 단감 (firm) or 홍시 (soft).
Saying 감이 써요 (bitter) for an unripe one; the right word is 떫어요 (astringent).

Counting 블루베리 with 개 for the whole container — buy it as 한 팩 (one pack).

examples.note: 골드키위 is the sweeter, premium type.

entries.nuance: 키위 (kiwi) is a popular everyday fruit in Korea, split into the sweeter 골드키위 and the tarter 그린키위 you'll see labeled separately at the mart. Beyond peeling it, a very common local habit is to halve it and 떠먹다 (scoop it out with a spoon), and unripe ones are described as 시큼하다 (sour).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Eating the fuzzy brown skin — Koreans always peel 키위 or scoop it out with a spoon.
Assuming all 키위 taste the same; 골드키위 (sweet) and 그린키위 (tart) are noticeably different.

entries.nuance: 브로콜리 (broccoli) is firmly part of healthy and diet eating in Korea, often appearing on 닭가슴살 (chicken breast) diet plates. The very Korean way to serve it is lightly 데친 (blanched) and dipped in 초고추장 (sweet chili-vinegar paste), and locals warn that overboiling makes it 물러지다 (mushy).

Counting 브로콜리 with 개 — a whole head is 한 송이.
Serving 브로콜리 raw and plain; the expected style is blanched with 초고추장.

entries.nuance: 가지 (eggplant) in Korea is the long, slender purple type, eaten mainly as the side dishes 가지나물 (seasoned steamed) and 가지볶음 (stir-fried). entries.nuance: 고구마 (sweet potato) is both a beloved food — especially winter 군고구마 (roasted) and the diet-friendly carb swap for rice — and a piece of modern slang. entries.nuance: 옥수수 (corn) shows up in everyday Korean life in three big ways: 찐 옥수수 (steamed on the cob) as a summer street snack, canned 옥수수 통조림 sprinkled on salads and even pizza, and 옥수수차 (corn tea) served free at many restaurants. You receive a 청첩장 (invitation) for this

examples.ko: 다음 주 토요일에 친구 결혼식이 있어서 못 가요.
examples.romanization: daeum ju toyoire chingu gyeolhonsigi isseoseo mot gayo.
examples.en: I can't go because I have a friend's wedding next Saturday.
examples.note: Weekend weddings are the norm in Korea, so this is a very common excuse

examples.en: Weddings usually end in 30 minutes to an hour.
examples.note: Korean weddings are short; the meal afterward matters more socially

examples.en: After the wedding, please eat at the dining hall before you leave.
examples.note: The buffet/meal after is expected; your 축의금 covers it

entries.nuance: 결혼식 is the ceremony itself, while 결혼 is the marriage/getting married. In Korea the ceremony is often surprisingly brief and the real social event is the meal afterward, which your cash gift (축의금) pays toward. Saying 결혼식에 가요 signals you're attending as a guest.

Don't confuse 결혼식 (the ceremony) with 결혼 (marriage); '결혼했어요' means you got married, not that you attended a wedding.
Avoid 결혼식을 가다; the natural particle is 에 — 결혼식에 가다.

examples.en: I went to the funeral and gave a condolence gift.

entries.nuance: Korean funerals (장례식) typically run three days and are held at a 장례식장, frequently located within a hospital. Attending the wake of a colleague's or friend's family member is a significant social duty, and you bring 조의금 in a plain white envelope. Wear muted, dark clothing.

Don't confuse the white-envelope 조의금 (funeral) with the wedding 축의금; mixing them up is a serious faux pas.

entries.nuance: 축의금 is the cash you give at a wedding, placed in a white envelope and handed in at the 접수처 (reception desk), where you sign so the couple can record it. Amounts run roughly 50,000 won and up depending on closeness, traditionally in odd denominations. If you can't attend, transferring it to their account is perfectly normal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 축의금 (weddings/happy events) with 조의금 (funerals); using the wrong word or envelope is a real social error.
Avoid even-numbered amounts like 60,000 or 80,000; odd amounts (50,000 / 70,000 / 100,000) are customary.

entries.nuance: 상견례 is the formal first meeting between the two families before a wedding, where both sets of parents (양가 부모님) are introduced over a meal. It's a significant, somewhat formal milestone usually held at a quiet, refined restaurant, and going smoothly signals the families approve of the union.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
상견례 specifically means the two families meeting before marriage — don't use it for any general first meeting between people.
It's a formal occasion, so dress and speak politely; treating it casually can offend the in-laws-to-be.

entries.nuance: 집들이 is the housewarming party thrown after moving into a new home (이사). The classic gifts are toilet paper (휴지) and laundry detergent (세제): the paper symbolizes things unrolling smoothly, the detergent's bubbles symbolize prosperity bubbling up. It's a warm, casual event where the host usually cooks or orders in for friends.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Bringing 휴지 or 세제 is a kind, traditional gesture, not a cheap one — don't assume it's an odd gift.
집들이 is the party; don't confuse it with 이사 (the act of moving) — you do 이사 first, then 집들이.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. The text giving the deceased's name, 빈소, and funeral times

examples.romanization: oneul achime bujangnim eomeonim bugoreul badasseoyo.
examples.en: This morning I received notice of our manager's mother's passing.
examples.note: Workplace 부고 messages circulate quickly and call for attendance

examples.ko: 부고 문자에 장례식장 위치가 적혀 있었어요.
examples.romanization: bugo munjae jangnyesikjang wichiga jeokyeo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The death-notice text had the funeral hall's location written on it.
examples.note: The message bundles 빈소 location and visiting hours

examples.en: On hearing of the death I prepared condolence money right away.
examples.note: Receiving a 부고 prompts 조의금 and a visit if you're close

entries.nuance: 부고 is the formal notification that someone has died, typically circulated by family or coworkers as a 부고 문자 listing the deceased, the 빈소 (wake location), and visiting times. In a workplace, receiving a colleague's family 부고 effectively signals that attending the funeral and giving 조의금 is expected. The word and tone are solemn.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
부고 is the death NOTICE, not the funeral itself (that's 장례식); you receive a 부고 and then attend the 장례식.
Respond to a 부고 soberly — no emoji or light replies in the KakaoTalk thread; a simple condolence message is right.

entries.explanation: 조용히 (joyonghi) means "quietly, calmly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조용히 해 주세요 ("please be quiet"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조용히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Polite way to ask for quiet in a library, cafe, or meeting
Describes lowering your voice so others aren't disturbed
Common reply about a calm, low-key lifestyle
Casual, slightly sharp; 좀 adds mild irritation

examples.en: Please keep quiet in the library.
examples.note: Standard sign and spoken request you hear everywhere

examples.en: The baby's sleeping, so come in quietly.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with action verbs like 들어오다

examples.ko: 요즘은 그냥 집에서 조용히 쉬고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun geunyang jibeseo joyonghi swigo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days I'm just resting quietly at home.
examples.note: Natural way to say you're keeping things low-key

entries.nuance: 조용히 is the adverb of 조용하다 and covers both literal quietness of sound and a calm, low-key way of doing things. It works for asking people to lower their voices and for describing a peaceful lifestyle, so it is far more common in speech than the adjective alone. Note the spelling ends in 히, and the meaning shifts gently from 'silently' to 'calmly' depending on context.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 조용이; the standard form is 조용히 with 히.
Using 조용히 to mean 'secretly' — for doing something on the sly, 몰래 is the right word.

examples.romanization: bam meokgi jeone soneul kkaekkeusi ssiseuseyo.

examples.note: Common in the move-out / deposit context

examples.en: I'll get the dishes done nice and clean.
examples.note: -아/어 놓다 = do in advance and leave it

entries.nuance: 깨끗이 is the adverb from 깨끗하다 and means doing something so the result is clean and complete, not just 'in a clean manner.' It is the natural partner for 씻다, 닦다, 청소하다, where it stresses thoroughness. Watch the spelling: it ends in 이, not 히, which trips up many learners and even some natives.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 깨끗히; the correct adverb is 깨끗이 with 이.
Using 깨끗이 only for surfaces — it also means finishing something completely, as in 깨끗이 잊다 (forget cleanly / put it behind you).

Asking someone to stop touching or meddling

usagePhrases.en: now that I think about it quietly

examples.ko: 주사 맞을 때 가만히 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: jusa majeul ttae gamanhi isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: You have to stay still when getting a shot.

examples.romanization: gamanhi jom isseo bwa, naega hae julge.
examples.en: Hold still a sec, I'll do it for you.
examples.note: Casual, gentle command to stop moving

examples.en: Thinking it over quietly, I realized I'd messed up.

entries.nuance: 가만히 has two everyday senses: physically staying still (가만히 있어) and doing something quietly or letting it be (가만히 둬, 가만히 생각하다). The phrase 가만히 두다 means 'leave alone / not interfere,' which is extremely common in daily life. There is also a warning tone in 가만히 안 둬 (I won't let this slide), so context decides whether it sounds gentle or threatening.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it only as 'quietly'; 가만히 often means 'without moving' or 'leave it be,' not silence.
Confusing 가만히 두다 (leave alone) with 가만히 있다 (stay still) — the verb changes the meaning.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 꼼꼼히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.en: Read the contract carefully before you sign.
examples.note: Essential advice for leases and contracts in Korea

examples.ko: 짐을 꼼꼼히 챙겼는데도 우산을 두고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jimeul kkomkkomhi chaenggyeonneundedo usaneul dugo wasseoyo.
examples.en: Even though I packed carefully, I left my umbrella behind.
The boss taught me the work thoroughly.

entries.nuance: 꼼꼼히 is the adverb of 꼼꼼하다 and describes doing something with careful attention to every detail, never skipping or rushing. It is a strong positive in Korea, where being 꼼꼼하다 is praised at work and in study. It pairs best with checking, reading, and preparing verbs, and ends in 히.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 꼼꼼이; the standard adverb is 꼼꼼히 with 히.
Using it for speed; 꼼꼼히 is about thoroughness, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 is contradictory — careful work is usually unhurried.

entries.explanation: "enough, sufficiently, plenty" is 충분히 (chungbunhi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충분히 자다 ("to sleep enough"). Watch the particle attached to 충분히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

examples.en: There's plenty of time, so take your time.

examples.note: 익히다 = to cook through; safety tip

entries.nuance: 충분히 means 'enough / sufficiently' and reassures that a quantity or degree has been fully met, whether sleep, time, or understanding. In conversation it often softens into 'completely / totally,' as in 충분히 이해해요 or 충분히 가능해요. It is polite and supportive, which is why it shows up constantly when comforting or encouraging someone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 충분히 (sufficiently) with 완전히 (completely/entirely); 충분히 means 'enough,' not '100%.'
Forgetting it can mean 'easily / readily' in phrases like 충분히 그럴 수 있어요, not just a literal amount.

entries.shortExplanation: 분명히 means "clearly, surely, definitely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 분명히 (bunmyeonghi) = "clearly, surely, definitely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 분명히 말하다 ("to say clearly / state plainly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 분명히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 분명히 말하다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 분명히.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come

examples.en: I definitely put it here, but I can't find it.
examples.note: Super common when something goes missing

examples.en: Please tell me clearly from next time.
You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.

entries.nuance: 분명히 has two linked uses: 'clearly' as in stating something plainly, and 'surely/definitely' as in expressing strong certainty. The second use is everywhere in spoken Korean, especially the frustrated 분명히 ...했는데 (I definitely did X, but...). It sounds confident and a little insistent, so it carries more conviction than the softer 아마 (probably).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 분명히 (definitely, your own certainty) with 확실히, which can also report objective certainty.
Using 분명히 for a mere guess; it claims real confidence, so a hedge like 아마 fits unsure situations.

entries.explanation: 확실히 (hwaksilhi) means "certainly, for sure, noticeably". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 확실히 알다 ("to know for sure"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 확실히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.en: After taking the medicine, I'm noticeably better.
examples.note: 확실히 = you can clearly tell the difference

examples.ko: 이건 확실히 해 둬야 나중에 문제가 없어요.
examples.romanization: igeon hwaksilhi hae dwoya najunge munjega eopseoyo.
examples.en: We should settle this clearly so there's no problem later.
examples.note: 확실히 해 두다 = make sure / nail down

examples.en: The new phone is definitely faster, I'll give it that.

entries.nuance: 확실히 means 'certainly / for sure' and, very usefully, 'noticeably' when you can clearly observe a difference (확실히 빠르다, 확실히 낫다). Compared with 분명히, which stresses the speaker's own conviction, 확실히 leans toward objective, verifiable certainty. The set phrase 확실히 하다 / 확실히 해 두다 means to make something definite, common at work and in agreements.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 확실히 and 분명히 as identical; 확실히 emphasizes objective certainty, 분명히 your personal conviction.
Overlooking the 'noticeably' sense; 확실히 다르다 means 'clearly different,' not just 'surely different.'

entries.explanation: "simply, briefly, lightly" is 간단히 (gandanhi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 간단히 설명하다 ("to explain briefly"). Watch the particle attached to 간단히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

examples.note: 때우다 = to make do with; very natural

examples.en: I'll keep the meeting short.
examples.note: Polite promise to be brief at work

examples.en: Simply put, the point is there isn't enough money.

entries.nuance: 간단히 is the adverb of 간단하다 and means doing something in a simple, brief, or light way. It is the go-to for eating something quick (간단히 먹다), keeping explanations short, and wrapping things up without fuss. The phrase 간단히 말하면 ('in short') is a handy connector for summarizing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 간단히 (simply/briefly) with 쉽게 (easily); a task can be done 간단히 yet not be 쉽게.
Using 간단히 for a big, elaborate meal — it implies something light and quick, not a full spread.

entries.nuance: 자세히 means 'in detail / closely' and is the natural opposite of 간단히. It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick summary. It is essential for daily life in Korea, where asking 자세히 설명해 주세요 helps you get the specifics on contracts, services, and instructions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 자세히 (in detail) with 정확히 (accurately/exactly); detailed is not the same as precise.
Using 자세히 about quantity; it describes thoroughness of explanation or observation, not amount.

Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

재질 = material/composition; staff use it when describing products.
(으)로 만든 = made of; specifies what something is built from.

examples.romanization: jeo geumsok allereugi isseoseo dareun geo eopseoyo?
examples.en: I have a metal allergy, so don't you have something else?
examples.note: A genuinely useful sentence when buying earrings or watches.

examples.en: These glasses frames are metal, so they're light and sturdy.
examples.note: 안경테 = glasses frame; 튼튼하다 = sturdy, a common product virtue.

examples.ko: 금속 부분이 녹슬 수 있으니까 물기를 닦아 주세요.
examples.romanization: geumsok bubuni nokseul su isseunikka mulgireul dakka juseyo.
examples.en: The metal parts can rust, so please wipe off the moisture.
examples.note: 녹슬다 = to rust; 물기 = moisture, practical care advice.

entries.nuance: 금속 is the general word for metal as a material, used for jewelry, frames, and hardware. The single most practical phrase is 금속 알레르기 (metal allergy), which you'll want when buying earrings, watches, or belts. For specific metals Koreans name them directly (금=gold, 은=silver, 스테인리스=stainless), but 금속 covers the category.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 금속 (metal, the material) with 금 (gold specifically) — 금 is just one metal.
Saying 철 (iron) when you mean metal generally; 철 is specifically iron/steel.

examples.ko: 이 신발 밑창이 고무라서 안 미끄러워요.

examples.en: The waist of these pants is elastic, so it's comfortable.

컵 (already known) + 도자기 for the material.
제품 = product; a category sign at homeware shops.
전통 = traditional; sold as Korean craft souvenirs.

examples.ko: 이 그릇 도자기예요? 전자레인지에 써도 돼요?
examples.romanization: i geureut dojagiyeyo? jeonjareinjie sseodo dwaeyo?
examples.en: Is this dish ceramic? Can I use it in the microwave?
examples.note: A practical check; most plain ceramic is microwave-safe but patterned ones may not be.

examples.en: Ceramic breaks right away if you drop it.
examples.note: 떨어뜨리다 and 깨지다 (already known); the fragility warning.

examples.en: I bought a pretty ceramic cup in Insadong.

entries.nuance: 도자기 covers ceramics and pottery, from everyday dishes to traditional craft pieces sold in places like Insadong. It's a popular gift and souvenir category, often described as 전통 도자기. A 천 가방 (cloth/tote bag) is especially common in Korea as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic bags.

examples.romanization: i o tapseongseomyuraseo jal an gugyeojyeoyo.

examples.note: 땀 (already known); slow-drying sweat is a known downside for everyday wear.

examples.en: Do you prefer natural fibers or synthetic ones?
examples.note: Natural vs. synthetic is the basic fabric distinction when shopping.

entries.nuance: 합성섬유 means synthetic fiber, the umbrella term for man-made fabrics like 폴리에스터 (polyester), as opposed to 천연섬유 (natural fibers) such as 면, 울, and 실크. Clothing tags use these category words, so recognizing 합성섬유 100% tells you a garment is fully man-made. Synthetics resist wrinkles but can feel less breathable, which matters in humid Korean summers.

examples.romanization: swineun sigani jjalbaseo maejeomeun neul sarami manayo.

편의점과 혼동하지 마세요. 매점은 보통 24시간이 아니고 학교 운영 시간에만 엽니다.

회사에 가는 건 '출근'이에요. 학교에 가는 건 등교로 구분하세요.

entries.explanation: 사탕 (satang) means "candy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사탕 하나 주세요 ("One candy, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사탕 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 사탕 하나 주세요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 사탕.

usagePhrases.note: Counting small candies with 하나/한 개 is the most natural way at a register.
Drop the subject in casual talk; context makes 'you' clear.
막대(stick) + 사탕 — a fixed compound, written as one word.

usagePhrases.en: Want me to unwrap the candy for you?
usagePhrases.note: 까다 (to peel/unwrap) is the everyday verb for opening wrapped candy.

examples.en: I bought a bag of candy at the convenience store.
examples.note: 봉지 is the counter for a bag/packet of snacks.

examples.ko: 목 아플 때 사탕 하나 먹으면 좀 나아요.
examples.romanization: mok apeul ttae satang hana meogeumyeon jom naayo.
examples.en: When my throat hurts, eating a candy helps a bit.
examples.note: Many Koreans treat throat-soothing candy as a mild remedy.

examples.en: The kids only want to eat candy, so I'm worried.

entries.nuance: 사탕 covers hard candy and lollipops, not gummies (those are 젤리) or chocolate (초콜릿). On Valentine's Day women give 초콜릿, and on White Day (March 14) men reciprocate with 사탕, so the word carries a small romantic-gift nuance in season.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling gummy candies 사탕 — soft chewy ones are 젤리, not 사탕.
Saying 사탕을 열다 to mean 'unwrap a candy'; Koreans say 사탕을 까다.

entries.explanation: "chocolate" is 초콜릿 (chokollit). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 초콜릿 한 개 ("one piece of chocolate"). Watch the particle attached to 초콜릿 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. 녹다 (to melt) is the verb you'll hear in summer.
Loanword modifiers like 다크/밀크 sit directly before 초콜릿.

usagePhrases.en: Cut back on chocolate a little
usagePhrases.note: 줄이다 = to reduce; common health-talk phrasing.

examples.note: Giving 초콜릿 on Feb 14 is a big custom in Korea.

examples.romanization: pigonhal ttae chokollin meogeumyeon gibuni jom joajyeoyo.

examples.ko: 이 빵 안에 초콜릿이 들어 있어요.
examples.romanization: i ppang ane chokollisi deureo isseoyo.
examples.en: There's chocolate inside this bread.
examples.note: 들어 있다 = to be contained inside.

entries.nuance: Note the spelling: 초콜릿, not 초콜렛 (a very common misspelling even among natives). The standard counter for a bar is 판, while individual squares or pieces use 개. Chocolate is the default Valentine's gift from women to men, mirrored by 사탕 on White Day.

entries.shortExplanation: 팝콘 means "popcorn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "popcorn" is 팝콘 (papkon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 팝콘 한 통 ("one tub of popcorn"). Watch the particle attached to 팝콘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 통 (tub/bucket) is the cinema counter for popcorn.
Flavor sits before 팝콘; 카라멜/치즈 are most common.
튀기다 (to fry/pop) is the standard verb.
Cinemas let you split flavors; 반반 = half-half.

examples.ko: 영화관에서 팝콘 큰 거 하나 시켰어요.
examples.romanization: yeonghwagwaneseo papkon keun geo hana sikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ordered one large popcorn at the cinema.
examples.note: 큰 거 = the big one; 시키다 = to order.

examples.ko: 고소한 팝콘 냄새 때문에 안 사고는 못 배겨요.
examples.romanization: gosohan papkon naemsae ttaemune an sagoneun mot baegyeoyo.
examples.en: The savory popcorn smell makes it impossible not to buy some.
examples.note: 고소하다 = nutty/savory; idiomatic 못 배기다 = can't resist.

examples.en: I made microwave popcorn at home.
examples.note: 돌리다 = to run (the microwave), then 먹다.

entries.nuance: 팝콘 is strongly tied to the cinema in Korea, where caramel and cheese (and half-and-half, 반반) are the default choices, often bundled with a drink in a 콤보 set. The cinema counter is 통, while microwave popcorn at home uses 봉지. The smell is classic 고소하다 (savory-nutty).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Ordering popcorn by 개 — at a cinema you ask for 한 통 (one tub).
Forgetting that flavored popcorn is the norm; plain butter is less common than caramel/cheese.

examples.ko: 겨울에 길거리에서 따뜻한 호떡 먹는 게 최고예요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure gilgeorieseo ttatteutan hotteong meongneun ge choegoyeyo.
examples.en: Eating warm hotteok on the street in winter is the best.
examples.note: Hotteok is a quintessential winter street food; -는 게 최고예요 = is the best.

examples.ko: 호떡 안에 흑설탕이 흘러나와서 입천장 데었어요.
examples.romanization: hotteok ane heukseoltangi heulleonawaseo ipcheonjang deeosseoyo.
examples.en: The brown sugar oozed out of the hotteok and I burned the roof of my mouth.
examples.note: 흑설탕 = brown sugar; the molten filling is famously hot.

examples.ko: 호떡 한 입 베어 물자마자 너무 뜨거웠어요.
examples.romanization: hotteo kan ip beeo muljamaja neomu tteugeowosseoyo.
examples.en: The moment I bit into the hotteok it was way too hot.
examples.note: 베어 물다 = to bite into; -자마자 = as soon as.

entries.nuance: 호떡 is a chewy griddle-fried pancake with a molten brown-sugar-and-cinnamon center, sold piping hot from winter street carts. Expecting 호떡 to be savory — the classic filling is sweet brown sugar.

슈크림 fillings now rival the classic 팥(red bean).

usagePhrases.en: Do you eat the head or tail first?

examples.en: These days it's hard to find a place selling bungeoppang.

examples.ko: 붕어빵은 팥이 꼬리까지 꽉 차 있어야 진짜죠.
examples.romanization: bungeoppangeun pachi kkorikkaji kkwak cha isseoya jinjjajyo.
examples.en: A real bungeoppang has red bean packed all the way to the tail.
examples.note: 꽉 차다 = packed full; locals judge stalls by this.

examples.ko: 추운 날 붕어빵 봉지 들고 호호 불면서 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: chuun nal bungeoppang bongji deulgo hoho bulmyeonseo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: On a cold day I ate bungeoppang from the bag, blowing on it.
examples.note: 호호 불다 = to blow (to cool); cozy winter image.

entries.nuance: 붕어빵 is a fish-shaped waffle-batter pastry filled with sweet red-bean paste, the iconic Korean winter street snack alongside 호떡 and 군고구마. Stalls have grown rare enough that fans share locations via a 'bungeoppang map' app, and locals fondly debate eating head-first vs. tail-first.

entries.explanation: 어묵 (eomuk) means "fish cake". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어묵 한 꼬치 ("one skewer of fish cake"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어묵 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

entries.nuance: 어묵 is the standard word for fish cake, eaten street-style on skewers (꼬치) with a free, endlessly refilled hot 국물 in winter. Many speakers casually call it 오뎅 from Japanese, though 어묵 is the 'proper' term. Busan (부산어묵) is the famous home of it, and packaged versions are common gifts and soup ingredients.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 오뎅 is wrong — it's extremely common in speech, just not the standard term.
Forgetting the broth is self-serve and refillable; you don't pay per cup.

entries.nuance: 튀김 means deep-fried, battered snacks in the Korean tempura tradition — fried squid, shrimp, sweet potato, and 김말이 (seaweed-noodle rolls) — sold at 분식 stalls next to 떡볶이 and 순대. Expecting one item — 튀김 usually refers to an assortment; specify the ingredient (오징어 튀김 etc.) to order one kind.

entries.nuance: 약과 is a traditional Korean confection (한과): wheat-flour dough fried and soaked in honey or grain syrup, historically a holiday and ritual-table sweet. It has surged back into fashion among 20-30s as part of the '할매니얼' retro-snack trend, with cafes selling 미니 약과 and yakgwa-topped desserts. It's quite sweet and pleasantly chewy (쫀득하다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 약과 contains medicine because of 약(藥) — the name is historical; it's just a honey cookie.
Grouping it with Western 과자 — 약과 is specifically a 한과 (traditional confection).

entries.shortExplanation: 축구 means "soccer, football" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 축구 (chukgu) means "soccer, football". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 축구 좋아해요? ("Do you like soccer?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 축구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Let's play a game of soccer
usagePhrases.note: 판 is the casual counter for a round/match of a game; 한 판 하다 = 'play a round'.

usagePhrases.en: Want to go watch a soccer game?
usagePhrases.note: 보러 가다 = 'go to watch'; used for stadium games or a sports bar.

examples.en: I play soccer with my friends every weekend.
examples.note: 축구 하다 (no 를 needed in speech) = 'play soccer'; 마다 = 'every'.

examples.ko: 어젯밤에 손흥민 나오는 축구 경기 봤어요?
examples.romanization: eojetbame sonheungmin naoneun chukgu gyeonggi bwasseoyo?
examples.en: Did you watch the soccer match Son Heung-min was in last night?
examples.note: EPL games with 손흥민 are huge water-cooler talk; 나오다 = 'appear/be featured'.

examples.ko: 한국이 일본을 이겨서 축구 팬들이 다 난리 났어요.
examples.romanization: hangugi ilboneul igyeoseo chukgu paendeuri da nalli nasseoyo.
examples.en: Korea beat Japan, so all the soccer fans went wild.
examples.note: 난리 나다 = 'go crazy/be in an uproar'; the Korea-Japan rivalry is intense.

entries.nuance: 축구 is the default national sport for casual conversation, especially men's chat — knowing 손흥민 (Son Heung-min) buys instant rapport. The verb is 축구(를) 하다 for playing and 축구(를) 보다 for watching; in speech the 를 is usually dropped. Note the spelled-out compound 조기 축구 (dawn amateur soccer), a cultural fixture worth recognizing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 풋볼 — Koreans always say 축구, and 풋볼 sounds like American football to them.
Using 게임 for a match; a soccer match is 축구 경기, not 축구 게임.

usagePhrases.note: Korea's most-attended pro sport (KBO); a safe, friendly small-talk topic.

usagePhrases.en: Which team do you root for?
usagePhrases.note: Asking someone's KBO team is a classic bonding question; 응원하다 = 'cheer for'.

usagePhrases.en: Let's go to a baseball game
usagePhrases.note: KBO stadiums are famous for loud, fun fan culture with chants and food.
The KBO season runs spring through fall; 시즌 is the everyday loanword.

examples.ko: 주말에 잠실 가서 야구 볼 거예요.
examples.romanization: jumare jamsil gaseo yagu bol geoyeyo.
examples.en: I'm going to Jamsil this weekend to watch baseball.
examples.note: 잠실 (Jamsil Stadium) is Seoul's main baseball venue; locals say just 잠실 가다.

examples.en: When you go to a baseball stadium, chicken and beer are a must.
examples.note: 치맥 (chicken+beer) at the ballpark is iconic; 필수 = 'a must'.

examples.en: Our team came from behind in the 9th, it was such a thrill.

entries.nuance: 야구 (KBO league) is arguably the sport Koreans are most passionate about attending in person — the stadium experience, team chants, and bringing your own 치맥 are a whole culture. Asking 어느 팀 응원해요? signals you want to connect. The verb pattern mirrors 축구: 야구(를) 하다 / 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For a pro game, Koreans usually name the venue (잠실 가다, 고척 가다) rather than saying 야구장 가다 — 야구장 sounds more like a generic/amateur field.
Confusing 회 (inning) with 회 (raw fish) — context and number make it clear, but 9회 here means the ninth inning.

entries.shortExplanation: 농구 means "basketball" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 농구 (nonggu) = "basketball". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 농구 할 줄 알아요? ("Do you know how to play basketball?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 농구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 농구 할 줄 알아요?. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 농구.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know how to play basketball?
usagePhrases.note: 할 줄 알다 = 'know how to do'; common when proposing a pickup game.

usagePhrases.en: Let's play a game of basketball
usagePhrases.note: 게임 works naturally for pickup hoops; 한 게임 = 'one game'.
골대 = the hoop/goal post; you'll see them at parks and schoolyards.
Many younger Koreans follow the NBA closely; the acronym is said in English letters.

examples.en: After work I go play basketball with coworkers.
examples.note: 하러 가다 = 'go to do'; a popular after-work activity for young men.

examples.ko: 키 크면 농구 잘할 것 같다는 말 많이 들어요.
examples.romanization: ki keumyeon nonggu jalhal geot gatdaneun mal mani deureoyo.
examples.en: People often tell me I'd be good at basketball since I'm tall.
examples.note: Common stereotype-based small talk; 잘하다 = 'be good at'.

examples.en: I played a game with strangers at the neighborhood court.
examples.note: Pickup games (픽업 게임) at outdoor courts are common; 농구장 = 'basketball court'.

entries.nuance: 농구 had a huge cultural moment in the 90s (the drama 'Last Match' / 만화 'Slam Dunk' generation), and pickup games at neighborhood 농구장 remain popular among younger men. You can say either 농구 경기 (formal match) or 농구 게임 (casual pickup); 게임 is fine here, unlike with pro soccer. Verb is 농구(를) 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 바스켓볼 — Koreans only say 농구.
Saying 농구 문 for the hoop; the correct word is 골대 (or 농구 골대).

entries.shortExplanation: 배구 means "volleyball" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배구 (baegu) means "volleyball". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배구 좋아해요? ("Do you like volleyball?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Women's pro volleyball (V-리그) has a strong, growing fanbase in Korea.

usagePhrases.en: Did you watch the volleyball match?
usagePhrases.note: 경기 is the standard word for a formal match in any sport.
국가대표 (national team) often comes up around 김연경 and the Olympics.
배구 was a common P.E. and 체육대회 (sports day) sport for many Koreans.

examples.ko: 김연경 선수 덕분에 배구 팬이 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: gimyeongyeong seonsu deokbune baegu paeni manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to Kim Yeon-koung, volleyball gained a lot of fans.
examples.note: 덕분에 = 'thanks to'; 김연경 is a beloved volleyball star.

examples.ko: 우리 회사 체육대회 때 배구 시합 했어요.
examples.romanization: uri hoesa cheyukdaehoe ttae baegu siha paesseoyo.
examples.en: We had a volleyball match at our company sports day.
examples.note: 시합 = match/contest, interchangeable with 경기 in casual use; 체육대회 = company/school sports day.

examples.ko: 배구는 키가 큰 선수들이 유리한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: baeguneun kiga keun seonsudeuri yurihan geot gatayo.
examples.en: It seems taller players have an advantage in volleyball.

entries.nuance: 배구 surged in popularity thanks to women's pro volleyball and especially 김연경 (Kim Yeon-koung), making it a warmer small-talk topic than it once was. It's also a nostalgic schoolyard and company sports-day (체육대회) game. You can use 경기 or the slightly more casual 시합 for a match.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 발리볼 — the Korean word is 배구.
Mixing up 배구 (volleyball) with 배 (boat/stomach/pear) — the full word 배구 avoids confusion.

entries.shortExplanation: 탁구 means "table tennis, ping-pong" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "table tennis, ping-pong" is 탁구 (takgu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 탁구 칠 줄 알아요? ("Can you play table tennis?"). Watch the particle attached to 탁구 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 탁구 칠 줄 알아요?. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 탁구.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Note the verb: 탁구는 치다 ('hit'), not 하다 — like other racket/paddle sports.

usagePhrases.en: Shall we play a round of ping-pong?
usagePhrases.note: 치다 + 판; a common spontaneous suggestion at a community center.
Dedicated 탁구장 are common in neighborhoods and apartment complexes.
Called 라켓; the table itself is 탁구대.

examples.en: During lunch we play ping-pong in the office lounge.
examples.note: 휴게실 = 'break room'; many Korean offices have a 탁구대.

examples.ko: 탁구는 운동도 되고 재미도 있어서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: takguneun undongdo doego jaemido isseoseo joayo.
examples.en: Table tennis is good because it's both exercise and fun.

examples.ko: 아파트 주민센터에 탁구대가 있어서 자주 쳐요.
examples.romanization: apateu juminsenteoe takgudaega isseoseo jaju chyeoyo.
examples.en: There's a table tennis table at the apartment community center, so I play often.
examples.note: 주민센터/커뮤니티 facilities often include a 탁구대; 치다 is the verb.

entries.nuance: Crucially, table tennis uses the verb 치다 (to hit), not 하다 — 탁구를 치다. It's an accessible, low-cost activity found in 탁구장, apartment community rooms, and office break rooms, so it's a realistic way to socialize. The table is 탁구대 and the paddle is 라켓.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 탁구 하다 instead of the natural 탁구 치다.

entries.explanation: "skiing, ski" is 스키 (seuki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스키 탈 줄 알아요? ("Do you know how to ski?"). examples.en: This winter I'm going to Gangwon-do to ski.
examples.note: 강원도 has Korea's main ski resorts; 타러 가다 = 'go to ski'.

examples.note: 초보자 코스 = 'beginner course'; 처음이라 = 'since it's my first time'.

examples.note: 넘어지다 = 'fall down'; note 스키 타다 throughout.
