entries.nuance: 마라톤 fits the current 러닝 (running) boom among Koreans in their 20s-30s — running crews and weekend 마라톤 대회 are genuinely trendy social scenes. The verb is 뛰다 or 달리다 (to run), 완주 means finishing the full distance, and many start with a 하프 마라톤 before attempting the 풀코스.

Saying 마라톤 하다 — more natural is 마라톤(을) 뛰다 or 달리다.
Assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km; in casual use it can refer to any race distance at a 마라톤 대회.

entries.shortExplanation: 경기 means "match, game (sporting event)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "match, game (sporting event)" is 경기 (gyeonggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 경기 봤어요? ("Did you watch the game?"). Watch the particle attached to 경기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 경기 봤어요?. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 경기.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 경기 is the standard word for a sports match in any sport.
시작하다 = 'begin'; said when a match kicks off.
결과 = 'result'; 경기 결과 is how you ask the final score/outcome.
있다 = 'there is'; common check before planning to watch.

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 중요한 축구 경기가 있어요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge jungyohan chukgu gyeonggiga isseoyo.
examples.en: There's an important soccer match this evening.
examples.note: Attach 경기 after the sport: 축구 경기, 야구 경기, etc.

examples.ko: 경기가 너무 박빙이라 끝까지 손에 땀을 쥐었어요.
examples.romanization: gyeonggiga neomu bakbingira kkeutkkaji sone ttameul jwieosseoyo.
examples.en: The game was so close I was on edge until the end.
examples.note: 박빙 = 'neck and neck'; 손에 땀을 쥐다 = idiom 'be on the edge of one's seat'.

examples.en: The game was canceled today because of rain.
examples.note: 취소되다 = 'be canceled'; outdoor 경기 often gets rained out.

entries.nuance: 경기 is the all-purpose word for a sporting match and pairs with any sport (축구 경기, 야구 경기). It's more formal/neutral than the loanword 게임, which fits casual pickup play; for pro and broadcast sports, 경기 is the right choice. 시합 is a near-synonym leaning slightly toward 'contest/bout.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 게임 for a pro match — use 경기 for real sporting events.
Confusing this 경기(sports match) with the homophone 경기(the economy), as in 경기가 안 좋다; context disambiguates.

entries.shortExplanation: 심판 means "referee, umpire" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 심판 (simpan) = "referee, umpire". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 심판이 휘슬 불었어요 ("The referee blew the whistle") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 심판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 심판이 휘슬 불었어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 심판.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 휘슬(을) 불다 = 'blow the whistle'; signals a foul or stoppage.
판정 = 'ruling/decision'; 심판 판정 often sparks fan complaints.
A typical heated shout from fans/players at a bad call; 똑바로 = 'properly'.
오심(誤審) = a refereeing error; a very common sports-news word.

examples.ko: 심판이 우리 팀한테만 불리하게 판정하는 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: simpani uri timhanteman bullihage panjeonghaneun geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: It felt like the referee was ruling unfairly against only our team.
Anyone can see that play was a wrong call.
examples.note: 누가 봐도 = 'no matter who looks / obviously'; 오심 = 'bad call'.

examples.ko: 요즘은 비디오 판독으로 심판 오심을 줄여요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun bidio pandogeuro simpan osimeul juryeoyo.
examples.en: These days they reduce referee errors with video review.

entries.nuance: 심판 is the referee/umpire across all sports, and the related noun 오심 (a wrong call) plus 판정 (a ruling) are essential for following sports talk and complaints. Fans frequently grumble about 심판 판정, and 비디오 판독 (video review) is the modern fix. The whistle collocation is 휘슬을 불다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 레퍼리 — Koreans say 심판, not the English loanword.
Confusing 심판 (referee) with the religious/judgment sense of 심판 (e.g., 최후의 심판 'the Last Judgment'); in sports it's strictly the official.

entries.shortExplanation: 망치 means "hammer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 망치 (mangchi) means "hammer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 망치 ("hammer"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 망치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday tool for driving nails; a basic item in any 공구함.

usagePhrases.en: to drive a nail in with a hammer
usagePhrases.note: 못을 박다 = to hammer a nail in; (으)로 marks the tool.
Noun + 질 turns it into the activity; 망치질하다 = to hammer.

usagePhrases.en: Could you lend me a hammer?
usagePhrases.note: Common favor to ask a neighbor or building manager.

examples.ko: 벽에 액자 걸려고 망치로 못을 박았어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge aekja geollyeogo mangchiro moseul bagasseoyo.
examples.en: I hammered a nail into the wall to hang a frame.
examples.note: 걸려고 = in order to hang; 박다 is the verb for driving nails in.

examples.ko: 망치질할 때 손가락 안 다치게 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: mangchijilhal ttae songarak an dachige josimhaseyo.
examples.en: Be careful not to hurt your fingers when you hammer.
examples.note: 안 다치게 = so as not to get hurt; practical safety caution.

examples.ko: 고무망치는 가구 조립할 때 흠집 안 나서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gomumangchineun gagu joripal ttae heumjip an naseo joayo.
examples.en: A rubber mallet is good for assembling furniture since it doesn't leave marks.
examples.note: 고무망치 = rubber mallet, common for IKEA-style furniture.

entries.nuance: 망치는 못을 박을 때 쓰는 가장 기본적인 공구라 자취방에 하나쯤 있으면 액자나 선반을 달 때 편합니다. 가구를 조립할 때는 흠집이 안 나는 '고무망치'를 따로 쓰기도 합니다. 동사로는 '망치로 못을 박다'처럼 쓰고, 행위 자체는 '망치질'이라고 부릅니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 망치를 치다 — the natural phrase is 못을 박다 (drive the nail), with 망치로 as the tool.
Confusing 망치 (hammer) with 못 (nail); the hammer hits, the 못 is what gets hit.

entries.explanation: "nail (for hammering)" is 못 (mot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 못 ("nail"). usagePhrases.note: The metal nail you hammer in; not to be confused with 못 'cannot' before a verb.
박다 = to drive/embed; the standard verb that pairs with 못.
빼다 = to pull out; use pliers (펜치) or the claw of a hammer.
The hole left in the wall; too many can mean a deposit deduction.

examples.romanization: i moseun neomu jjalbaseo byeoge an bakyeoyo.
examples.en: This nail is too short, so it won't go into the wall.
examples.note: 박히다 = to get driven in (passive of 박다).

examples.ko: 전셋집이라 못 박는 거 조심해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeonsetjibira mot bangneun geo josimhaeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: It's a jeonse place, so I have to be careful about hammering nails.
examples.note: Landlords may deduct from the deposit for wall damage.

examples.ko: 벽에 못 자국 남으면 보증금에서 깎일 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge mot jagung nameumyeon bojeunggeumeseo kkakkil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If nail marks are left on the wall, it could be deducted from the deposit.
examples.note: 못 자국 = nail marks; 깎이다 = to get docked.

entries.nuance: 못은 망치로 벽이나 나무에 박는 금속 핀으로, '못을 박다 / 빼다'처럼 동사와 함께 씁니다. 한국에서는 전세·월세 집 벽에 못을 박으면 보증금에서 수리비를 깎을 수 있어서, 요즘은 못 대신 떼었다 붙이는 무타공 걸이를 많이 씁니다. 동사 앞에 붙어 '못 가요(못 간다)'처럼 쓰이는 부정 표현과 글자는 같지만 전혀 다른 단어입니다.

Mixing up the noun 못 (nail) with the adverb 못 used for inability (못 해요).

십자 = cross-shaped; the most commonly needed type at home.
일자 = straight line; for slotted screws.

entries.nuance: 드라이버는 나사를 풀고 조이는 손공구로, 집에 하나 두려면 '십자'와 '일자'가 한 세트로 있는 게 편합니다. 같은 외래어가 골프채(드라이버)나 운전자(driver) 뜻으로도 쓰여서 문맥으로 구분해야 합니다. 나사와 함께 '풀다(loosen) / 조이다(tighten)' 동사를 짝지어 외워 두면 좋습니다.

usagePhrases.en: to measure with a tape measure

examples.en: Measure the spot where the fridge will go with a tape measure first.
examples.note: 들어갈 자리 = the spot it'll fit into; 재 보다 = to try measuring.

examples.ko: 줄자가 없어서 핸드폰 앱으로 대충 쟀어요.
examples.romanization: juljaga eopseoseo haendeupon aebeuro daechung jaesseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't have a tape measure, so I roughly measured with a phone app.
examples.note: 대충 = roughly; phone AR measure apps are common.

examples.ko: 이 책상 가로세로 좀 재 줄래? 새 방에 들어갈지 봐야 돼.
examples.romanization: i chaeksang garosero jom jae jullae? sae bange deureogalji bwaya dwae.
examples.en: Can you measure this desk's width and length? I need to see if it fits the new room.
examples.note: 들어갈지 = whether it'll fit; useful when moving.

entries.nuance: 줄자는 가구나 가전이 들어갈 공간의 치수를 잴 때 쓰는 도구로, 이사하거나 가구를 살 때 꼭 필요합니다. 동사는 '재다'를 쓰고, 공간을 잴 때는 '가로세로'라는 표현을 자주 같이 씁니다. 요즘은 줄자가 없으면 휴대폰 계측 앱으로 대신 재기도 하지만 정확도는 줄자가 낫습니다.

Saying 길이를 보다; you 재다 (measure) a length, you don't 보다 it.

usagePhrases.note: For reaching high places; a folding step ladder is common at home.
올라가다 = to go up; 에 marks where you climb onto.
The truck-mounted lift used for moving (이삿짐) on moving day in Korea.
A popular way to decide who pays/loses; drawing ladder lines.

examples.ko: 전등 갈아야 하는데 사다리 좀 잡아 줄래?
examples.romanization: jeondeung garaya haneunde sadari jom jaba jullae?
examples.en: I have to change the light — can you hold the ladder for me?
examples.note: 잡아 주다 = to hold (for safety); common request.

examples.en: When moving, it was the 5th floor, so we called a ladder lift truck.
examples.note: Reflects how Korean apartment moves usually work.

examples.ko: 누가 커피 살지 사다리 타기로 정하자.
examples.romanization: nuga keopi salji sadari tagiro jeonghaja.
examples.en: Let's decide who buys coffee with a ladder game.
examples.note: 사다리 타기 = the random ladder picker game.

entries.nuance: 사다리는 높은 곳에 올라갈 때 쓰는 도구로, 집에서는 접이식 사다리를 흔히 씁니다. 한국에서 이사할 때 높은 층으로 짐을 올릴 때 부르는 '사다리차'도 꼭 알아 두면 좋습니다. 또 '사다리 타기'는 커피 내기처럼 누가 할지 정할 때 하는 놀이를 가리키는 일상 표현입니다.

Forgetting 사다리차 on moving day; high-floor moves in Korea rely on it.

usagePhrases.note: Wall/furniture paint; the loanword from English.
칠하다 = to coat/paint; the standard verb with 페인트.
페인트 + 칠; 페인트칠하다 = to do the painting.
묻다 = to get smeared; warn people about wet paint.

examples.ko: 방 분위기 바꾸려고 한쪽 벽에 페인트 칠했어요.
examples.romanization: bang bunwigi bakkuryeogo hanjjok byeoge peinteu chilhaesseoyo.
examples.en: To change the room's mood, I painted one wall.
examples.note: 분위기 = mood/vibe; accent-wall DIY is popular.

examples.en: Don't touch it until the paint dries.
examples.note: 마르다 = to dry; 만지다 = to touch.

examples.en: I bought a roller and masking tape to paint it myself.
examples.note: 셀프 = DIY/by oneself; 롤러 = paint roller.

entries.nuance: 페인트는 벽이나 가구에 칠하는 도료로, 동사는 '칠하다'를 쓰고 행위는 '페인트칠'이라고 합니다. 요즘 2030 세대는 방 분위기를 바꾸려고 한쪽 벽만 다른 색으로 칠하는 '셀프 페인트칠'을 많이 합니다. 칠한 뒤에는 '페인트가 마를 때까지' 만지지 않도록 주의해야 합니다.

examples.romanization: keibeultaineun han beon joimyeon jareugi jeonen mot pureoyo.
examples.en: Once you tighten a zip tie, you can't undo it without cutting.
examples.note: 조이다 = to tighten; they're one-way unless reusable.

examples.ko: 다이소에서 케이블타이 한 봉지 사면 한참 써요.
examples.romanization: daisoeseo keibeultai han bongji samyeon hancham sseoyo.
examples.en: If you buy a pack of zip ties at Daiso, they last a long time.
examples.note: 한 봉지 = one pack; 한참 = for a good while.

examples.romanization: eoduunde haendeupon sonjeondeung jom kyeo jullae?
examples.en: It's dark — can you turn on your phone flashlight?
examples.note: Everyday request; phone light is the default these days.

넣어 두다 = to put away and store; 에 marks the location.
A boxed set of basic tools; a handy one-buy for a new home.

examples.en: When I moved, I got myself a basic toolbox.
Put the screwdriver back in the toolbox.
examples.note: 다시 넣어 두다 = to put it back and store it.

examples.ko: 공구함에 망치랑 드라이버, 줄자 정도는 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gongguhame mangchirang deuraibeo, julja jeongdoneun isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: A toolbox should at least have a hammer, screwdriver, and tape measure.

묶다 = to tie/bind; the core verb with 노끈.

풀다 = to undo/untie; opposite of 묶다.

examples.en: Tie the newspapers with twine and put them out for recycling.

examples.ko: 노끈이 약해서 무거운 거 묶으면 끊어져요.
examples.romanization: nokkeuni yakaeseo mugeoun geo mukkeumyeon kkeuneojyeoyo.
examples.en: The twine is weak, so it snaps if you tie heavy things.
examples.note: 끊어지다 = to snap/break; use stronger cord for heavy loads.

entries.explanation: "chilly, nippy (cool air)" is 쌀쌀하다 (ssalssalhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 쌀쌀하다 ("to be chilly"). polite present; the go-to weather small talk in spring and fall

examples.en: These days it's chilly morning and evening, so bring a jacket.
examples.note: classic seasonal advice you'll hear and use constantly

examples.ko: 오늘 좀 쌀쌀하지 않아요? 가디건 입고 올걸.
examples.romanization: oneul jom ssalssalhaji anayo? gadigeon ipgo olgeol.
examples.en: Isn't it a bit chilly today? I should've worn a cardigan.
examples.note: natural office or cafe small talk

examples.en: The wind's blowing so it's chillier than I expected.

entries.nuance: 쌀쌀하다 is a mild, brisk chill — the kind that makes you want a light jacket, typical of spring and autumn. It can also describe a person's cold, distant attitude (쌀쌀맞다 / 쌀쌀하게 대하다), so context tells you whether it's weather or personality.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for deep winter cold — that's 춥다 or 매섭다, not 쌀쌀하다.
Confusing it with 싸늘하다, which feels colder and often carries an eerie or tense undertone.

entries.explanation: 포근하다 (pogeunhada) = "mild and cozy (unusually warm)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 포근하다 ("to be mild/cozy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 포근하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: gently warm, especially a winter day that's warmer than usual; also a soft, snug feeling
polite present; said happily when winter cold eases up
날(이) + adjective is a natural weather frame

examples.en: Even though it's midwinter, the day is so mild today.
examples.note: the typical context: a surprisingly warm winter day

examples.en: The blanket is so cozy I don't want to get up.
examples.note: 포근하다 also describes soft, snug things, not just weather

examples.ko: 눈이 와도 바람이 없어서 포근한 느낌이에요.
examples.romanization: nuni wado barami eopseoseo pogeunhan neukkimieyo.
examples.en: Even though it's snowing, there's no wind so it feels cozy.
examples.note: 포근한 느낌 = a warm, gentle vibe

entries.nuance: 포근하다 carries a warm, comforting feeling — mostly used for a winter day that turns out mild, or for soft, snuggly things like blankets. It's emotionally positive; you say it with relief or contentment, unlike neutral 따뜻하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for hot summer warmth — 포근하다 is for gentle/mild warmth, never summer heat.
Forgetting it also means 'soft and cozy' for objects; don't limit it to weather.

examples.en: This summer is unusually sweltering, so everyone's struggling.

examples.romanization: bamedo an sigeoseo mudeoun yeoldaeyaga gyesokdwaeyo.

usagePhrases.note: comfortable coolness, especially early autumn after summer heat breaks

examples.ko: 이제 아침 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 딱 좋아요.

examples.en: The night breeze is nice and cool, so I'll leave the window open.

examples.en: The heat has died down a bit and it's gotten cool.
examples.note: 한풀 꺾이다 = (heat) to ease off; a very Korean expression

Pairing it with summer heat; 선선하다 implies the heat has already passed.

usagePhrases.note: high moisture in the air; the defining feature of Korean summer and the rainy season
습한 before a noun; also 습한 공기 (damp air)
습하다 + 덥다 is the classic summer combo

examples.ko: 장마철엔 너무 습해서 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren neomu seupaeseo ppallaega jal an mallayo.
examples.en: During the rainy season it's so humid that laundry doesn't dry well.
examples.note: a very real apartment-life problem in Korea

examples.ko: 방이 습한 것 같아서 제습기를 틀었어요.
examples.romanization: bangi seupan geot gataseo jeseupgireul teureosseoyo.
examples.en: The room felt damp so I turned on the dehumidifier.
examples.note: 제습기 (dehumidifier) is a summer essential here

examples.en: Today's not humid and feels nice and dry — so pleasant.
examples.note: 보송보송하다 = pleasantly dry; the opposite feeling

entries.nuance: 습하다 focuses on moisture/dampness in the air, separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool day. In Korea it's the word behind summer misery: damp laundry, mold (곰팡이), and the constant hum of the 제습기.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 덥다 (hot); 습하다 is about moisture, not heat, even if they often go together.
Using it for dry conditions — the opposite is 건조하다.

usagePhrases.note: low humidity in the air; the hallmark of Korean winter and spring
polite present; also used for dry skin (피부가 건조해요)
건조주의보 is a real warning issued in dry, fire-risk seasons

examples.ko: 겨울엔 너무 건조해서 가습기를 꼭 틀어요.
examples.romanization: gyeouren neomu geonjohaeseo gaseupgireul kkok teureoyo.
examples.en: In winter it's so dry that I always run a humidifier.
examples.note: 가습기 (humidifier) is a winter must-have in Korea

examples.en: The weather's so dry my lips keep chapping.
examples.note: 트다 = (skin/lips) to chap; common winter complaint

examples.ko: 피부가 건조할 땐 보습 크림을 발라요.
examples.romanization: pibuga geonjohal ttaen boseup keurimeul ballayo.
examples.en: When my skin is dry, I put on moisturizing cream.
examples.note: 건조하다 applies to skin as well as air

entries.nuance: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air, the opposite of 습하다 — typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season. It applies equally to skin (피부가 건조하다) and can describe a dry, dull personality or tone, so let context guide you.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing it up with 습하다; 건조하다 = dry, 습하다 = humid.
Forgetting the skin/personality uses — it's not only a weather word.

entries.explanation: 매섭다 (maeseopda) = "bitterly cold, biting (wind, cold)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매섭다 ("to be biting/fierce") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매섭다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 매섭다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 매섭다.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular; piercing winter cold or a sharp, cutting wind
매서운 바람/추위 are the standard pairings

examples.en: The wind was so biting that my ears froze.
examples.note: the visceral feeling of a Seoul winter wind

examples.ko: 오늘 추위가 매서우니까 패딩 단단히 입으세요.
examples.romanization: oneul chuwiga maeseounikka paeding dandanhi ibeuseyo.
examples.en: The cold is biting today, so bundle up well in your padded coat.
examples.note: 패딩 (padded coat) is the Korean winter uniform

examples.en: On top of the cold wave, a knife-like wind blew bitterly.
examples.note: 칼바람 (knife wind) + 매섭다 is very natural

entries.nuance: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing quality — most often a biting winter wind or sharp cold that hurts your skin. Note the ㅂ-irregular (매서워요, 매서운). It can also describe a sharp, severe gaze or scolding (매서운 눈빛), reflecting its core sense of 'cutting/intense'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it as 매섭어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 매서워요.
Using it for mild cold — 매섭다 is reserved for harsh, painful cold or wind.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 따사롭다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

the natural subject is sunlight, not air temperature

examples.ko: 봄 햇살이 따사로워서 벤치에 한참 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: bom haetsari ttasarowoseo benchie hancham anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The spring sunshine was so warm and gentle that I sat on the bench for a while.
examples.note: the cozy feeling of basking in spring sun

examples.ko: 창문으로 따사로운 볕이 들어와서 기분이 좋아요.
examples.romanization: changmuneuro ttasaroun byeochi deureowaseo gibuni joayo.
examples.en: Gentle sunlight is coming through the window, so I feel good.
examples.note: 볕 = sunlight; 볕이 들다 = sun shines in

examples.en: Even though it's winter, the sunshine is gentle and warm, so I came out for a walk.
examples.note: often used to describe a sunny winter or spring afternoon

entries.nuance: 따사롭다 is a softer, more poetic cousin of 따뜻하다, used almost exclusively for sunlight (햇살/햇볕) and warm feelings. It evokes a gentle, soothing warmth and a peaceful mood, so it's common in casual writing, captions, and heartfelt speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it as 따사롭어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 따사로워요.
Using it for general air temperature — for that say 따뜻하다; 따사롭다 is mainly for sunshine.

usagePhrases.note: a sharper, colder chill than 쌀쌀하다; air that's gone genuinely cold
싸늘한 + 공기/날씨; also 분위기 (atmosphere) for a tense mood
-아/어지다; weather or a mood suddenly going cold

examples.en: Once the sun set, the air suddenly turned cold.
examples.note: the chill that drops fast after sunset

examples.ko: 새벽엔 꽤 싸늘하니까 따뜻하게 입고 나가세요.
examples.romanization: saebyeogen kkwae ssaneulhanikka ttatteutage ipgo nagaseyo.
examples.en: It's quite cold at dawn, so dress warmly when you go out.
My joke made the mood turn cold.
examples.note: very common figurative use: an awkward, frozen atmosphere

entries.nuance: 싸늘하다 is colder and sharper than 쌀쌀하다, often with an unsettling or tense edge. Beyond weather, Koreans use it constantly for a cold atmosphere — 분위기가 싸늘하다 means a room has gone awkwardly silent or frosty, like after a bad joke.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 쌀쌀하다 — 싸늘하다 is colder and can feel eerie or tense.

entries.explanation: 푹푹 찌다 (pukpuk jjida) = "to be boiling/scorching (oppressively hot)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 푹푹 찌다 ("to be sweltering/boiling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 푹푹 찌다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 푹푹 찌다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 푹푹 찌다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: vivid idiom: heat so heavy the air feels steamed; standard spacing is 푹푹 찌다
pairs with 더위 (heat) for peak-summer days

examples.ko: 요즘 날씨가 푹푹 쪄서 밖에 나가기 무서워요.
examples.romanization: yojeum nalssiga pukpuk jjyeoseo bakke nagagi museowoyo.
examples.en: The weather's been boiling lately, so I'm scared to go outside.
examples.note: everyday exaggeration locals use in a heat wave

examples.ko: 에어컨 없이는 푹푹 찌는 여름을 못 버텨요.
examples.romanization: eeokeon eopsineun pukpuk jjineun yeoreumeul mot beotyeoyo.
examples.en: Without AC, I can't survive the sweltering summer.
examples.note: 버티다 = to endure; relatable summer truth

examples.en: Maybe because it's the dog days of summer, it's really sweltering.
examples.note: 삼복더위 = the hottest stretch of summer (복날)

entries.nuance: 푹푹 찌다 literally means '(the heat) steams you,' an idiomatic, very colloquial way to say it's brutally, oppressively hot — stronger and more expressive than 무덥다. Standard spelling spaces it as 푹푹 찌다, and you'll hear it everywhere during a Korean heat wave.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 찌다 here with 찌다 'to gain weight' or 'to steam (food)' — context (날씨/더위) makes it 'sweltering'.
Writing it without the space; the standard form is 푹푹 찌다, not 푹푹찌다.

entries.shortExplanation: 많이 means "a lot, much, many" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 많이 (mani) means "a lot, much, many". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 많이 먹어요 ("I eat a lot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 많이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 많이 먹어요. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 많이.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Goes right before the verb; the most basic way to say 'a lot'
Handy when ordering food or asking for more
With adjectives 많이 can mean 'very', like 'a lot busy'
너무 많이 마셨어요 = I drank too much

examples.en: It's raining a lot today.
examples.note: 비가 오다 = it rains; 많이 shows the amount

examples.en: I like Korean food a lot.
examples.note: Put 많이 before 좋아해요 to say 'like a lot'

examples.en: Please eat a lot / Enjoy your meal.
examples.note: A warm, common thing hosts say at the table

entries.nuance: 많이 is the everyday word for 'a lot/much' and sits right in front of the verb it describes, such as 많이 먹어요 or 많이 자요. With feelings or states it can also mean 'very', so 많이 아파요 means 'it hurts a lot'. It is one of the first adverbs a beginner should learn because it works for both amount and degree.

Using the adjective 많다 where you need the adverb 많이; before a verb you say 많이 먹어요, not 많다 먹어요.
Putting 많이 after the verb; in Korean the adverb comes before the verb, so 먹어요 많이 sounds wrong.

entries.nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit' and is the natural partner to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. In fast speech it very often shrinks to 좀, so 조금만요 and 좀만요 are the same idea. It is gentle and polite, which makes it useful for softening requests and modest answers like 조금 해요.

Using 조금 for large amounts; it only ever means a small degree, so 조금 많이 is contradictory.

Using 좀 in very formal writing, where the full 조금 or a polite request form fits better.

entries.nuance: 그냥 means 'just / simply / for no particular reason' and is one of the most useful filler-style words in casual Korean. It can soften a statement (그냥 좀 그래요), mean 'plain/as-is' (그냥 주세요), or answer 'why?' with a light 'no reason' (그냥). Beginners hear it constantly, so recognizing it makes everyday speech much easier to follow.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 그냥 as having one fixed translation; its meaning shifts with context between 'just', 'plain', and 'no reason'.
Overusing it in formal settings; 그냥 is casual and can sound too vague in business writing.

entries.nuance: 꼭 means 'definitely / without fail' and adds strong intention or a firm request to a sentence. With promises it sounds sincere (꼭 갈게요), and with requests it makes them warm but firm (꼭 오세요). Confusing 꼭 (for sure) with 곧 (soon); they look and sound similar but mean different things.
Using 꼭 for casual maybes; it implies real certainty or a firm wish, not 'perhaps'.

Assuming 바로 only means 'immediately'; it also means 'exactly/right' for places and things.

entries.explanation: 빨리 (ppalli) means "quickly, fast, hurry". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 빨리 가요 ("Let's go quickly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빨리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

Repeated for emphasis; a famous Korean phrase
더 빨리 해 주세요 = please do it faster

examples.en: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
examples.note: Everyday urging when in a rush

examples.en: I ate quickly.

examples.note: A caring set phrase to a sick person

entries.nuance: 빨리 means 'quickly / fast' and is among the first action adverbs beginners need. Doubled as 빨리빨리, it captures the well-known Korean 'hurry, hurry' spirit and adds urgency. It pairs with almost any action verb (빨리 가요, 빨리 먹어요) and appears in warm set phrases like 빨리 나으세요 (get well soon).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.nuance: 푹 means doing something deeply and thoroughly, and it shows up most in 푹 쉬다 (rest well) and 푹 자다 (sleep soundly), which beginners hear all the time as caring wishes. usagePhrases.en: I opened the door. Then a cat came out.

entries.nuance: 그러자 means 'and then / just then' and is used when telling a past story, marking the event that happened right after another. The second event is usually someone or something else's reaction. It almost always appears with past-tense sentences.

usagePhrases.note: Two things happening together or said with another.

usagePhrases.en: She smiles. And at the same time waves her hand.

entries.nuance: 그러면서 means 'while doing that' and links two actions happening at the same time, often by the same person. It can also hint that someone says or does one thing while doing another. It connects back to the action in the previous sentence.

entries.nuance: 몸 means the physical body as a whole, and 'my body hurts' (몸이 아파요) is the most natural everyday way to say you feel sick. It also appears in set phrases like 몸조심하세요 (take care) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (I don't feel well). Beginners use 몸 far more than the formal word 신체.

Don't confuse 몸 (body) with 봄 (spring); they look and sound similar but are different words.

entries.nuance: 살 is the soft flesh of the body, and in daily life it is used constantly to talk about weight: 살이 찌다 (gain weight) and 살이 빠지다 / 살을 빼다 (lose weight). Use 살이 쪘어요 for 'gained weight,' not 살이 컸어요 — 크다 (to grow big) is wrong here.
Don't mix up 살 (flesh/age counter) with 쌀 (uncooked rice); the tense ㅆ sound changes the meaning.

Don't use the medical word 혈액 in casual speech about a cut; 피 is the natural choice.

entries.nuance: 아무 means anyone or any, but it almost never stands alone; it needs a partner particle. With 도 and a negative verb it means nobody or nothing (아무도 없어요 = no one is here), and with 나 it means anyone or anything at all (아무나 = anyone). Using 아무도 with a positive verb; 아무도 must go with a negative like 없어요 or 안 와요.
Saying 아무 alone to mean anyone; you need 아무나 or 아무도 to complete the meaning.

entries.nuance: 아저씨 is the everyday word for a middle-aged or grown man, and it doubles as a friendly way to address a male stranger, shopkeeper, or driver, similar to mister. It is informal and warm, but calling a man who feels too young an 아저씨 can sound rude. Its female counterpart is 아주머니.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 아저씨이에요 instead of the correct 아저씨예요.
Calling a young man 아저씨; he may feel offended since it implies he looks middle-aged.

entries.nuance: 주변 means the area or things around a spot, a bit wider than 근처 ('the vicinity'). Travelers use it constantly for 'around the hotel/station'. It is almost always followed by 에 (location) or used as N + 주변.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주변 식당 without 에; for location say 주변에 식당이 있어요.
Confusing 주변 (the surrounding area) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar but are unrelated.

entries.nuance: 끝 is the physical or time 'end/tip' of something. Note the spelling has the rare final consonant ㅌ, and it is pronounced 'kkeut'. It pairs naturally with 에 for a place ('at the end') and with 맨 for emphasis ('the very end').

entries.explanation: "place, spot" is 곳 (got). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 곳 ("place"). entries.nuance: 곳 is a slightly more written or polite word for 'place' than 데. It often follows an adjective or a modifying clause (조용한 곳, 가 본 곳). For a location use 곳에서 (action there) or 곳에 (existence there).

entries.nuance: 이거 is the casual, everyday version of 이것 and means 'this thing' near the speaker. This is the form you will actually hear and use most in daily life — shopping, ordering food, pointing at things. It contracts to 이게 (subject), 이걸 (object), and 이건 (topic) in fast speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.nuance: 저기 means 'over there,' a place far from both people, completing the set 여기 (here) / 거기 (there, near you) / 저기 (over there). It doubles as a soft attention-getter: 저기요 is how Koreans politely say 'excuse me' to a stranger or call a waiter. The filler 저기... also works like English 'um' when you hesitate.

Using 저기 for a place near the listener — that is 거기.

Saying 무엇을 좋아해요 fine, but dropping the marker as 뭐 좋아해요 in speech — both occur, just keep them consistent.

entries.nuance: 자기 has two common everyday uses: it is a reflexive pronoun meaning 'oneself' (자기 일 = one's own work), and it is also a sweet way couples call each other, like 'honey' (자기야). Context makes the meaning clear. As a reflexive, it points back to the subject already mentioned in the sentence.

In casual talk, 인내심 sounds more natural than bare 인내.
Add 하다 for the verb: 인내하다, and remember 참다 covers everyday 'put up with'.

entries.explanation: "I; me (casual)" is 나 (na). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 나 ("I / me (casual)"). Watch the particle attached to 나 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: First-person pronoun used with close friends, younger people, or family. Plain, not polite.
나 changes to 내 before the subject marker 가. Say 내가, never 나가, for 'I (subject).'
나 + 는. Often shortened to 난 in speech.
나 + 를. Often shortened to 날 in speech.

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: 나 with the topic marker 는; the 요-ending is still polite even though 나 is casual.

examples.en: Can you give this to me?

entries.nuance: 나 is the casual word for 'I/me' and is what you use with close friends, people younger than you, and family. Saying 나가 for 'I (subject)'; the correct form is 내가.
Using 나 with a boss, elder, or stranger — use the humble 저 instead to stay polite.

entries.nuance: 너 is the casual word for 'you' and is only safe with close friends and people clearly younger than you. With elders, strangers, coworkers, or anyone you respect, Koreans avoid 너 entirely — they use the person's name plus a title, a role word, or simply drop 'you' from the sentence. Note the subject form 네가 is often pronounced like '니가' in real speech, because 네가 and 내가 sound almost identical.

Using 너 with an elder, stranger, or boss — it sounds rude; use their name or title instead.
Saying 너가 for 'you (subject)'; the written form is 네가 (commonly pronounced 니가).

entries.explanation: 저 (jeo) means "I; me (humble/polite)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저 ("I / me (humble)"). usagePhrases.note: Polite, humble first-person pronoun for elders, strangers, and formal situations.
저 changes to 제 before the subject marker 가. Say 제가, never 저가, for 'I (subject).'
저 + 는. The standard polite way to introduce yourself.

examples.en: I am Korean.
examples.note: 저 + 는 is the standard polite self-introduction.

examples.en: I'll help you.
examples.note: 저 becomes 제 before 가, giving 제가 for 'I (subject).'

examples.en: Do you remember me?

entries.nuance: 저 is the humble, polite word for 'I/me' and is the safe default with elders, strangers, customers, and anyone you are not close to. It lowers yourself to show respect, so it pairs naturally with 요-form and formal speech. Like 나, it has an irregular subject form: 저 + 가 becomes 제가, not '저가.' Note this 저 (I) looks the same as 저 meaning 'that over there,' but context makes them clear.

Saying 저가 for 'I (subject)'; the correct form is 제가.
Using casual 나 where 저 is expected — with strangers and elders, 저 is the polite choice.

entries.nuance: 당신 is a formal word for 'you,' but it is tricky: said to a stranger it can sound cold, distant, or even like you are picking a fight (it shows up in arguments). Its warm, natural homes are between spouses ('dear/honey'), in song lyrics, in poetry, and in formal writing or ads that address 'you, the reader.' In ordinary polite conversation Koreans almost never say 당신 to someone's face — they use a name, a title, or no word for 'you' at all.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 당신 with a stranger to mean a neutral 'you' — it can sound cold or aggressive; use a name or title.
Assuming 당신 is the polite everyday 'you'; in real speech Koreans usually avoid a direct 'you' word entirely.

entries.nuance: 낮 means the daytime, the bright hours between morning and evening, and it stands in contrast to 밤 (night). The final ㅈ links to a following vowel, so 낮에 is pronounced like '나제.' A very common compound is 낮잠 (a nap). Do not confuse 낮 (daytime) with 낯 (face), which sounds similar but is a different, less common word.

Confusing 낮 (daytime) with the look-alike 낯 (face) or 낫 (sickle / to be better).
Forgetting the liaison: 낮에 is pronounced '나제,' not 'nat-e.'

usagePhrases.note: Everyday word for color; slightly warmer than the shorter 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is.

examples.en: What color do you like?
examples.note: 색깔 as the object with 을 in a question.

examples.en: This bag has a pretty color.

entries.nuance: 색깔 is the everyday word for 'color' and feels a little fuller and warmer than the short form 색, which often attaches to a specific color name (파란색, 빨간색). You can ask 무슨 색깔이에요? (What color is it?) about almost anything. Both 색깔 and 색 are correct; 색깔 stands alone more naturally, while 색 is the building block inside color names.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Trying to attach a color directly to 색깔, like '파란색깔'; specific colors use 색, as in 파란색.
Asking 어떤 색깔 when 무슨 색깔 is the more natural way to ask 'what color.'

entries.nuance: 술 is the general word for any alcoholic drink, covering 소주, 맥주, 막걸리, and more. Like other drinks it takes the verb 마시다 (to drink), not 먹다, though in very casual speech you may hear 술을 먹다 too. Drinking culture is social in Korea: 술 한잔하다 (to have a drink) is a common friendly invitation, and pouring drinks for others is polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 먹다 with 술 in careful speech; the standard verb is 마시다 (술을 마셔요).
Confusing 술 (alcohol) with 물 (water) — one vowel apart but very different drinks.

Seen in 추상화 (abstract painting); rarely used alone

examples.en: The explanation was so abstract that it was hard to understand.

examples.ko: 사랑 같은 추상적인 개념은 말로 설명하기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: sarang gateun chusangjeogin gaenyeomeun mallo seolmyeonghagi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Abstract concepts like love are hard to explain in words.
examples.note: 추상적인 + 개념 is a very frequent collocation.

examples.ko: 너무 추상적으로 말하지 말고 예를 들어 주세요.
examples.romanization: neomu chusangjeogeuro malhaji malgo yereul deureo juseyo.
examples.en: Don't speak so abstractly; please give an example.

entries.nuance: 추상적이다 describes ideas that exist only as concepts, with no concrete detail — the direct opposite of 구체적이다. Writing 추상적이여서 — the correct form is 추상적이어서.

entries.explanation: "to be objective" is 객관적이다 (gaekgwanjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 객관적이다 ("to be objective"). Watch the particle attached to 객관적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 객관적으로 보면… is a common discourse opener.
Used in formal/academic writing: 객관성을 유지하다

examples.ko: 객관적으로 보면 두 사람 다 잘못이 있어요.
examples.romanization: gaekgwanjeogeuro bomyeon du saram da jalmosi isseoyo.
examples.en: Looking at it objectively, both people are at fault.
examples.note: 객관적으로 보면 is a set phrase for giving a fair view.

examples.ko: 기사에는 객관적인 사실만 담겨 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gisaeneun gaekgwanjeogin sasilman damgyeo isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: An article should contain only objective facts.
examples.note: 객관적인 + 사실 is a high-frequency pairing.

examples.ko: 감정을 빼고 좀 더 객관적으로 판단해 보세요.
examples.romanization: gamjeongeul ppaego jom deo gaekgwanjeogeuro pandanhae boseyo.
examples.en: Try to judge a bit more objectively, setting emotion aside.
examples.note: 객관적으로 판단하다 is the natural adverb + verb pairing.

entries.nuance: 객관적이다 means 'based on facts, not personal feelings,' and is the standard antonym of 주관적이다. Korean speakers very often start an opinion with 객관적으로 보면 ('objectively speaking') to signal fairness. It is common in news, essays, and workplace discussion.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 객관적 (objective) and 주관적 (subjective) — they are opposites and easy to swap by accident.
Forgetting the 으로 in the adverb: it is 객관적으로, never 객관적게 in normal usage.

usagePhrases.note: 주관이 뚜렷하다 = to have firm opinions

examples.ko: 맛에 대한 평가는 아무래도 주관적일 수밖에 없어요.
examples.romanization: mase daehan pyeongganeun amuraedo jugwanjeogil subakke eopseoyo.
examples.en: Evaluations of taste are inevitably subjective.
examples.note: 주관적일 수밖에 없다 = cannot help but be subjective.

examples.en: That is not a fact but a subjective opinion.

examples.ko: 너무 주관적으로만 보지 말고 다른 관점도 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: neomu jugwanjeogeuroman boji malgo dareun gwanjeomdo deureo boseyo.
examples.en: Don't see it only subjectively; listen to other viewpoints too.
examples.note: Pairs with the antonym idea 객관적으로.

entries.nuance: 주관적이다 describes something shaped by personal feelings, taste, or viewpoint — the opposite of 객관적이다. Swapping it with 객관적이다; remember 주(主, self) vs 객(客, guest/outside).
Using it for 'biased' in a strongly negative sense — for prejudice use 편견 instead.

examples.ko: 일반적으로 한국에서는 신발을 벗고 집에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: ilbanjeogeuro hangugeseoneun sinbareul beotgo jibe deureogayo.
examples.en: Generally, in Korea you take off your shoes before entering a house.
examples.note: 일반적으로 introduces a general fact or norm.

examples.ko: 그건 아주 일반적인 반응이니까 걱정하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: geugeon aju ilbanjeogin baneunginikka geokjeonghaji maseyo.
examples.en: That is a very common reaction, so don't worry.

examples.ko: 요즘은 재택근무가 점점 일반적인 일이 되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jaetaekgeunmuga jeomjeom ilbanjeogin iri doego isseoyo.
examples.en: These days remote work is gradually becoming common.
examples.note: 일반적인 일이 되다 = to become a common/normal thing.

entries.nuance: 일반적이다 means 'typical, common, what is usually the case,' and the adverb 일반적으로 is one of the most useful discourse words for stating a general rule. Dropping 적: 일반이다 means something different ('to be general public/regular'), so keep 일반적이다 for 'common/typical.'

entries.shortExplanation: 합리적이다 means "to be rational, reasonable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be rational, reasonable" is 합리적이다 (hamnijeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 합리적이다 ("to be rational/reasonable"). Watch the particle attached to 합리적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 합리적이다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 합리적이다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 이 가격이면 정말 합리적인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i gagyeogimyeon jeongmal hamnijeogin geot gatayo.
examples.en: At this price it really seems reasonable.
examples.note: 합리적인 가격 = a fair/reasonable price (very common in shopping).

examples.en: Let's judge rationally rather than emotionally.
examples.note: Often paired with the contrast 감정적으로.

examples.ko: 그 회사는 합리적인 근무 환경으로 유명해요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun hamnijeogin geunmu hwangyeongeuro yumyeonghaeyo.
examples.en: That company is famous for its reasonable working conditions.
examples.note: 합리적인 modifies abstract nouns like 환경, 제도.

entries.nuance: 합리적이다 covers both 'logical/rational' and 'reasonable (fair)' — for example 합리적인 가격 means a fair price, while 합리적으로 생각하다 means to think logically. It carries a positive evaluation in most contexts. Its opposite 비합리적이다 is formed simply with the prefix 비-.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming it only means 'cheap' — 합리적인 가격 implies a fair, justified price, not merely a low one.
Forgetting the prefix for the opposite: 'irrational' is 비합리적이다, not 안 합리적이다 in formal use.

entries.explanation: 현실적이다 (hyeonsiljeogida) = "to be realistic, practical". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 현실적이다 ("to be realistic/practical") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 현실적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 현실적이다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 현실적이다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 현실적으로 생각하면 그 계획은 좀 무리예요.
examples.romanization: hyeonsiljeogeuro saenggakamyeon geu gyehoegeun jom muriyeyo.
examples.en: Realistically thinking, that plan is a bit of a stretch.

examples.ko: 꿈도 좋지만 좀 더 현실적인 목표를 세워 보세요.
examples.romanization: kkumdo jochiman jom deo hyeonsiljeogin mokpyoreul sewo boseyo.
examples.en: Dreams are fine, but try setting a more realistic goal.
examples.note: 현실적인 목표 = an achievable, practical goal.

examples.en: That is too unrealistic to carry out.
examples.note: Shows the antonym 비현실적이다 in use.

entries.nuance: 현실적이다 describes something grounded in reality and actually feasible, often contrasted with idealistic dreams (이상적이다). Describing a person as 현실적이다 usually means practical and down-to-earth, which is generally positive. The adverb 현실적으로 is a frequent way to bring a discussion back to what is actually possible.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 현실적이다 (realistic) with 사실적이다 (factual/lifelike) — the latter is mostly used for art and description.
Calling a practical person 현실 — the adjective is 현실적이다; 현실 alone means 'reality.'

entries.shortExplanation: 이상적이다 means "to be ideal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이상적이다 (isangjeogida) means "to be ideal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이상적이다 ("to be ideal"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이상적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 이상이 높다 = to have high ideals

examples.ko: 집에서 가깝고 월급도 좋으니 이상적인 직장이네요.
examples.romanization: jibeseo gakkapgo wolgeupdo joeuni isangjeogin jikjangineyo.
examples.en: It's close to home and the pay is good, so it's an ideal job.
examples.note: 이상적인 + noun = perfect/ideal for a purpose.

examples.en: Ideally it sounds good, but reality is a bit different.
examples.note: 이상적으로는 … 현실은 contrasts ideal vs reality.

examples.ko: 모두가 만족하는 건 사실 좀 이상적인 생각이에요.
examples.romanization: moduga manjokaneun geon sasil jom isangjeogin saenggagieyo.
examples.en: Everyone being satisfied is, honestly, a somewhat idealistic notion.

entries.nuance: 이상적이다 means 'perfect in theory, ideal,' and is naturally contrasted with 현실적이다. The pattern 이상적으로는 …, 현실은 … ('ideally …, but in reality …') is extremely common in real conversation. Note the homonym 이상 also means 'strange' in 이상하다, so context matters.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing 이상적이다 (ideal) with 이상하다 (strange) — same 이상 sound, opposite feel.
Overusing it for everyday 'good'; reserve 이상적이다 for something close to perfect, otherwise use 좋다.

entries.explanation: "to be traditional" is 전통적이다 (jeontongjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전통적이다 ("to be traditional"). usagePhrases.note: 전통을 지키다 = to keep a tradition

examples.ko: 설날에는 전통적인 한복을 입는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: seolnareneun jeontongjeogin hanbogeul imneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: On Lunar New Year, many people wear traditional hanbok.
examples.note: 전통적인 + noun describes culturally inherited things.

examples.ko: 전통적으로 한국에서는 어른께 먼저 인사를 드려요.
examples.romanization: jeontongjeogeuro hangugeseoneun eoreunkke meonjeo insareul deuryeoyo.
examples.en: Traditionally in Korea, you greet your elders first.

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 세대는 전통적인 가치관과 조금 달라요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun sedaeneun jeontongjeogin gachigwangwa jogeum dallayo.
examples.en: These days the younger generation differs a little from traditional values.

entries.nuance: 전통적이다 means 'in keeping with long-standing tradition,' and is the natural adjective for describing food, clothing, customs, and values passed down over generations. The adverb 전통적으로 is a clean way to introduce a cultural norm. The noun 전통 appears constantly in 전통문화, 전통시장, and so on.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 전통 (tradition) with 정통 (orthodox/authentic) — similar sound, different meaning.
Using it for merely 'old' objects; for old-fashioned/outdated use 구식이다, while 전통적이다 has a respectful tone.

entries.shortExplanation: 대표적이다 means "to be representative, the most typical example" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 대표적이다 (daepyojeogida) = "to be representative, the most typical example". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 대표적이다 ("to be representative/typical") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대표적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 대표적이다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 대표적이다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Predicate use is less common; modifier form dominates.

examples.en: Kimchi is a representative food of Korea.
examples.note: 대표적인 + noun = the most iconic/typical example.

examples.en: As prime examples, Busan and Jeju are popular travel spots.
examples.note: 대표적으로 introduces leading examples in a list.

examples.ko: 이 작가의 대표적인 작품은 학교에서도 배워요.
examples.romanization: i jakgaui daepyojeogin jakpumeun hakgyoeseodo baewoyo.
examples.en: This author's representative works are even taught in school.

entries.nuance: 대표적이다 means 'standing as the most typical or famous example' of a category, and you will almost always meet it as 대표적인 + noun or as the list-opener 대표적으로. It is the natural way to say 'a leading/iconic example of X.' The root 대표 separately means a representative or company head.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Trying to use 대표적이다 as a stand-alone predicate ('이건 대표적이에요') sounds odd; prefer 대표적인 음식이에요 / 대표적인 예예요.
Confusing 대표적 (representative example) with 대신 (instead) — unrelated words.

entries.shortExplanation: 직접적이다 means "to be direct" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 직접적이다 (jikjeopjeogida) means "to be direct". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 직접적이다 ("to be direct"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 직접적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 직접적이다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 직접적이다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 직접 가다 = to go in person (distinct usage)

examples.en: Stress has a direct effect on health.
examples.note: 직접적인 영향/원인 are very common collocations.

examples.ko: 한국에서는 거절을 직접적으로 말하지 않는 경우가 많아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseoneun geojeoreul jikjeopjeogeuro malhaji anhneun gyeonguga manayo.
examples.en: In Korea, refusals are often not stated directly.
examples.note: Cultural point: 직접적으로 vs indirect refusal.

examples.ko: 그 질문은 너무 직접적이어서 대답하기 불편했어요.
examples.romanization: geu jilmuneun neomu jikjeopjeogieoseo daedapagi bulpyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: That question was so direct that it was uncomfortable to answer.

entries.nuance: 직접적이다 describes something direct, without anything in between — 직접적인 원인 (direct cause), 직접적인 영향 (direct impact), or a blunt 직접적인 표현 (direct expression). Note that the bare root 직접 works as an adverb meaning 'in person/by oneself' (직접 만들다), which is a different, very frequent usage. Its antonym is 간접적이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the adjective 직접적이다 with the adverb 직접 ('in person') — 직접 가다 ≠ 직접적으로 가다.
Writing 직접적이여서; the correct connective is 직접적이어서.

examples.ko: 적극적인 태도 덕분에 좋은 평가를 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeokgeukjeogin taedo deokbune joeun pyeonggareul badasseoyo.

examples.note: 적극적인 태도 is a common workplace phrase.

examples.ko: 저는 좀 소극적인 편이라 적극적인 사람이 부러워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jom sogeukjeogin pyeonira jeokgeukjeogin sarami bureowoyo.
examples.en: I'm rather passive, so I envy proactive people.

entries.nuance: 적극적이다 describes an energetic, take-initiative attitude and is very common in workplace and school contexts (적극적인 참여, 적극적으로 나서다). In Korean the particle or ending next to 결과 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 결과 + noun: the result of something
natural collocation for results being announced/released
attaches to a verb to express consequence: 노력한 결과 = as a result of trying
discourse connector linking a cause sentence to its outcome

examples.ko: 열심히 준비한 결과 좋은 점수를 받았어요.
examples.romanization: yeolsimhi junbihan gyeolgwa joeun jeomsureul badasseoyo.
examples.en: As a result of preparing hard, I got a good score.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 결과 turns the first clause into the cause of the second

examples.ko: 검사 결과가 아직 안 나와서 기다리고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geomsa gyeolgwaga ajik an nawaseo gidarigo isseoyo.
examples.en: The test results haven't come out yet, so I'm waiting.
Do you think the result matters more than the process?
examples.note: common contrast pairing 과정 vs 결과

entries.nuance: 결과 is the end outcome of an action or event and pairs naturally with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear). It often contrasts with 과정 (process). The pattern -(으)ㄴ 결과 is a frequent intermediate connective meaning 'as the result of having done X.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 결과 takes 이/가 with 나오다: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; use 원인 or 이유 for the reason.

entries.explanation: "cause" is 원인 (wonin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사고의 원인 ("the cause of the accident"). Watch the particle attached to 원인 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 원인 is the objective, often negative, cause of a problem or event
natural collocation for investigating what caused something
X이/가 원인이 되다 = X causes/leads to
common with 근본적(인) when discussing root causes

examples.ko: 화재의 정확한 원인은 아직 밝혀지지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hwajaeui jeonghwakan wonineun ajik balkyeojiji anasseoyo.
examples.en: The exact cause of the fire hasn't been determined yet.
examples.note: 원인 is used for problems, accidents, and phenomena

examples.ko: 스트레스가 여러 질병의 원인이 될 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseuga yeoreo jilbyeongui wonini doel su isseoyo.
examples.en: Stress can become the cause of various illnesses.

examples.ko: 문제의 원인을 먼저 찾는 것이 중요해요.
examples.romanization: munjeui wonineul meonjeo channeun geosi jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: It's important to first find the cause of the problem.

entries.nuance: 원인 refers to the objective cause of a result, usually a problem, accident, or phenomenon, and pairs with 결과 as cause-and-effect. It is more analytical and impersonal than 이유, which is the personal reason/justification someone gives. You investigate an 원인 but you explain an 이유.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 원인 for personal reasons like 'the reason I'm late' — use 이유 there.
원인이 되다 (becomes a cause), not 원인을 되다.

usagePhrases.note: common on immigration forms and in formal contexts
describes having an intended aim behind an action
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states a purpose

examples.en: What's the purpose of this gathering?
examples.note: asking for the aim of an event

examples.ko: 이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.
examples.romanization: i peurogeuraemui mokjeogeun oegugineul domneun geosieyo.
examples.en: The purpose of this program is to help foreigners.
I just started without a clear purpose.

entries.nuance: 목적 is the conscious aim or intention behind an action and is more goal-oriented than 이유 (reason) or 원인 (cause). It is common in formal/written contexts such as immigration forms (방문 목적) and reports. To say what something is for, use N의 목적은 ~는 것이다.

commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 과장 (exaggeration / section chief) when you mean 과정 (process) — different word.
Use 거치다 with 과정 for 'go through stages,' not 가다.

usagePhrases.en: be related, have to do with

examples.en: The relationship with my coworkers is really important.

examples.ko: 그 일은 저와는 아무 관계가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu ireun jeowaneun amu gwangyega eopseoyo.
examples.en: That matter has nothing to do with me.
examples.note: 관계가 없다 = unrelated, none of one's business

examples.ko: 두 사건은 서로 깊은 관계가 있어요.
examples.romanization: du sageoneun seoro gipeun gwangyega isseoyo.
examples.en: The two incidents are deeply related to each other.

entries.nuance: 관계 covers both personal relationships (인간관계, 친구 관계) and abstract relations/connections between facts or events. With 있다/없다 it often means 'to be related / have to do with,' so 관계없다 is a common way to say 'irrelevant' or 'none of my business.' Use 와/과 to mark the other party.

Don't say 관계를 있다; it's 관계가 있다.
관심 (interest) and 관계 (relationship) look similar but mean different things — don't mix them up.

usagePhrases.note: X이/가 Y에게/에 영향을 주다 = X affects Y
X에게/에서 영향을 받다 = to be affected by X
more formal than 주다; common in writing
pairs with 좋은/나쁜/큰 to describe the effect

examples.en: The weather has a big effect on my mood.
I was greatly influenced by my parents.

examples.ko: 이 정책은 사회 전체에 영향을 미쳐요.
examples.romanization: i jeongchaegeun sahoe jeonchee yeonghyangeul michyeoyo.
examples.en: This policy has an impact on society as a whole.
examples.note: 영향을 미치다 is the formal/written form

entries.nuance: 영향 is the influence or impact one thing has on another and works in two directions: 영향을 주다/미치다 (to affect) and 영향을 받다 (to be affected). 미치다 is more formal and frequent in written or news Korean, while 주다 is everyday speech. Mark the affected target with 에 (things) or 에게/께 (people).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap the direction: the affecter 주다/미치다, the affected 받다.
Use 에 or 에게 for the target, not 을/를: 환경에 영향을 주다 (not 환경을 영향을 주다).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 상황 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 현재 상황. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 상황.

usagePhrases.note: 상황 follows an adjective/noun describing the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation

examples.ko: 지금 상황이 너무 복잡해서 설명하기 어려워요.
examples.romanization: jigeum sanghwangi neomu bokjapaeseo seolmyeonghagi eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: The situation is so complicated right now that it's hard to explain.

examples.ko: 이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireon sanghwangeseoneun eotteoke haeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.

examples.ko: 답은 상황에 따라 달라질 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: dabeun sanghwange ttara dallajil su isseoyo.
examples.en: The answer can change depending on the situation.

entries.nuance: 상황 describes the overall set of circumstances surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (case/instance). The phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is extremely common and useful for hedging. 이런/그런 상황에서 frames advice or reactions to a set of conditions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 상황 (situation) with 상태 (state/condition of a thing or body).
Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation,' not 으로: 상황에 따라.

entries.explanation: "condition, requirement, terms" is 조건 (jogeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조건이 좋다 ("the conditions/terms are good"). 조건 follows a noun naming the relevant terms
조건에 맞는 사람 = a person who fits the requirements

examples.ko: 이 회사는 근무 조건이 정말 좋은 편이에요.
examples.romanization: i hoesaneun geunmu jogeoni jeongmal joeun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: This company's working conditions are really quite good.

examples.ko: 지원하려면 몇 가지 조건을 갖춰야 해요.
examples.romanization: jiwonharyeomyeon myeot gaji jogeoneul gatchwoya haeyo.
examples.en: To apply, you have to meet a few requirements.

examples.ko: 그 조건에 맞으면 누구나 신청할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu jogeone majeumyeon nuguna sincheonghal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you meet those conditions, anyone can apply.

entries.nuance: 조건 means both the requirements that must be satisfied and the terms/conditions of an arrangement (jobs, contracts, deals). With 갖추다 or 만족하다 it means 'fulfill requirements,' and with 맞다 it means 'fit/match the conditions.' It is more concrete than 상황 — 조건 are the specific terms, not the overall circumstances.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 조건 for an if-clause grammar point; 'if' is expressed with -(으)면, while 조건 is the noun 'condition.'
조건에 맞다 (fit the conditions), not 조건을 맞다.

usagePhrases.note: 기준이 높다/낮다/엄격하다 describe how strict a standard is

usagePhrases.en: based on / using N as the standard
usagePhrases.note: 성적을 기준으로 = on the basis of grades
기준에 맞추다 = to align with the standard
기준 follows a noun naming what the standard is for

examples.en: The hiring criteria differ from company to company.
We lined up based on age.
examples.note: N을 기준으로 = using N as the criterion

examples.ko: 이 제품은 안전 기준을 모두 통과했어요.
examples.romanization: i jepumeun anjeon gijuneul modu tonggwahaesseoyo.
examples.en: This product passed all the safety standards.

entries.nuance: 기준 is the standard or yardstick against which things are measured, judged, or sorted. The phrase N을/를 기준으로(하다) means 'taking N as the basis/reference point' and is very common for explaining how something is organized or decided. Unlike 조건 (a requirement to meet), 기준 is the measuring criterion itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't drop 으로 in the set phrase: it's N을/를 기준으로, not N을 기준.
기준 (standard) is not 기분 (mood) — be careful with the vowel.

usagePhrases.en: to some degree, roughly how much
usagePhrases.note: 어느 정도 알아요 = I know to some extent
그 정도면 충분해요 = that much is enough
한 시간 정도 = about an hour
울 정도로 = to the point of crying

examples.ko: 한국어를 어느 정도 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul eoneu jeongdo hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can speak Korean to some degree.

examples.ko: 여기서 공항까지 한 시간 정도 걸려요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo gonghangkkaji han sigan jeongdo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: It takes about an hour from here to the airport.
I was tired to the point that I couldn't even speak.

entries.nuance: 정도 expresses degree or extent and, after a number, means 'about/approximately,' similar to 쯤 but slightly more flexible. The set phrases 어느 정도 ('to some extent') and 그 정도 ('that much') are essential intermediate vocabulary. The grammar -(으)ㄹ 정도로 means 'to the extent/point that,' showing how strong something is.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
정도 after a number means 'about,' so don't add 약 unnecessarily — 한 시간 정도 already means 'about an hour.'
Don't confuse 정도 (degree/extent) with 제도 (system/institution).

lesson.canDo: Use 정도 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.

entries.shortExplanation: 변화 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "change" is 변화 (byeonhwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 변화가 생기다 ("a change occurs"). Watch the particle attached to 변화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 변화가 생기다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 변화.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: natural way to say a change appears/arises
분위기에 변화를 주다 = add a change to the mood
pairs with 급격한/큰/작은 to describe scale

examples.en: These days the weather changes are too severe.
examples.note: 변화가 심하다 = the change is severe

examples.ko: 새 환경의 변화에 적응하는 데 시간이 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: sae hwangyeongui byeonhwae jeogeunghaneun de sigani geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took time to adapt to the changes in the new environment.
I want to make a small change in my life.

entries.nuance: 변화 is the noun 'change,' used for changes in states, trends, weather, society, or life, and is more abstract than the verb 변하다 (to change). 변화를 주다 means 'to introduce/make a change' (often for variety), while 변화가 생기다 means a change 'occurs.' Mark what one adapts to with 에: 변화에 적응하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use the verb 변하다/바뀌다 to say 'something changes'; 변화 is the noun, so don't say 변화하다 to mean a simple everyday change (it sounds formal/scientific).
변화를 주다 (make a change), not 변화를 하다 in this 'add variety' sense.

entries.shortExplanation: 의미 means "meaning, significance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 의미 (uimi) = "meaning, significance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 의미가 있다 ("be meaningful/significant") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 의미, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 의미가 있다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 의미.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 의미 있는 일 = a meaningful thing
common way to say something has no point

usagePhrases.en: in the sense that / meaning that
usagePhrases.note: 축하하는 의미에서 = in the sense of celebrating
결과에 의미를 두다 = to attach significance to the result

examples.romanization: i daneoneun du gaji uimiga isseoyo.
examples.en: This word has two meanings.
examples.note: 의미가 있다 in the literal 'meaning' sense

examples.en: I prepared a small gift to express my gratitude.

examples.ko: 혼자 여행한 것은 저에게 큰 의미가 있었어요.
examples.romanization: honja yeohaenghan geoseun jeoege keun uimiga isseosseoyo.
examples.en: Traveling alone had great significance for me.

entries.nuance: 의미 covers both the literal 'meaning' of a word and the deeper 'significance/value' of an experience, so 의미가 있다 can mean 'is meaningful' as well as 'has a meaning.' The pattern -는 의미에서 ('in the sense/spirit of doing') is a useful intermediate connector for explaining intentions behind an action. 뜻 is a near-synonym but leans toward literal word meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For asking 'what does this word mean?' both 의미 and 뜻 work, but in casual speech 뜻 is more common: 무슨 뜻이에요?
Don't say 의미를 있다 — it's 의미가 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 역할 means "role, part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 역할 (yeokal) means "role, part". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 역할을 하다 ("play a role"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역할 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 역할을 하다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 역할.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 중요한 역할을 하다 = to play an important role
맡다 = to be in charge of a role/part
common when sharing tasks in a team

examples.en: Within a family, each person has their own role.
examples.note: 역할이 있다 = to have a role

examples.en: Teachers play an important role for students.
examples.note: 역할을 하다 = to play a role

examples.ko: 이번 프로젝트에서 제가 발표 역할을 맡았어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon peurojekteueseo jega balpyo yeokareul matasseoyo.
examples.en: I took on the presentation role in this project.
examples.note: 역할을 맡다 = take on a role

entries.nuance: 역할 is the role or part someone or something plays, used for people in groups, family members, or even the function of objects and factors. 역할을 하다 means 'to play/serve a role,' while 역할을 맡다 stresses being assigned or taking on the part. Note the pronunciation: 역할 sounds like [여칼].
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 역활 — the correct spelling is 역할.
Use 맡다 for taking on a role, not 잡다: 역할을 맡다, not 역할을 잡다.

entries.explanation: "chance; opportunity" is 기회 (gihoe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기회가 있어요 ("there is a chance"). Watch the particle attached to 기회 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.ko: 저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oegugeseo ilhal gihoereul japgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to seize a chance to work abroad.

entries.nuance: 기회 means an opportunity or chance to do something, often one that may not come again. The natural verbs are 기회를 잡다 to seize it and 기회를 놓치다 to miss it, rather than 기회를 하다. 기회가 되면 is a common phrase meaning if I get the chance.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기회를 하다 instead of 기회를 잡다 or 기회가 있다
Marking it 기회를 있다 instead of 기회가 있다

entries.explanation: 태도 (taedo) = "attitude". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 태도가 좋아요 ("the attitude is good") shows how it actually behaves. entries.nuance: 태도 means the attitude or stance someone shows through behavior, especially toward work, people, or a situation. It is often paired with 에 대한 to mean attitude toward something. Unlike 자세, which can be a physical posture, 태도 is mostly about one's mental and behavioral disposition.

examples.romanization: iri maneunde deoguna saramkkaji bujokaeseo yageuni jajayo.
examples.en: There's a lot of work, and on top of that we're short-staffed, so we often work late.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 비싸요. 더구나 맛도 별로였어요.

entries.nuance: 더구나 stacks an additional fact onto the previous statement, usually intensifying a negative situation ('and to make matters worse'). Use it when the second point makes the overall picture more extreme, not for simply listing neutral items.

Using 더구나 to add a positive, neutral item (e.g. a plain shopping list) where 그리고/게다가 fits better.
Treating it as a sentence object; it is an adverb that opens or links a clause, not a noun.

examples.romanization: jeoneun gwaireul joahaneunde, teuki ttalgireul jeil joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like fruit, and I especially like strawberries the most.
examples.note: Picks out one favorite from a category

examples.ko: 이번 시험은 특히 듣기 부분이 어려웠어요.

examples.note: Narrows a general statement to a specific case

entries.nuance: 특히 points to one member of a group as standing out from the rest, equivalent to 'especially' or 'in particular.' It naturally follows a general statement and then zooms in on the exception.

Placing it so far from the highlighted item that it's unclear what is being singled out.

entries.explanation: "mainly; mostly; usually" is 주로 (juro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주로 V해요 ("I mainly do V"). Marks the typical place something happens
Identifies the chief object or target

examples.note: Describes a typical pattern of behavior

examples.en: Mostly students come to this cafe.

examples.ko: 점심은 주로 회사 근처에서 간단히 먹어요.
examples.romanization: jeomsimeun juro hoesa geuncheoeseo gandanhi meogeoyo.
examples.en: I usually eat lunch simply near the office.
examples.note: Marks a habitual choice without claiming 'always'

entries.nuance: 주로 means 'mainly/mostly' and describes what is typical or dominant, leaving room for exceptions. It overlaps with 보통 (usually) and 대부분 (for the most part), but 주로 emphasizes the principal case among options rather than pure frequency. Use it to describe habits, typical locations, or the main kind of thing involved.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 주로 to mean 'absolutely always'; it implies a tendency, not 100%.
Swapping it with 주로/주류 (mainstream) as a noun; here it is strictly an adverb.

examples.en: This neighborhood is relatively quiet.
examples.note: Hedges the claim against other areas

examples.ko: 오늘은 비교적 일이 적어서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun bigyojeok iri jeogeoseo iljjik toegeunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Today there was comparatively little work, so I left early.

examples.ko: 한국어 발음은 비교적 규칙적이라서 배우기 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo bareumeun bigyojeok gyuchikjeogiraseo baeugi swiwoyo.
examples.en: Korean pronunciation is relatively regular, so it's easy to learn.

entries.nuance: 비교적 means 'relatively/comparatively' and hedges an adjective or quantity against an implied standard. It tells the listener that the quality holds only in comparison, not absolutely, which makes statements sound more careful and intermediate. It is more formal and measured than 꽤 or 좀, and unlike 별로 it carries no negative bias.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it as 비교적이에요; 비교적 is an adverb and should modify, e.g., 비교적 쉬워요.
Using it where there is truly no point of comparison; a baseline (even implicit) should exist.

대체로 stresses the general trend, not a count

examples.romanization: hotereun daechero kkaekkeutaetjiman waipaiga jom neuryeosseoyo.
