entries.shortExplanation: 적당하다 means "to be moderate, just right, adequate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 적당하다 (jeokdanghada) means "to be moderate, just right, adequate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 적당한 ("moderate / just-right (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 적당하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 적당한. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 적당하다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 적당한 운동 'moderate exercise', 적당한 크기 'a suitable size'.
Polite present; very common in everyday speech.
Adverb: 적당히 하다 'do something in moderation / not overdo it'.

usagePhrases.en: give it a rest / don't overdo it
usagePhrases.note: Casual idiom telling someone to stop going too far.

examples.ko: 국이 너무 짜지 않고 간이 적당해요.
examples.romanization: gugi neomu jjaji anko gani jeokdanghaeyo.
examples.en: The soup isn't too salty; the seasoning is just right.
On weekends I rest a moderate amount and work a moderate amount.

examples.ko: 이 정도 가격이면 적당한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i jeongdo gagyeogimyeon jeokdanghan geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think this price is reasonable.

entries.nuance: 적당하다 expresses a comfortable middle — not too much, not too little, neither extreme. It is more casual and quantity/degree-focused than 적절하다. The adverb 적당히 can be positive ('in moderation') or carry a slightly negative 'just enough to get by / half-heartedly' nuance depending on context and tone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
적당히 can imply doing something carelessly or half-heartedly ('적당히 했어' = 'I just did it roughly'); read the tone before assuming it's positive.
Don't swap with 적절하다 in formal evaluations — 적절하다 sounds more proper there.

entries.explanation: "to be enough, sufficient, ample" is 충분하다 (chungbunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충분한 ("enough / sufficient (+ noun)"). Watch the particle attached to 충분하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 충분한. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 충분하다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 충분한 시간 'enough time', 충분한 준비 'sufficient preparation'.
Adverb already in the app as a separate word; here as a derived form: 충분히 이해해요 'I fully understand'.
Softer than 부족하다 for saying 'that's not quite enough'.

examples.en: There's enough time to prepare, so take your time.

examples.ko: 이 정도면 두 명이 먹기에 충분해요.
examples.romanization: i jeongdomyeon du myeongi meokgie chungbunhaeyo.
examples.en: This much is enough for two people to eat.
I fully understand how you feel.
examples.note: 충분히 as an intensifying adverb = 'fully, well enough'.

entries.nuance: 충분하다 means a quantity, time, or degree reaches or exceeds what is needed. It is the natural opposite of 부족하다. The adverb 충분히 is extremely useful and often means 'fully/plenty' rather than just 'enough' (e.g., 충분히 가능해요 'it's totally possible'). It works for tangible amounts and abstract things like understanding or rest.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say '충분 있어요'; 충분하다 is an adjective, so use 충분해요 or 충분한 N.
충분하다 vs 풍부하다: 충분하다 = 'enough for the need'; 풍부하다 = 'abundant/rich', emphasizing plentifulness beyond mere sufficiency.

entries.english: to be lacking, insufficient, short of
entries.shortExplanation: 부족하다 means "to be lacking, insufficient, short of" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부족하다 (bujokada) = "to be lacking, insufficient, short of". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부족한 ("lacking / insufficient (+ noun)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부족하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 부족한. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 부족하다.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 부족한 부분 'the lacking part', 부족한 점 'shortcomings'.
잠이 부족하다 'be short on sleep', 경험이 부족하다 'lack experience'.
Set humble phrase: 부족하지만 잘 부탁드립니다.

examples.en: I've been short on sleep lately, so I'm really tired.
examples.note: 잠이 부족하다 is a fixed collocation.

examples.ko: 아직 경험이 부족해서 더 배우고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: ajik gyeongheomi bujokaeseo deo baeugo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I still lack experience, so I want to learn more.
I have many shortcomings, but I'll work hard.

entries.nuance: 부족하다 is the direct opposite of 충분하다 and marks the thing in short supply with 이/가 (잠이 부족하다, 돈이 부족하다). Beyond literal shortages it is also a humble, polite way to describe one's own abilities or work ('부족하지만…'). Korean speakers use this self-deprecating 부족하다 frequently to sound modest.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mark the short item with 이/가, not 을/를: 시간이 부족해요 (not 시간을 부족해요).

entries.nuance: 독특하다 describes something noticeably different from the ordinary — distinctive, original, one-of-a-kind. For food, design, or style it is usually positive ('unique, characterful'). examples.en: I want to learn how to use time effectively.

entries.nuance: 효과적이다 means something actually works well and produces the intended result — effective. It is a ~적이다 adjective, so remember the patterns: 효과적인 N (modifier), 효과적이에요 (predicate), 효과적으로 (adverb). It is closely related to 효율적이다, but focuses on whether the desired effect is achieved at all, not on resource economy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't drop 이: it's 효과적이다 / 효과적이에요, not '효과적다'.
Before a noun use 효과적인, and as an adverb use 효과적으로 — mixing these up is a very common error.

entries.explanation: 효율적이다 (hyoyuljeogida) means "to be efficient (good output for the input)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 효율적인 ("efficient (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 효율적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 효율적인 동선 'an efficient route/flow', 효율적인 일 처리 'efficient handling of work'.
Adverb: 시간을 효율적으로 관리하다 'manage time efficiently'.

examples.en: If you do it this way, you can work more efficiently.
examples.note: 효율적으로 + 하다, very common at work.

examples.en: Our team runs meetings efficiently.
I bought an appliance that uses energy efficiently.

entries.nuance: 효율적이다 is about getting the most result with the least time, effort, or resources — efficiency. It pairs naturally with work, time management, and energy use. The key contrast with 효과적이다: 효과적이다 asks 'does it work?', while 효율적이다 asks 'is it worth the input?'. Something can be effective but not efficient, and vice versa.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Keep the patterns straight: 효율적인 N, 효율적이에요, 효율적으로 (adverb).
Don't use it as a synonym for 효과적이다 — efficiency (cost) and effectiveness (result) are different ideas.

examples.en: Korea is a country with four distinct seasons.

He is a person with clear-cut opinions.

entries.nuance: 뚜렷하다 means something stands out clearly and is well-defined — distinct seasons, a sharp difference, a firm opinion, a vivid memory. Don't use 뚜렷하다 to mean 'certain that something is true' — for that, prefer 확실하다 or 분명하다.

examples.romanization: chaegim sojaega myeonghwakaji anaseo munjega saenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It wasn't clear who was responsible, so a problem arose.

entries.nuance: 명확하다 means clearly defined and free of ambiguity — explicit criteria, unambiguous answers, well-defined responsibilities. It is more formal/written than 분명하다 and is preferred in work, rules, and academic writing. It is the natural opposite of 모호하다, emphasizing that nothing is left vague or open to interpretation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
명확하다 (clear/unambiguous) vs 정확하다 (accurate/correct): clarity is not the same as correctness.
Use the modifier 명확한 before a noun, and 명확하게/명확히 as the adverb.

entries.explanation: 모호하다 (mohohada) means "to be vague, ambiguous, unclear". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모호한 ("vague / ambiguous (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모호하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 모호한 태도 'an ambiguous attitude', 모호한 표현 'a vague expression'.
Emphatic compound; very common in speech.

examples.ko: 대답이 너무 모호해서 무슨 뜻인지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: daedabi neomu mohohaeseo museun tteusinji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: The answer is so vague that I can't tell what it means.
If the criteria are vague, each person understands them differently.

examples.ko: 그는 태도가 모호해서 속을 알 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: geuneun taedoga mohohaeseo sogeul al su eopseoyo.
examples.en: His attitude is ambiguous, so I can't read his true feelings.

entries.nuance: 모호하다 is the opposite of 명확하다/뚜렷하다 — blurry, unclear, open to multiple interpretations. It applies to language, criteria, attitudes, and boundaries. In daily speech you'll often hear the stronger compound 애매하다 or 애매모호하다 for 'wishy-washy / hard to pin down'. It frequently carries a mildly negative tone of frustration that something isn't clear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
In casual speech 애매하다 is more common than 모호하다 for 'iffy/unclear'; 모호하다 sounds a touch more formal/written.
Don't confuse with 헷갈리다 ('to be confused/mixed up'), which describes the listener's confusion, not the thing's vagueness.

entries.shortExplanation: 사회 means "society" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "society" is 사회 (sahoe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 현대 사회 ("modern society"). Watch the particle attached to 사회 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Very common collocation; 사회 often pairs with an adjective-like noun in front.
Compound noun used constantly in news and writing.

usagePhrases.en: social life / life in the working world
usagePhrases.note: Note: this usually means working life and getting along with people, not 'social life' in the party sense.

usagePhrases.en: to go out into society (e.g., after school)
usagePhrases.note: Idiomatic for entering the workforce / adult world.

examples.ko: 우리 사회에는 아직 해결해야 할 문제가 많아요.
examples.romanization: uri sahoeeneun aji kaegyeolhaeya hal munjega manayo.
examples.en: There are still many problems our society needs to solve.
examples.note: 해결해야 할 = 'that must be solved'; 사회 takes 에 for 'in society'.

examples.en: Once you graduate from university, you really start your working life.
examples.note: 사회생활 here = professional/adult life, a key nuance.

examples.ko: 인터넷이 우리 사회를 크게 바꿔 놓았어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi uri sahoereul keuge bakkwo noasseoyo.
examples.en: The internet has greatly changed our society.
examples.note: 바꿔 놓다 = 'has changed (and left it that way)', natural with 사회.

entries.nuance: 사회 covers 'society' as the whole community of people, but in everyday Korean 사회생활 and 사회에 나가다 specifically point to working life and entering the adult world. When Koreans say someone is good at 사회생활, they mean that person handles workplace relationships and social obligations well, not that they go to many parties.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 사회생활 means 'social life / hanging out with friends' — it almost always means working life and getting along at work.
Using 사회 for a small social gathering; for that use 모임 instead.

entries.shortExplanation: 전통 means "tradition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전통 (jeontong) = "tradition". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전통 문화 ("traditional culture") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 전통 문화. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 전통.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 전통 is frequently used attributively before another noun without 의.
지키다 ('protect, keep') is the standard verb that goes with 전통.
The adjective form; e.g. 전통적인 결혼식 = a traditional wedding.
오랜 ('long, longtime') is the natural modifier, not 긴.

examples.ko: 한국의 전통을 지키려고 노력하는 사람들이 많아요.
examples.romanization: hangugui jeontongeul jikiryeogo noryeokaneun saramdeuri manayo.
examples.en: Many people are working to preserve Korea's traditions.
examples.note: 지키려고 노력하다 = 'try to preserve', a common pattern with 전통.

examples.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i maeureun oraedoen jeontongeul geudaero ieo gago isseoyo.
examples.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
examples.note: 이어 가다 = 'carry on / continue', natural with 전통.

examples.ko: 저는 전통적인 음악보다 현대 음악을 더 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jeontongjeogin eumakboda hyeondae eumageul deo joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like modern music more than traditional music.

entries.nuance: 전통 refers to customs, values, or practices handed down over generations. Use the adjective 전통적이다 (전통적인 + noun) when you describe something as 'traditional'; 전통 by itself is the abstract noun. It carries a respectful, valued tone, unlike the more neutral 습관 ('habit'), which is personal and routine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 긴 전통 for 'long tradition' — Koreans say 오랜 전통.
Confusing 전통 (tradition) with 습관 (personal habit); 전통 is shared and inherited, 습관 is individual.

entries.shortExplanation: 현대 means "modern times; the present age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 현대 (hyeondae) means "modern times; the present age". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 현대 사회 ("modern society"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 현대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 현대 사회. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 현대.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 현대 commonly modifies another noun directly: 현대 사회, 현대 미술, 현대 의학.
Adjective form; 현대적인 디자인 = a modern design.
현대 + 인 (person) = the people of today; very common in essays.

usagePhrases.en: entering modern times; in the modern era
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for 'in modern times', often starting a sentence.

examples.ko: 현대 사회에서는 스마트폰 없이 살기 어려워요.
examples.romanization: hyeondae sahoeeseoneun seumateupon eopsi salgi eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: In modern society it's hard to live without a smartphone.
examples.note: 현대 사회에서는 = 'in modern society', a frequent opener.

examples.en: People today live constantly chased by time.

examples.ko: 이 건물은 전통과 현대가 잘 어우러져 있어요.
examples.romanization: i geonmureun jeontonggwa hyeondaega jal eoureojyeo isseoyo.
examples.en: This building blends tradition and modernity well.
examples.note: 전통과 현대 is a common paired contrast; 어우러지다 = 'harmonize'.

entries.nuance: 현대 means the modern/contemporary age and is usually used as a noun modifier (현대 사회, 현대 미술) rather than standing alone. For the descriptive sense 'modern, up-to-date in style', use the adjective 현대적이다. It is often contrasted with 전통 to set up old-versus-new comparisons.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 현대 to mean 'recently' — for that use 최근 or 요즘.
Forgetting the adjective form: say 현대적인 디자인, not 현대 디자인, when you mean 'modern-style design'.

entries.shortExplanation: 국가 means "nation; state; country" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "nation; state; country" is 국가 (gukga). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 민주 국가 ("a democratic nation"). Watch the particle attached to 국가 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 민주 국가. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 국가.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 국가 is the formal word for a country as a political entity; 나라 is the everyday word.
국가 modifies many official nouns: 국가 정책, 국가 기관.
Formal, often heard about public service or soldiers.
국가적 + noun, e.g. 국가적 행사 = a national event.

examples.en: The state must take responsibility for its citizens' safety.
examples.note: 국가 paired with 국민; 책임지다 = 'take responsibility'.

examples.ko: 이번 행사는 국가적인 차원에서 준비되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon haengsaneun gukgajeogin chawoneseo junbidoego isseoyo.
examples.en: This event is being prepared on a national level.
examples.note: 국가적인 차원에서 = 'at a national level', a formal collocation.

examples.ko: 여러 국가가 이 문제를 함께 논의했어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo gukgaga i munjereul hamkke nonuihaesseoyo.
examples.en: Several nations discussed this issue together.

entries.nuance: 국가 is the formal, institutional word for a country as a political and legal entity, used in news, law, and academic contexts. In casual speech, Koreans say 나라 instead (우리 나라, not usually 우리 국가). Choose 국가 when the emphasis is on government, policy, or the state as an institution.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 우리 국가 in casual conversation — the natural phrase is 우리 나라.
Treating 국가 and 나라 as fully interchangeable; 국가 is formal/institutional, 나라 is everyday.

entries.shortExplanation: 정부 means "government" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정부 (jeongbu) = "government". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정부 정책 ("government policy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 정부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 정부 정책. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 정부.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: Extremely common in news; 정부 modifies the noun directly.
발표하다 is the standard verb for official government statements.
Often heard regarding funding, benefits, or aid.

examples.en: The government announced a new real estate policy.
examples.note: 정부 + 발표하다, the textbook news collocation.

examples.ko: 많은 사람들이 정부의 결정에 반대하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: maneun saramdeuri jeongbuui gyeoljeonge bandaehago isseoyo.
examples.en: Many people are opposing the government's decision.

examples.ko: 정부에서 소상공인을 위한 지원을 늘리기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbueseo sosanggongineul wihan jiwoneul neulligiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The government decided to increase support for small business owners.
examples.note: 정부에서 (subject marked with 에서 for organizations) is natural and common.

entries.nuance: 정부 means the government as an administrative body. Note that when an organization is the subject of an action, Korean often marks it with 에서 (정부에서 발표했어요) as well as 가 (정부가 발표했어요); both are correct, with 에서 feeling slightly more institutional. Pair it with formal verbs like 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 정부 (the government/administration) with 정치 (politics, the activity); 정부 is the body, 정치 is the field.
Using only 가 as the subject marker; with organizations like 정부, the 에서 form (정부에서) is equally natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 정치 means "politics" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정치 (jeongchi) means "politics". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정치에 관심이 있다 ("to be interested in politics"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 정치에 관심이 있다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 정치.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 관심이 있다/없다 is the go-to phrase for topics like 정치.
정치 + 인; the person who does politics.
Adjective form; 정치적인 문제 = a political issue.

usagePhrases.en: to go into / be in politics
usagePhrases.note: 하다 here means to be active in the political arena.

examples.en: I'm not very interested in politics.
examples.note: 정치에 관심이 없다, the standard way to talk about interest.

examples.ko: 요즘 정치 뉴스를 보면 답답할 때가 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeongchi nyuseureul bomyeon dapdapal ttaega manayo.
examples.en: These days, watching political news often feels frustrating.

examples.ko: 그 문제는 너무 정치적이라서 이야기하기 조심스러워요.
examples.romanization: geu munjeneun neomu jeongchijeogiraseo iyagihagi josimseureowoyo.
examples.en: That issue is too political, so I'm careful about discussing it.

entries.nuance: 정치 is the abstract field of politics, while 정부 is the concrete governing body and 정치인 is an individual politician. The adjective 정치적이다 describes something as 'political' (often with an undertone of being calculated or sensitive). Koreans frequently treat 정치 as a touchy topic, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many avoid in polite company.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 정치 (politics) and 정부 (government) — politics is the activity/field, government is the institution.
Saying 정치 사람 for 'politician'; the correct word is 정치인 (or 정치가).

entries.shortExplanation: 경제 means "economy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "economy" is 경제 (gyeongje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 경제가 어렵다 ("the economy is bad / struggling"). Watch the particle attached to 경제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 경제가 어렵다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 경제.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial'. 경제적인 부담 = financial burden.
경제 takes modifiers like 세계, 한국, 지역 directly.

examples.ko: 요즘 경제가 어려워서 다들 지갑을 닫고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gyeongjega eoryeowoseo dadeul jigabeul datgo isseoyo.
examples.en: The economy is tough these days, so everyone is tightening their wallets.
examples.note: 경제가 어렵다 + 지갑을 닫다 ('close one's wallet') = natural idiomatic pairing.

examples.ko: 정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbuneun gyeongje seongjangeul wihae yeoreo jeongchaegeul naenoasseoyo.
examples.en: The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
examples.note: 경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward'.

examples.en: Using public transportation is much more economical.
examples.note: 경제적이다 here means 'economical/cost-saving', the everyday sense.

entries.nuance: 경제 means 'economy' as a system, but the adjective 경제적이다 splits into two everyday meanings: 'economical' (saves money) and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden). To say the economy is doing badly, Koreans say 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다 rather than translating 'bad' literally.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 'the economy is bad' word-for-word with 나쁘다 — natural Korean is 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다.
Forgetting that 경제적이다 can mean 'economical (saves money)', not only 'economic'.

lesson.canDo: Use 경제 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.

lesson.pronunciationTip: 경제 is written gyeongje. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

entries.shortExplanation: 제도 means "system; institution (a set of rules/structures)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 제도 (jedo) = "system; institution (a set of rules/structures)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교육 제도 ("the education system") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 제도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 교육 제도. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 제도.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 제도 = an organized social system of rules; pairs with 교육, 의료, 복지.
바꾸다 ('change') and 고치다 ('fix') are common verbs with 제도.
도입하다 ('introduce, adopt') is the formal verb for bringing in a 제도.

examples.ko: 한국의 의료 제도는 외국인들에게도 잘 되어 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugui uiryo jedoneun oegugindeuregedo jal doeeo isseoyo.
examples.en: Korea's healthcare system is well set up even for foreigners.
examples.note: 의료 제도 = 'medical system'; 잘 되어 있다 = 'is well established'.

examples.en: The company newly introduced a work-from-home system.
examples.note: 제도 + 도입하다, the standard collocation for adopting a system.

examples.ko: 이건 한 사람의 잘못이 아니라 제도적인 문제예요.
examples.romanization: igeon han saramui jalmosi anira jedojeogin munjeyeyo.
examples.en: This isn't one person's fault but a systemic problem.
examples.note: 제도적인 문제 = 'systemic/structural problem', a useful set phrase.

entries.nuance: 제도 refers to an established system of rules or an institution in the abstract sense — an education system, a welfare system, a company policy framework. It is more structural than 법률 (specific laws) and more formal than 규칙 ('rules' for daily situations). The adjective 제도적이다 is handy for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than individual.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 제도 (a system/framework of rules) with 규칙 (everyday rules); 제도 is large-scale and institutional.
Using 제도 for a physical institution/building — for a building use 기관 or the specific place name.

lesson.canDo: Use 제도 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.

entries.shortExplanation: 법률 means "law (formal/legal term)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 법률 (beomnyul) means "law (formal/legal term)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 법률을 지키다 ("to obey the law"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 법률 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 법률을 지키다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 법률.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 지키다 ('keep, observe') is the standard verb; cf. 법을 어기다 = break the law.
법률 modifies formal nouns: 법률 상담, 법률 문제, 법률 전문가.
제정하다 is the formal verb for legislating; very written/news register.

examples.en: A new law goes into effect starting next month.
examples.note: 법률 + 시행되다 ('be enforced/take effect'), formal collocation.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 법률 전문가의 도움이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i munjeneun beomnyul jeonmungaui doumi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: This issue needs help from a legal expert.
examples.note: 법률 전문가 = 'legal expert'; 도움이 필요하다 = 'need help'.

examples.en: All citizens are equal before the law.
examples.note: 법률 앞에서 평등하다 = 'equal before the law', a formal set expression.

entries.nuance: 법률 is the formal, written term for 'law' (as in legislation and the legal system), common in documents, news, and academic contexts. In everyday speech, Koreans usually shorten it to 법 (법을 어기다 = break the law). Use 법률 when the register is official or when referring to laws as a body of legislation; use 법 in casual conversation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 법률 in casual speech where 법 is natural — say 법을 어기다, not 법률을 어기다, when chatting.
Confusing 법률 (the law itself) with 법원 (the court); 법원 is the institution that applies the law.

examples.romanization: gwollyeogeul gajin saramilsurok deo chaegimgameul gajyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: The more power a person has, the more responsibility they should bear.
examples.note: 권력을 가지다 + V-(으)ㄹ수록 ('the more...'), a strong intermediate combo.

examples.ko: 그 정치인은 권력을 남용해서 결국 자리에서 물러났어요.

examples.en: Looking at history, power is not eternal.
examples.note: 권력은 영원하지 않다 = 'power is not eternal', a reflective set sentence.

entries.nuance: 권력 specifically means political power or authority — the power to control people and decisions — and carries a weightier, often serious or negative tone (권력 남용 = abuse of power). entries.shortExplanation: 국민 means "the people; citizens of a nation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 국민 (gungmin) = "the people; citizens of a nation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 국민의 권리 ("the rights of the people") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 국민, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 국민 pairs with 권리 ('rights') and 의무 ('duties') in civic contexts.
전 ('whole') + 국민 = everyone in the country.
Fixed compound; a vote by all citizens.
뽑다 ('choose, elect') is the natural verb in election contexts.

examples.ko: 국가는 국민의 안전과 행복을 위해 일해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gukganeun gungminui anjeongwa haengbogeul wihae ilhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: The state should work for the safety and happiness of its citizens.
examples.note: 국가 + 국민, the classic civic pairing.

examples.ko: 이 정책은 전 국민에게 영향을 줘요.
examples.romanization: i jeongchaegeun jeon gungminege yeonghyangeul jwoyo.
examples.en: This policy affects all citizens.
examples.note: 전 국민 = 'all citizens'; 영향을 주다 = 'have an effect on'.

examples.en: The people directly elect the president.
examples.note: 국민이 뽑다 = 'the people elect', simple civic sentence.

entries.nuance: 국민 means the people as citizens of a particular nation — a civic, collective term tied to rights, duties, and the state. It differs from 사람들 ('people' in general) and 시민 ('citizens', which leans toward city residents or civil society). Use 국민 when talking about the population in relation to government, law, or national identity.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 국민 to mean 'people' in a casual, general sense — for that use 사람들.
Confusing 국민 (citizens of a nation) with 시민 (citizens in the civil-society / city-resident sense).

entries.shortExplanation: 환경 means "environment; surroundings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 환경 (hwangyeong) means "environment; surroundings". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환경을 보호하다 ("to protect the environment"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환경 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 환경을 보호하다. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 환경.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 보호하다 (protect) is the standard verb in eco contexts.
Very common compound; pairs with pollution, climate, etc.
환경 also means the conditions around you, not just nature.

usagePhrases.en: to be good for the environment
usagePhrases.note: Use 에 to mark what the effect is on.

examples.ko: 요즘 환경 문제에 관심을 가지는 사람이 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hwangyeong munjee gwansimeul gajineun sarami manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: These days more people have become interested in environmental issues.
examples.note: 관심을 가지다 = to take an interest in.

examples.ko: 일회용품을 줄이는 것이 환경을 보호하는 첫걸음이에요.
examples.romanization: ilhoeyongpumeul jurineun geosi hwangyeongeul bohohaneun cheotgeoreumieyo.
examples.en: Reducing disposables is the first step to protecting the environment.
examples.note: 첫걸음 = first step; common in essays.

examples.ko: 이 회사는 근무 환경이 좋아서 직원들이 오래 다녀요.
examples.romanization: i hoesaneun geunmu hwangyeongi joaseo jigwondeuri orae danyeoyo.
examples.en: This company has a good work environment, so employees stay long.
examples.note: 환경 used for workplace conditions, not nature.

entries.nuance: 환경 covers both the natural environment (nature, pollution, climate) and the conditions surrounding a person, such as a 근무 환경 (work environment) or 가정 환경 (home environment). In intermediate texts it most often appears in discussions of ecology and society. Pair it with 보호하다 for protection and 오염되다 for pollution.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 환경 only for nature — it also means general surroundings/conditions (근무 환경, 주변 환경).
Saying 환경을 좋다 — use 환경이 좋다 (the environment is good) or 환경에 좋다 (good for the environment).

entries.explanation: "knowledge" is 지식 (jisik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지식을 쌓다 ("to build up knowledge"). entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 쌓다 (to pile up) is the natural verb, not 만들다.
전문 = specialty; common in job descriptions.
풍부하다 = abundant; a compliment about someone.
Useful when talking about understanding a topic.

examples.ko: 책을 많이 읽으면 다양한 지식을 쌓을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: chaegeul mani ilgeumyeon dayanghan jisigeul ssaeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you read a lot of books, you can build up varied knowledge.

examples.ko: 이 일을 하려면 어느 정도의 전문 지식이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i ireul haryeomyeon eoneu jeongdoui jeonmun jisigi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: To do this job you need a certain level of specialized knowledge.

examples.ko: 배경 지식이 있으면 기사를 이해하기가 훨씬 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: baegyeong jisigi isseumyeon gisareul ihaehagiga hwolssin swiwoyo.
examples.en: If you have background knowledge, articles are much easier to understand.

entries.nuance: 지식 is knowledge as accumulated information and facts, the kind you gain from study or experience. It differs from 지혜 (wisdom), which is the good judgment to use that knowledge well. The everyday verb is 지식을 쌓다, picturing knowledge as something you stack up over time.

Confusing 지식 (knowledge/facts) with 지혜 (wisdom/judgment).

entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) is the standard verb from the learner's side.
With 하다 it becomes a verb meaning to teach/train.
공 = public; contrasts with 사교육 (private education).

examples.ko: 한국 부모들은 자녀 교육에 정말 많은 관심을 가져요.
examples.romanization: hanguk bumodeureun janyeo gyoyuge jeongmal maneun gwansimeul gajyeoyo.
examples.en: Korean parents take a great deal of interest in their children's education.

examples.ko: 회사에서 신입 사원들을 대상으로 교육을 진행했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo sinip sawondeureul daesangeuro gyoyugeul jinhaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: The company carried out training for the new employees.
examples.note: 교육 also means workplace training, not just school.

examples.ko: 좋은 교육을 받는 것은 모든 아이의 권리예요.
examples.romanization: joeun gyoyugeul banneun geoseun modeun aiui gwolliyeyo.
examples.en: Receiving a good education is every child's right.
examples.note: 권리 = right; common in social topics.

entries.nuance: 교육 means education in a broad sense, covering schooling, parenting, and on-the-job training. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교육을 하다 when you mean to study — that means to provide training; learners use 교육을 받다.
Limiting 교육 to schools — it also covers corporate 교육 (training sessions).

usagePhrases.note: 작품 = work; the standard pairing for novels, poems.

examples.en: I want to major in Korean literature at university.

examples.ko: 이 소설은 한국 현대 문학의 대표 작품이에요.
examples.romanization: i soseoreun hangu kyeondae munhagui daepyo jakpumieyo.
examples.en: This novel is a representative work of modern Korean literature.

examples.ko: 문학을 통해 그 시대 사람들의 삶을 엿볼 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: munhageul tonghae geu sidae saramdeurui salmeul yeotbol su isseoyo.
examples.en: Through literature you can glimpse the lives of people of that era.

entries.nuance: 문학 means literature as an art form built from language: novels, poetry, drama, and essays. It is one branch under 예술 and is the academic word, not casual; for everyday reading people just say 소설 (novel) or 책 (book). Using 문학 for a single novel — a specific book is 소설/작품; 문학 is the whole field.

모국 = homeland; the language you grew up with.

examples.ko: 새로운 언어를 배우는 것은 쉽지 않지만 정말 재미있어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun eoneoreul baeuneun geoseun swipji anchiman jeongmal jaemiisseoyo.
examples.en: Learning a new language isn't easy, but it's really fun.

examples.ko: 언어는 그 나라의 문화를 이해하는 열쇠예요.
examples.romanization: eoneoneun geu naraui munhwareul ihaehaneun yeolsoeyeyo.
examples.en: Language is the key to understanding a country's culture.

examples.ko: 그분은 언어 능력이 뛰어나서 통역사로 일해요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun eoneo neungnyeogi ttwieonaseo tongyeoksaro ilhaeyo.
examples.en: She has excellent language ability, so she works as an interpreter.

entries.nuance: 언어 is the abstract concept of language in general, while a specific language usually takes the suffix 어 (한국어 Korean, 영어 English, 일본어 Japanese). So you study 한국어 but discuss 언어 as a phenomenon. The native-Korean near-synonym 말 is more casual and also means 'speech/words.'

Saying 한국언어 — a named language uses the suffix 어: 한국어, not 한국언어.
Using 언어 for casual 'words/talk' — that everyday sense is 말.

entries.explanation: "population" is 인구 (ingu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 인구가 많다 ("to have a large population"). usagePhrases.note: Describe size with 많다/적다, not 크다.
감소 = decrease; a major social topic.
고령 = old age; e.g. 고령 인구 증가.

examples.en: Seoul has a large population, so it's always crowded.

examples.ko: 요즘 한국은 인구 감소 문제가 심각해요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hangugeun ingu gamso munjega simgakaeyo.
examples.en: These days population decline is a serious problem in Korea.

examples.ko: 이 지역은 젊은 인구가 점점 줄고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jiyeogeun jeolmeun inguga jeomjeom julgo isseoyo.
examples.en: The young population in this area is gradually shrinking.

entries.nuance: 인구 means the number of people living in a place, the population. Describe its size with 많다 (many) or 적다 (few), and its change with 늘다 (increase) or 줄다 (decrease); avoid 크다/작다, which suit physical size. In contemporary Korea, 인구 감소 and 고령화 (aging) are constant news themes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 인구가 크다 — population is 많다/적다 (many/few), not 'big/small'.
Confusing 인구 (population) with 인기 (popularity) — they look similar but are unrelated.

사회 = society; 지역 사회 = the local community.

examples.en: Dialects and food differ a little from region to region.

examples.ko: 지역 주민들이 환경 보호 활동에 적극적으로 참여했어요.

entries.nuance: 지역 means a geographic region or local area, and by extension the local community (지역 사회). It is more formal and neutral than 동네, which is your immediate, familiar neighborhood. Use 지역 for administrative or news-style talk (지역 경제, 지역 주민) and 동네 for the friendly block where you live.

Using 지역 for your cozy neighborhood — that warmer sense is 동네.

examples.ko: 대학원에서 한국어 교육에 대해 연구하고 있어요.

entries.nuance: 과거 is the past as an abstract span of time, and it contrasts directly with 현재 (present) and 미래 (future). The present matters more than the past or future.

entries.nuance: 현재 means 'the present' as a noun and also works as an adverb meaning 'currently / at present,' a bit more formal than 지금. In writing and news it often replaces 지금: 현재 상황, 현재까지. 현재 is more formal than 지금; in casual chat 지금 sounds more natural.
Don't add 에 when using it as an adverb — say 현재 살고 있어요, not 현재에 살고 있어요.

usagePhrases.note: time adverbial for things to come
pairs with 밝은/어두운 to describe outlook
가까운/먼 미래 = the near / distant future

examples.en: In the future, cars might fly through the sky.

examples.romanization: aideurui balgeun miraereul wihae yeolsimhi ilhaeyo.

examples.ko: 먼 미래보다 가까운 미래를 먼저 계획하세요.
examples.romanization: meon miraeboda gakkaun miraereul meonjeo gyehoekaseyo.

Don't use 미래 to mean 'later today / soon' — use 나중에 or 이따가 for near, casual future.
'In the future I'll...' as a personal plan is more naturally 앞으로 ~할 거예요 than 미래에 ~.

entries.explanation: "moment, instant" is 순간 (sungan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그 순간 ("at that moment"). 보는 순간 = the instant one sees
adverb form describing a split-second reaction
pairs with 마지막/결정적인 for a crucial instant

examples.en: At that moment my mind went blank.
examples.note: 그 순간 = at that very instant

examples.en: The moment I opened the door, I was startled.
Happy moments always pass by quickly.

entries.nuance: 순간 is a single instant or fleeting moment, much shorter than 동안 (a stretch of time) or 시기 (a period). The pattern Verb-는 순간 means 'the moment/instant that something happens' and is extremely common for dramatic timing. 순간적으로 describes a reflexive, split-second action. Note it pairs with 지나가다 (pass by) for moments slipping away.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 순간 for a duration like 'for a moment, please wait' — that's 잠깐/잠시, not 순간.
-는 순간 takes the present 는 even for past events: 문을 여는 순간 놀랐어요, not 연 순간.

entries.explanation: 시기 (sigi) = "period, time (season of)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이 시기 ("this period") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

시기 follows a noun naming the phase
pairs with 적절한/적당한 for opportune timing

examples.en: Now is the best time to move.
examples.note: 시기 = an opportune period for doing something

examples.en: During the period of job hunting, there's a lot of stress.
I hurried so as not to miss the good timing.

entries.nuance: 시기 is a period or phase of time defined by what is happening in it, broader than a 순간 but more specific than 시대 (an era). It often carries the sense of 'the right timing' for an action, as in 적절한 시기 or 시기를 놓치다. Compare 시기 (a phase, e.g., 성장 시기) with 기간 (a measured duration with a start and end, e.g., 시험 기간).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 시기 (period/timing) with the homophone 시기 meaning 'envy/jealousy' — context disambiguates, but they are different words.
Use 기간 when you mean a measured duration (3-day period); 시기 is a phase or the right moment.

usagePhrases.note: the most common form, referring to a past time already in context

examples.note: 당시 placed before the clause it frames

entries.nuance: 당시 means 'at that (past) time' and always points back to a specific time established in context, so it is most often used as 그 당시 or N 당시 (사고 당시, 졸업 당시). 당시 refers only to a past time; don't use it for 'now' or the future.

entries.explanation: "simultaneity, the same time" is 동시 (dongsi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 동시에 ("at the same time, simultaneously"). expresses two things happening together or a dual quality

entries.nuance: 동시 means 'the same time' and is nearly always used as 동시에 (simultaneously) or in the pattern -는/-인 동시에. With a verb it means two actions happen together; with a noun (N인 동시에) it means something has two qualities at once ('is X and also Y'). It differs from 한꺼번에, which stresses doing things 'all in one go' rather than precisely at the same instant.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
동시 is rarely used bare — say 동시에, not just 동시, when you mean 'at the same time.'
Don't confuse 동시에 (simultaneously) with 한꺼번에 (all at once / in a single batch).

entries.nuance: 평생 means one's entire life span and is most often used adverbially ('for my whole life') without a particle, or as 평생 동안. It carries emotional weight, common in promises (평생 사랑할게요) and statements of rarity (평생 한 번). Compare 일생 (a lifetime, more bookish/biographical) — 평생 is the everyday word and feels heartfelt rather than clinical.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
평생 already implies 'whole life,' so don't add 전체; 평생 동안 is the natural way to stress duration.
Don't write 평셍 or 평성 — the correct spelling is 평생.

entries.explanation: 순서 (sunseo) means "order, sequence, turn". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 순서대로 ("in order, in sequence"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 순서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. entries.nuance: 순서 is the order or sequence in which things are arranged or done, and also a person's 'turn.' The set phrase 순서대로 ('in order') is essential, as is 순서를 지키다 ('wait your turn / keep the order'). It differs from 차례, a close synonym that leans toward 'one's turn' in a rotation; 순서 emphasizes the overall arrangement or sequence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 순서대로 (with 대로) for 'in order'; 순서로 alone sounds incomplete.
For 'it's my turn now,' 차례 is often more idiomatic: 이제 제 차례예요.

entries.nuance: 시초 means the very beginning or origin of something, the point from which it all started. It is more formal and 'historical/origin' in flavor than the everyday 처음 (first time / at first) or 시작 (start of an activity). Use 시초 when tracing where something originated (a company, a custom, a conflict), often as N의 시초 or 시초가 되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 시초 for 'at first / in the beginning' in casual speech — use 처음(에) for that.
시초 names the origin point; for starting an action use the verb 시작하다, not 시초하다 (not a word).

entries.shortExplanation: 막바지 means "the final stage, the home stretch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막바지 (makbaji) = "the final stage, the home stretch". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막바지에 ("in the final stretch") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막바지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 막바지에. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 막바지.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

entries.nuance: 막바지 refers to the very last phase of something that has been going on for a while — a season, a project, a year — equivalent to 'the home stretch' or 'final stage.' Don't use 막바지 for 'the last item/one' — that's 마지막; 막바지 is the final phase of an ongoing process.
Pair it with 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 for 'reach the home stretch,' not 가다.

examples.note: 그사이에 = in the gap when one was absent

entries.nuance: 그사이 (also written 그 사이) means 'in the meantime / during that interval,' referring to the gap between two moments — typically while someone was away or time quietly passed. It often appears as 그사이에 and frequently pairs with comments about unexpected change. Compare 그동안, which covers a longer ongoing stretch ('all this while'); 그사이 stresses a shorter in-between gap.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
그사이 is commonly written as one word, but 그 사이 (spaced) is also accepted; keep it consistent.
Don't confuse 그사이 (a short interval) with 그동안 (the whole period up to now), which spans a longer time.

entries.shortExplanation: 상점 means "store" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상점 (sangjeom) means "store". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상점에서 옷을 사요. ("I buy clothes at the store."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 상점에서 옷을 사요.. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 상점.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

examples.en: That store is kind.

entries.nuance: A general word for a shop or store, slightly formal and broad in everyday Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 상점 with 식당, which means restaurant.

entries.shortExplanation: 만 means "ten thousand (Sino number)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 만 (man) means "ten thousand (Sino number)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 만 분 ("ten thousand minutes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 만 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize 만 분. Then read the examples and notice the particle or ending attached near 만.
entries.contextHint: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.

usagePhrases.note: order / line number also uses Sino

examples.en: This is ten thousand won.
It is one ten thousand now.
It is on the ten thousand floor.

entries.nuance: Sino-Korean number for "ten thousand". Use it for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors, and counting above 100.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use this for hours or age — those take native numbers (하나, 둘 …).

lesson.canDo: Use 만 inside a real beginner sentence, not only as an isolated translation.
studyFlow: Say the word first: 만. Check the romanization only after trying the Hangul.
Memorize one useful chunk: 만 분.
Notice which particle, place marker, or ending appears around the word.
Make one personal sentence by changing only one noun, place, time, or adjective.
lesson.teacherNote: 만 should be taught as a sentence ingredient. The student needs the common frame more than a dictionary definition.
lesson.pronunciationTip: 만 is written man. Use audio and Hangul together because romanization is only a helper.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Learn the word with a frame
beginnerPath.body: Do not stop at "ten thousand (Sino number)". Start with 만 분, because that shows how the word behaves in Korean.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Notice the grammar beside it
beginnerPath.body: Look for particles and endings around the word. Those small pieces tell you whether it is a topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Use it in one real situation
beginnerPath.body: Use this word when talking about basic everyday communication. The examples show whether it naturally works with 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 로/으로, or a descriptive ending.
